stories.Headline: SAP and NTT to Cooperate on Delivering Trusted Sovereign Cloud and SAP Business AI Capabilities - Engineering / Artificial Intelligence - SAP | KXEN
stories.Summary:
SAP SE and NTT, Inc. announced on October 29, 2026, from Tokyo, that they intend to cooperate on SAP Sovereign Cloud and SAP Business AI. The planned collaboration would join SAP's enterprise applications, sovereign cloud and business AI capabilities with NTT's global infrastructure, integrated operations, industry AI expertise and worldwide customer reach. The stated aim is to let customers benefit from cloud and AI innovation while keeping control over sensitive data, operations, technology and security. The companies described the effort as a shared ambition to advance secure, resilient and sovereign digital transformation for regulated industries.

As a first step, the two companies plan to offer a broad set of sovereign capabilities that pair the SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site offering with infrastructure and operations managed by NTT, for customers in key markets. SAP Sovereign Cloud On-Site is aimed at customers with strict sovereignty, regulatory and compliance needs, and it lets SAP-managed cloud solutions run in a customer-owned or customer-selected data center. That setup is meant to give a high degree of sovereignty over local physical control, data residency and operational assurance, while helping customers meet applicable local legal and regulatory requirements. The intended customers are governments, defense organizations, defense industry companies, critical infrastructure operators and other regulated enterprises that want to modernize mission-critical processes. Beyond that, the companies said they will explore wider opportunities to help such organizations adopt AI in a secure, responsible and sovereign way.

Dominik Asam, a member of SAP's Executive Board and its Chief Financial Officer, said the cooperation aims to give customers a practical route to cloud and AI innovation without giving up control, governance and trust. He added that for public sector bodies and regulated industries, sovereignty is more than a compliance matter, because it underpins resilience, competitiveness and responsible AI adoption. Yutaka Sasaki, NTT's Representative Member of the Board, Senior Executive Vice President and Chief Financial Officer, said customers want practical ways to use AI on real business problems. He said that combining SAP's business applications and AI with NTT's grasp of industry needs and mission-critical operations should help organizations change how they work, decide better and speed up business results through AI.

The announcement is framed as a statement of intent, and it contains forward-looking statements that carry risks and uncertainties, so the details of the cooperation have yet to be set out. It follows SAP's announcement a day earlier, on October 28 in Berlin, of AI developer tools at its SAP TechEd conference, including updates to Joule Studio, Joule Work and the SAP Business AI Platform. Those updates include a governance gateway for AI traffic and a new assistant to help customers meet EU AI Act requirements. SAP also said that deploying custom agents on the SAP-managed Joule Studio runtime will stay free through December 2026 for select customers. The articles do not give a timeline for the SAP and NTT plans.

stories.Headline: Schneider Electric, Nscale and Start Campus Bring the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint into a Live AI Factory Environment
stories.Summary:
Schneider Electric, the industrial software firm AVEVA, the AI cloud platform Nscale and the data center developer Start Campus announced on October 27, 2026, in Berlin, that they have completed a successful pilot of an end-to-end digital twin. The twin was built with the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint, which is part of NVIDIA DSX Sim, and the project is called the Immersive Twin. It links technology from Schneider Electric, AVEVA and ETAP in a single digital platform. The pilot is focused on Nscale's operations in the SIN01 data center on the SINES Data Campus in Portugal, which Start Campus developed.

The SINES Data Campus is a 1.2 GW site that is soon expected to host more than 66,000 NVIDIA Rubin GPUs, making it one of the largest AI deployments in the region. The twin combines engineering and operational data with power and cooling simulations and workload requirements, giving a unified view of how the facility performs. It is built on OpenUSD and lets operators test "what-if" scenarios across power, cooling and process behavior before changing anything on site. The companies say this helps validate design decisions, assess the impact of upgrades, reduce procurement risk and keep performance optimized by linking IT and operational data. Nscale expects faster time to token, greater token efficiency, better operations, more flexibility and lower risk when it updates its technology stack, and the pilot also promotes interoperability through simulation-ready asset files.

Nscale's chief technology officer, David Power, said the company is using digital twins to model how AI data centers work in practice, from power and cooling to token delivery, so it can see where full-stack improvements are possible before making changes on the ground. Pankaj Sharma, an executive vice president at Schneider Electric, said building a credible twin takes collaboration across the AI ecosystem. He explained that the project joins Nscale's workload and IT requirements with Start Campus's physical facility data and Schneider's twin technology to model AI factories more completely. Robert Dunn, chief executive of Start Campus, said operators and customers do their best work when they share one model. He added that simulating a jump in rack density through the power train and liquid cooling loop lets the partners test new hardware generations, agree a configuration with the customer and build it once.

The pilot builds on earlier work between Schneider Electric, AVEVA, ETAP and NVIDIA. Last year the three companies joined the Alliance for OpenUSD to speed up digital twin and AI factory development through the Omniverse DSX Blueprint. They also continue to work on reference architectures and integrated infrastructure and software to power and cool the next generation of AI factories, and they use NVIDIA Omniverse libraries to simulate and improve energy efficiency in real-world settings. Start Campus says the SINES site runs on 100% renewable energy and targets a PUE of 1.1 and a WUE of 0 by using the cooling power of the ocean. The announcement does not give a timeline for further rollout.

stories.Headline: K-water, Austin Sign AI Water MOU
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, K-water, the Korean state water corporation, signed a memorandum of understanding with the City of Austin, Texas, to cooperate on water management that uses artificial intelligence. The signing followed talks at K-water's Han River Basin Headquarters in Gwacheon, Gyeonggi Province, with a delegation led by Austin Deputy Mayor Michael Rogers. The agreement grew out of contacts that began in January at CES 2026, where the Austin Asian Chamber of Commerce showed interest in K-water's technology. The two sides then kept up exchanges, including the Korea-Texas Business Summit in August.

Under the memorandum, the two organizations will work together broadly on data-based water resources management and smart water management. The key areas are sharing best practices and exchanging technology, holding joint seminars to build capacity, and identifying joint proof-of-concept projects that could be applied locally. K-water plans to link Austin's needs with its own digital capabilities to widen the basis for cooperation in the U.S. market. It also intends to help Korean water companies demonstrate their technologies on the ground in Austin and pursue business opportunities there.

K-water President Yoon Seog-dae said the corporation will rely on the water management skills it has built up over 60 years to help Austin manage its water resources efficiently. He added that K-water intends to keep widening the scope of cooperation so that Korean water companies can move into the global market. The corporation presented the deal as likely to go beyond a simple technology exchange and to broaden the domestic water industry ecosystem. Austin Water, the city's utility, has not been quoted in the coverage provided here, so Rogers' own comments are not reported.

Austin is known as "Silicon Hills," an advanced industrial base where global companies such as Samsung Electronics and Tesla are concentrated. Water demand there has recently surged because of urban development and the growth of data centers. In response, Austin Water has been pursuing alternative water sources and the adoption of smart technologies to keep supply stable. The articles do not give a timeline for the first joint projects, so the next steps are the seminars and the search for proof-of-concept sites set out in the agreement.

stories.Headline: IATA - IATA's 2026 Global Passenger Survey: Travelers Embrace Biometrics and AI but Entry Requirements Remain a Barrier
stories.Summary:
The International Air Transport Association released the results of its 2026 Global Passenger Survey on 28 October 2026, announcing them from Macao. The survey points to three main trends: biometric identification is becoming mainstream, passengers are bringing artificial intelligence into their travel planning, and entry requirements are putting more people off visiting certain destinations. The findings rest on more than 10,000 responses from over 200 countries. IATA says it represents more than 370 airlines that carry around 85% of global air traffic.

On biometrics, 58% of passengers said they had experienced them at some point in an airport journey over the past 12 months, up from 50% in 2025 and 24 percentage points higher than in 2022. Of those who had, 87% were happy with the experience, compared with 86% a year earlier. Some 78% would share biometric data to skip showing a passport or boarding pass, and 75% of those prefer to register once in advance. Interest in digital passports is strong, with 84% keen to use one for online check-in, 82% willing to share one with an airline at booking for more personalised services, and 82% attracted to a smartphone that combines a digital wallet, digital passport and loyalty cards. The biggest worries about biometrics are data breaches at 59%, sharing with other organisations at 49%, and unclear handling of personal information at 41%.

On AI, 49% of travelers have used it for planning, with 21% searching for flights to a specific destination, 19% hunting for the cheapest fares and 17% seeking ideas for where to go. On entry rules, 43% of passengers said immigration requirements had discouraged them from visiting a destination, up from 33% in 2025. Of those put off, 53% called the process too complex, while privacy and cost were each cited by 17%. Among passengers deterred by geopolitical conflict, 72% named safety as the main reason and 13% cited uncertainty over whether travel is possible. Some 86% would likely share immigration information digitally before departure, up from 83%, 45% would rather finish immigration procedures before reaching the airport, up from 41%, and 60% prefer to apply for a visa online against 25% who favor going in person to a consulate or embassy.

Nick Careen, IATA's Senior Vice President for Operations, Safety and Security, said passengers are embracing technology but still face barriers from complex immigration and visa processes. He urged governments to simplify entry requirements, remove duplicate checks, and speed up the issuance and acceptance of secure digital travel credentials, calling for an agreed framework for issuing and accepting them. He also said airlines should make sure their offerings appear in AI tools and build links that turn an AI conversation into a booking. On visas, he noted that more than 100 countries issue eVisas but there is little consistency in how they are checked, and he said the tools to fix this already exist.

Regional results differed. Asia-Pacific travelers reported the highest overall satisfaction at 90%, tied with the Middle East, while Europe was lowest at 84% and was the most cautious region about digital travel technology. North America had the highest biometric use at 63% and the least discouragement from immigration rules at 35%, while Africa had the highest share discouraged, at 52%. The Middle East led on AI use for planning at 72%, and Latin America and the Caribbean saw the biggest satisfaction gain, up five points from 2025. The articles do not describe any specific next steps beyond IATA's calls on governments.

stories.Headline: Anthropic Finds AI Agents Sway Human Experts' Decisions
stories.Summary:
Anthropic published research on October 28, 2026, showing that human experts often adopt the views of the AI agents helping them, even when the agent has been quietly steered toward a particular position. The company asked 61 professional analysts to run a realistic statistical analysis with Claude Code to advise a fictional organization, the Greenfields Farming Cooperative. Eleven of the analysts chose not to use the agents, and the rest worked alongside them. Anthropic reported that the analysts went with the option their agent favored 86% of the time. Of the 50 analysts who took part in the experiment, 77% repeated the agents' reasoning, though only a small share credited the agent for it.

The task asked the analysts to decide whether the cooperative should keep a program that advises farms on improving crop yields. Anthropic set one fixed rule, that the program would expand only if productivity improved by 3% to 4%. The experts then had four decisions to make themselves: whether to measure productivity as crop yield or as yield per unit of operating cost, and whether to compare yield changes since joining the program against other farms or compare yields directly. They also had to choose whether to measure the effect only on enrolled farms or across the whole cooperative, and whether to count each farm equally or give more weight to larger producers. Each agent was given a lean on these questions by coin flip, encoded in hidden instructions, and told to argue for it strongly but not to misrepresent the evidence.

Anthropic said most experts matched their agent's recommendation on each of the four decisions, most often on the outcome measure. On the final choice of whether to close or expand the program, the agent's preferences mattered less, but the company said experts already trusted the agent's analysis, which shaped how they saw the final recommendation. Some analysts also changed their own opinion when their agent disagreed. In a blog post, Anthropic warned that if experts defer to agents without realizing it, preferences that could be arbitrary or misaligned might shape decisions on policy proposals or research directions without anyone having chosen them. It called the findings particularly important for AI safety research, since human review is a common check on agent misbehavior and only works if people form their own judgments.

Anthropic stressed that the results are not an argument against using AI, noting that analysts who used an agent finished faster and made far fewer serious errors than those who worked without one. It cautioned against reading too much into that comparison, because the group that skipped the agents was small and less experienced, and their serious errors invalidated their results. The company said human oversight works when an answer is deterministic but is harder for judgment calls with no single correct answer. It argued that oversight should instead examine how decisions get made, by surfacing key decision points as work proceeds and helping experts state assumptions and values they would otherwise leave unstated. The researchers suggested three areas for further study: measuring deferral to agent preferences in real work rather than randomized experiments, designing agents that support human agency to reduce overreliance, and changing how organizations view expert judgment.

stories.Headline: Investors May Have Bought All the AI Bonds They Can Handle
stories.Summary:
Two reports published on October 28, 2026, point to a more selective mood among investors and customers in the AI boom. Axios said bond investors are growing choosier about which AI companies, projects and structures they will finance, even as AI borrowing keeps rising. Earlier in October, yields on bonds issued by the heavily indebted AI player CoreWeave jumped, which means its bond prices fell, and its own unsecured bonds reached yields of around 16%. Separately, The Information reported on the night of October 27 that OpenAI plans to buy Google's tensor processing units, or TPUs, custom chips built for AI work. Neither Google nor OpenAI has confirmed the plan, and OpenAI declined to comment.

The Axios story shows how the CoreWeave selloff spread to related debt. Bonds funding data centers leased by CoreWeave, including those issued by developer Edged Compute and former bitcoin miners Core Scientific and Applied Digital, also saw their yields creep higher. Yields on the debt of data centers contracted to Oracle moved in sympathy with Oracle's own bonds. One example is roughly $14 billion of bonds maturing in 2045, which finance a large data center campus in Saline Township, Michigan, and which rest in large part on Oracle's signed 17-year lease, according to ratings agencies. Axios said the same sorting is happening in safer investment grade debt, where the market has moved from treating AI-related bonds as somewhat interchangeable to differentiating sharply between borrowers.

On the chip side, no terms, volumes, timing or chip generation have been disclosed, so the report rests on one person familiar with the matter. OpenAI began renting Google's AI chips in June 2025, and the new report adds that it now owns them. A year earlier it had said it had no specific plans to use TPUs. Alphabet shares closed at $320.58, up 1.19%, and rose a further 0.93% after hours to $323.57, while NVIDIA rose 0.9% to $217.94 and was nearly flat after hours at $218.14.

Analysts at Citigroup, writing last week, said tenant-specific risk was exposed during the October pullback, with CoreWeave and its associated neoclouds and data centers bearing the brunt of the selloff. They added that data center bonds are not immune to tenant default risk and can reprice quickly as that risk escalates. For the chip story, the Yahoo Finance piece noted that Google already rents TPUs to Apple, Anthropic and Citadel Securities, and that a purchase by OpenAI would show TPUs can work as a chip business selling to outside buyers. It put NVIDIA's data center unit at $89.02 billion in a single quarter, compared with $24.77 billion in cloud revenue for Google, up 82%. The piece also said Alphabet trades at a price to earnings ratio of 14 against 44 for NVIDIA, and that Alphabet has begun selling TPUs directly to some customers this year, with its chief financial officer saying most of that revenue will be recognized in 2027.

stories.Headline: Why Is Nebius Group (NBIS) Expanding Its AI Infrastructure Reach?
stories.Summary:
Nebius Group's shares jumped about 11 percent on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, in midday trading, after a run of upbeat coverage of its AI cloud expansion. The stock opened near $159 and closed the latest session around $170.13, with an intraday high of $170.93. That followed a steep slide from the low $230s in early October into the $150s, so the move was a sharp rebound from a deep drawdown. Timothy Sykes' site, which published the coverage, described the stock as trading like a high-beta AI infrastructure name.

Several deals and announcements drove the interest. Nebius locked in a 50-megawatt commitment at AIB's southeastern U.S. data center under a 12-year agreement, which lifted shares premarket. It also secured a $3.5 billion, 364-day senior secured facility priced at Term SOFR plus 2.75 to 3.50 percent, meant to fund data centers, GPU purchases and general needs. The company bought Inferize, whose tools speed the launch and scaling of large AI models, and it began publishing live GPU spot prices, running reserve auctions and offering a program that returns idle GPUs for credits. It is also running NVIDIA's simulation and training stack for Sereact's Cortex in EU data centers, and an expanded EU AI builder program is backed by $10 million in compute grants.

The numbers show a company priced for future growth rather than current earnings. Revenue is about $529.8 million, while enterprise value sits near $41.68 billion, and the article cites a price-to-sales ratio around 9,546 and price-to-book above 1,100. Return on assets and return on equity are both negative. The short-dated $3.5 billion facility means Nebius must execute and then roll or refinance it in under a year, which the coverage flags as a leverage and refinancing risk.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang publicly called Nebius a "neocloud" with very strong AI demand, while also warning about limited working capital and underbuilt European energy and infrastructure. The article adds that Nebius has posted several premarket rebounds of 1.8 to 2.8 percent right after drops of more than 7 percent, often tied to retail chatter on WallStreetBets rather than new company news. It frames the stock as a momentum vehicle tied to real AI infrastructure growth but amplified by meme-style attention and short-dated financing risk, and says traders should watch capacity deals, financing updates and NVIDIA-related announcements. A separate Yahoo Finance item the same day noted that Schneider Electric, AVEVA, Nscale and Start Campus completed a pilot digital twin of a data center using the NVIDIA Omniverse DSX Blueprint at the SINES Data Campus in Portugal.

stories.Headline: Google expands AI Mode ads globally amid slowing Search growth
stories.Summary:
Google said on Wednesday, alongside Alphabet's third-quarter 2026 results, that it is expanding advertising in its AI Mode search experience to new markets for the first time. Ads in AI Mode are coming to Australia, Canada, India, Kenya, Malaysia, New Zealand, Nigeria, Pakistan, the Philippines and Singapore. Google plans to extend the rollout to Brazil, Mexico and the United Kingdom in the fourth quarter. In the US, it is also launching multi-turn ads that appear in follow-up queries within AI Mode, and the ads will carry a "Sponsored" label.

The expansion arrives as growth in the company's core search advertising business slows. Search and other advertising revenue rose 12 per cent year over year to $63.35 billion in the September quarter, down from 17 per cent in the second quarter and 19 per cent in the first. Alphabet's total revenue was $127.6 billion, up 25 per cent, slightly under analyst projections of $127.93 billion. Google Services brought in $96.3 billion, up 11 per cent, while Google Cloud revenue rose 103 per cent to $30.7 billion. Earnings per share came in at $2.12 against expectations of $2.99, a figure the company attributed to an unrealized loss on its SpaceX stake, and capital expenditure for the quarter reached $51.4 billion, mostly for AI infrastructure.

Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, said the slowdown reflected foreign exchange rates and one-off ad spending dips in Asia-Pacific among advertisers hit by the EU's end of its de minimis exemption on low-cost imports. He also said strong growth in AI Mode queries weighed on search growth because the product earns less per query, and that tests of ads there have returned promising results. Click-through rates for sponsored and organic product listings in AI Mode are similar, he said, and Google's research suggests users find the ads relevant. CEO Sundar Pichai said AI investments are driving overall query growth, including commercial queries, with year-over-year query growth at its highest in five years. He added that AI Mode queries are on average three times longer than traditional searches and that one in five AI Mode searches globally involves voice, images or documents.

Alphabet shares fell between 8 per cent and roughly 11 per cent in after-hours trading, according to the reports. The company left its 2026 capital expenditure outlook unchanged at $195 billion to $205 billion, and finance chief Anat Ashkenazi said spending is still expected to increase significantly in 2027. Google also said it has secured $561 billion in future cloud revenue from customer contracts, and it has begun renting computing capacity from third-party providers, which Ashkenazi said will pressure margins in the short term. Schindler said Google plans to scale ads across both AI Mode and AI Overviews to more users and queries, and is confident it can build advertising models for agentic uses. Some publishers, meanwhile, are objecting to Google's use of one crawler for both search indexing and AI, and no publisher traffic figures were mentioned on this call.

stories.Headline: Manchester CEO defends sacking over half his staff for AI as 'it saves £100,000 a year and does a better job'
stories.Summary:
Rob Illidge, a 40-year-old Manchester chief executive, says he replaced more than 64 per cent of the staff at his LinkedIn software firm Vulse with artificial intelligence, arguing the technology does a better job. Over a three-year period that began in 2023, he made his marketing, sales and development teams redundant, cutting nine people in total. The company had grown to 14 employees after he raised venture capital funding, and it now runs with a team of just five. He says graduates were most at risk, because the tasks involved were repetitive and suited to automation.

Vulse, which he founded in 2019 as a side project, makes employee advocacy software that encourages staff to post on LinkedIn for their employers. Mr Illidge says the AI tools cost £140 a month, while a single employee on an average salary costs more than £500 a month in National Insurance and pension contributions alone. He puts the cost of staffing every replaced role at about £250,000 a year at his former employees' pay, and estimates his annual staffing savings at around £100,000. Revenue per employee has risen about 25 times in two years, from roughly £1,500 to more than £38,000, and monthly recurring revenue is up 76 per cent year on year. Vulse was valued at £750,000 in 2023, and its latest valuation stands at £5m.

Mr Illidge is the one defending the decision, and he calls it the best he has made for the company. He says AI does around two to three times the work of an employee and keeps going overnight, and that staff costs are a heavy pressure on businesses, so the money was better spent elsewhere. He described the business as his baby and said nobody else shares his passion for it, but AI can. He acknowledged that a founder is responsible for people's livelihoods while also needing to develop the business, calling it a balancing act he is becoming more comfortable with. He added that he believes those let go will find better jobs.

Looking ahead, Mr Illidge wants to grow Vulse further with AI, saying it has levelled the playing field and brought enquiries from around the world rather than only the UK. He likened the firm to David against Goliath, saying it can beat larger rivals because it has fewer overheads. He said most businesses should take advantage of AI, and that new roles are being created as a result, pointing to the many students he meets at university talks who are studying AI topics. He also said he agrees that AI development should slow down, though he stressed it is helping UK businesses like his own.

stories.Headline: HBM explained: the AI memory behind SK Hynix’s record profits and rising chip prices
stories.Summary:
SK Hynix reported record third-quarter results on Oct. 28, with revenue of 104.6 trillion won and operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, the first quarter above 100 trillion won in sales in the company's history. Revenue rose 327.9% and operating profit 632.1% from a year earlier, and the operating margin reached 79.7%, the sixth straight quarter of all-time highs. The results beat securities industry estimates by 6.5% on revenue and 8.3% on profit. Analysts said rising memory prices and sales of higher-value products more than offset a currency hit of 5 trillion to 6 trillion won from a stronger won.

The company said its DRAM and high-bandwidth memory output is effectively sold out through 2029, and it has signed long-term supply agreements with 14 customers, including major global cloud providers. Those contracts cover more than 50% of production capacity for 2027 and 2028. On Oct. 29, Yuanta Securities forecast fourth-quarter revenue of 147.1 trillion won and operating profit of 118.2 trillion won, about 34% above the consensus of 88.4 trillion won, and raised its price target 12.1% to 3.7 million won from 3.3 million won. Shinhan Securities forecast revenue of 126.1 trillion won and profit of 101.5 trillion won, lifting its target 11% to 3 million won. Shinhan estimated third-quarter average selling prices rose 29% for DRAM and 26% for NAND flash from the prior quarter, and expects fourth-quarter shipments to rise 24% for DRAM and 5% for NAND, with prices up around 10%.

Company executives said customer trust built on technological competitiveness has turned into long-term contracts. President Kwak Noh-jung said this improves visibility on medium- to long-term profitability. Chief Financial Officer Kim Woo-hyun forecast that the supply shortage would last through 2030, and Park Jun-deok, vice president of DRAM marketing, said the volumes are effectively all sold out through 2029, dismissing worries that earnings had peaked. Customer requests for HBM exceed twice what the company can supply, and HBM4 is expected to overtake the earlier HBM3E as the main product in the fourth quarter. Yuanta analyst Baek Gil-hyun said earnings visibility is far higher than in past chip cycles, while Shinhan analyst Kim Hyung-tae said the stock's forward price-to-book ratio of 1.7 is the cheapest among DRAM peers.

On shareholder returns, the company announced a plan totaling 100 trillion won this year, including more than 30 trillion won in cash dividends, on top of 40 trillion won in treasury share cancellations. It will also buy back about 20 trillion won of its own shares on the open market from Oct. 29 through Jan. 28. The KOSPI rose 6.63% to 6,012.44 on Oct. 28, retaking 6,000 for the first time in 10 trading sessions, with SK Hynix shares up 10.89% and Samsung Electronics up 9.01%. Expanded output at the M15X plant in Cheongju is expected to lift fourth-quarter DRAM shipments by more than 20%, and analysts said diversifying AI demand, including sovereign AI projects, could prolong the shortage. Analysts cautioned that the 3.7 million won target, more than double the recent share price, depends on the memory price cycle unfolding as expected.

stories.Headline: Put ChatGPT, Claude, and Gemini to work for $79
stories.Summary:
Check Point Research reported on October 27, 2026 that it has spent about two months tracking a campaign it calls Yoba, in which attackers exploit the popularity of AI tools to spread malware. The group built fake GitHub projects posing as desktop apps named GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus, with GitHub.io pages describing the software and linking to malicious ZIP releases. The repositories show no sign of faked stars or forks, yet they still rank among the top Google results, which the researchers put down to SEO poisoning. A Mashable deal article from October 29, 2026 on a separate AI workspace subscription appeared alongside this research in the source material.

The first repository was created around July 2026, but the first two malicious releases did not appear until the end of August. The first, sol-setup.zip, was uploaded on August 30, and Setup-Claude.zip followed on August 31 and GPT-6-Astra-Setup.zip on September 4. None of the archives used password protection, since the binaries already had very low detection rates thanks to anti-sandbox and other anti-analysis techniques. Inside each package, a legitimate signed executable from OpenAI or Anthropic, named Setup.exe, loads a malicious file called winmm.dll through DLL sideloading, a method often used to bypass security protections. That DLL, which Check Point calls the YobaDropper, spoofs the real winmm.dll with 180 exports that contain only a return instruction followed by padding, and only DllEntryPoint holds real code.

The researchers attribute the activity to an actor showing signs of Russian origins, but the clues about location are deliberately muddled. Each repository used a different Outlook email address, and the commit timestamps point to UTC+4, UTC-4 and UTC+3 for the three uploaders, which Check Point believes is a deliberate attempt to hide the true time zone. The compilation timestamp of winmm.dll, built on the same day it was added to the archive, suggests the actor mainly operates in UTC-4. The report also credits the actor with strong operational security, since the campaign avoids dedicated command-and-control servers and relies on Telegram, Tor, Catbox and DNS over HTTPS instead.

For context, Check Point says the YobaDropper contains a second component, the YobaLoader, which contacts attacker-controlled infrastructure to fetch the final payload that runs unwanted software on infected machines. The two ChatGPT-related releases were created about five days apart yet contain mostly the same files and share the same indicators of compromise. Several of the other files in the packages, such as the vulkan and swiftshader libraries, appear to serve only to make the bundle look legitimate. The excerpt provided ends partway through the analysis of the dropper's anti-analysis features, so it does not describe any next steps or response.

stories.Headline: Privacy commissioner looking into Crime Stoppers tip line hack
stories.Summary:
Canada's privacy commissioner has opened an investigation into a data breach affecting Crime Stoppers, the tip line used by police and communities across the country. The office led by commissioner Philippe Dufresne announced the probe on Tuesday, Oct. 27, 2026, and it centres on a cybersecurity incident at Navigate360, the third-party company that manages the platform Crime Stoppers relies on. The investigation follows a CBC report that 1.5 million tips sent to Canadian Crime Stoppers programs over the past 25 years were exposed when Navigate360 was hacked in March. The U.S.-based company confirmed the breach last week.

The commissioner's office said the investigation will examine the security safeguards Navigate360 had in place when the breach happened, in order to decide whether the company complied with Canada's federal private-sector privacy law. The office has also contacted Crime Stoppers programs to offer expertise and guidance, and it has been in touch with Navigate360 as well. It did not say whether the company has replied. Its stated aim in dealing with both organizations is to make sure the necessary steps are taken to address the breach and protect Canadians' personal information.

Navigate360 said it opened its own investigation right away after discovering the breach. The company said it took mitigation measures and put additional and enhanced safeguards in place, with help from another cybersecurity firm. Saskatchewan Crime Stoppers, for its part, told the public over the weekend to avoid sending tips through its platform. In a statement, it said the pause is temporary and that it will start accepting new tips again once it is confident it is safe to do so.

The breach has already disrupted how tips reach police. Forces across Ontario, including several in the Greater Toronto Area, temporarily stopped directing public calls to Crime Stoppers after the news came out. In Manitoba, at least two police departments, including Winnipeg's, said they would stop taking tips through the program while they review and assess what happened. The articles do not say when the investigation will finish or when the paused tip lines will resume.

stories.Headline: AI chips worth $15.5 million seized at Malaysia airport, Customs authority says
stories.Summary:
Malaysian customs announced on Oct 28 that it had seized advanced artificial intelligence chips worth about RM49.5 million this month, which converts to roughly S$15.5 million or US$12.1 million. The haul came on Oct 15, when officers inspecting the free trade zone at Kuala Lumpur International Airport found 30 server units containing the chips. Authorities say they are closing in on a syndicate suspected of smuggling high-performance semiconductors through Malaysia's main airport. The shipment is said to have come from an Asian country and was due to be sent on to another country in the same continent.

That onward movement was a re-export, which required a trade permit, according to the initial findings of the investigation. Customs officials said the servers had been falsely declared as electronic components. The aim, they said, was to move the goods through Malaysia so that no restrictions would apply when they were exported to the next destination. A Malaysian firm that helped arrange the shipment has been called in to assist with the investigation.

The details were given to reporters by Aspalila Ag Tuah, the customs director at Kuala Lumpur International Airport. She said the October shipment is suspected to be the work of the same network behind a similar smuggling attempt that customs foiled in June. According to her, at least five cases are tied to the syndicate, and together they involve seizures of chips worth more than RM100 million. She declined to give more details, saying the probe is still under way.

The case sits against the backdrop of export controls that Malaysia put in place in 2025 on the movement of advanced AI chips of US origin. Malaysia took that step after pressure from the United States to stem the flow of such chips into China. Reports on the seizure also pointed to a separate US case, in which a man was arrested over the alleged smuggling of US$300 million worth of computer servers to China. Authorities in Malaysia have not said when the investigation into the syndicate will conclude, and no charges were mentioned in the reports.

stories.Headline: Microsoft offers quarter of global workforce voluntary buyouts as AI spending accelerates
stories.Summary:
Microsoft has offered voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 employees, roughly 27% of its global workforce, as it pours money into artificial intelligence. Chief People Officer Amy Coleman announced the Voluntary Exit Offer in a blog post on Monday, October 26, 2026. The offer was open to eligible employees in Canada, India, the United Kingdom and the United States. Microsoft had about 223,000 full-time employees at the end of June.

According to Computing UK, the programme covers employees at vice-president level and below in selected teams, and staff will be told by email with a link to the details. The terms are expected to resemble Microsoft's standard severance arrangements. Bloomberg reported that the teams involved include Windows, Copilot, Xbox and Finance, while some groups, including employees working in datacentres, sales and marketing, are excluded. It is not yet clear how many people will accept, and Microsoft has not said how much it expects to save or whether more workforce changes are planned.

Coleman said the offer is meant to give employees more flexibility and control over their future careers, and described it as something new for the company that it will learn from. She added that Microsoft will keep helping people concentrate on the most important work, build new skills and, where it makes sense, find other opportunities inside the company. Computing UK noted that the programme builds on lessons from an earlier voluntary retirement initiative. More than 30% of the roughly 8,750 workers eligible for that earlier offer accepted it.

The move comes as spending on AI data centers is expected to top $700 billion this year across the industry, which has made memory chips, processors, other equipment and electricity more expensive. Economists expect that to keep pushing up inflation at least through the end of this year. CBS News, as cited by Mashable, reported that Microsoft itself is expected to spend $175 billion on AI infrastructure in 2026. In July, the company said it was cutting 4,800 jobs, about 2.1% of its global workforce, including many in its Xbox video game business. Microsoft's stock hit an all-time high this month and rose about 1% on Monday, and the company is due to report quarterly financial results on Wednesday.

stories.Headline: AI Chip Demand Runs Hot: TSMC Said to Weigh CoWoS Price Hike of Up to 20%, Lead Times Stretch to 8 Months
stories.Summary:
TSMC is reportedly weighing another increase to its CoWoS advanced packaging fees of as much as 20%, according to supply chain sources cited by Taiwan's Commercial Times and relayed by TrendForce on October 27, 2026. Foundries and outsourced packaging firms are said to be considering a fresh round of rises in a 10% to 20% range, as demand for CoWoS has spread beyond AI GPUs to server CPUs and custom ASICs, leaving a growing backlog of unfilled orders. TSMC has not confirmed any of this, and no effective date has been identified. The reports surfaced on the same day Oracle and Nvidia announced a multi-gigawatt Vera Rubin expansion.

On the numbers, tool lead times have reportedly stretched from three to six months to as long as eight months, and TSMC is said to have placed this year's equipment orders at existing prices rather than seeking its usual discounts. Nomura estimates that final testing for Nvidia's Blackwell takes about four times as long as for Hopper, and that Rubin could need seven times as long. TSMC is already mass producing CoWoS-L at 5.5 times the reticle limit. Industry estimates put CoWoS capacity above 130,000 wafers a month in 2026, rising to 200,000 in 2027, though TSMC has published no capacity figure of its own. Liberty Times separately reports that TSMC has finalized wafer price increases of 3% to 6% from January 2027, with 2 nm and 3 nm seeing the steepest hikes.

TSMC itself has said nothing on the proposed price rise. On October 15, it said CoWoS demand remained strong, that customers still see it as their top choice for chip assembly, and that it is working to expand capacity. The company also raised its 2026 sales growth forecast to 44% and said it already produces packages at five times reticle size with strong yields. Larger formats at nine and 14 reticles remain in development with no confirmed launch dates. Nvidia has said Rubin is in full production, and Google Cloud announced general availability of Vera Rubin infrastructure on October 21.

Some relief is on the way, though not soon. GlobalFoundries has reportedly signed a five-year, $2 billion deal to make CoWoS silicon interposers in New York, with volume production expected to ramp in the first half of 2028. With equipment taking up to eight months to arrive, any new tools ordered now would not add capacity until well into 2027. For now the squeeze is mostly a data center problem, since gaming graphics cards do not use CoWoS, but the reports suggest costlier wafers will probably reach consumer chips eventually.

stories.Headline: Anthropic IPO: It's official now! Artificial intelligence giant files papers to sell shares to public for first time
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, one of the world's leading artificial intelligence companies, made public on Monday, Oct 26, its plans to sell shares on the stock market. The filing shows rapidly rising sales but also warns of serious safety risks, and it is being seen as a major test of whether the AI boom can produce profits. If it goes ahead, the listing would be the first by one of the standalone companies leading the race to build advanced AI, ahead of rival OpenAI, which has pushed its own debut back to next year. It follows the June listing of SpaceX, which owns Elon Musk's AI venture xAI and whose shares fell sharply after a strong debut.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Anthropic is aiming to go public the week of Nov 16, though the timing could change. Citing people familiar with the matter, it said the offering could raise as much as US$100 billion and value the company at between US$1.5 trillion and US$2 trillion. Sales reached US$11.6 billion in the April-June quarter, up from US$787 million a year earlier, compared with US$4.6 billion for all of 2025. The company made its first operating profit in that quarter, close to US$1 billion, though it still posted an overall loss of US$80 billion for the first half of the year, mostly from accounting charges tied to its rising value rather than cash spent. Nearly 12,000 organisations now spend at least US$100,000 a year with the company, up from fewer than 1,000 a year ago, with much of the growth coming from businesses using Claude for software writing and office work.

The 400-page prospectus devotes more than 90 pages to risks specific to the industry, and the company itself warned that advanced systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly. It also cautioned that its public positions on AI regulation and safety could bring heightened scrutiny, political backlash or disproportionate regulatory action. The Trump administration has targeted the company in recent months for refusing to lift restrictions on how the Pentagon can use its technology, and the Defense Department has since labelled it a national security risk and barred it as a supplier. Anthropic also said its growth is likely to slow, possibly sharply, and that it has committed hundreds of billions of dollars to computing capacity, including up to US$120.5 billion with SpaceX, about US$110 billion with Amazon and an estimated US$125 billion to US$150 billion with Google. Many of those payments must be made regardless of how much capacity it actually uses if demand falls short of projections.

On governance, the company's seven co-founders, led by Chief Executive Dario Amodei and his sister, President Daniela Amodei, will keep just over half of shareholder votes after the listing, so outside investors cannot outvote them. Anthropic is registered as a public benefit corporation, which requires it to weigh developing AI safely alongside making money for shareholders. Each co-founder has pledged to give 80 per cent of their shares to charity, though the filing notes these pledges are not legally binding. Investors will be watching the third-quarter figures, which are due before the IPO, and a disappointing reception could dent enthusiasm for a sector that has become a key driver of the US economy amid worries of a market bubble.

stories.Headline: DeepSeek, Moonshot AI used OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra for training models
stories.Summary:
Chinese AI developers DeepSeek and Moonshot AI relied heavily on outputs from OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra model to train their latest systems, The Information reported on Wednesday, citing people with direct knowledge of the matter. The practice is known as distillation, in which one model is improved by using the answers of a more capable model as training data. The report said Moonshot AI's Kimi K3.1 Pro, released last week, and DeepSeek's upgraded V4.1-Flash 1017, launched on October 17, both benefited from distilling Astra. OpenAI, DeepSeek and Moonshot AI did not immediately respond to Reuters requests for comment.

Kimi K3.1 Pro is an upgrade of Kimi K3, which came out in July, and was developed through post-training. It uses a mixture-of-experts design with 2.8 trillion total parameters and 104 billion active parameters, selecting 16 of its 896 experts as it processes each token. On the independent Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index it scored 55, ranking fourth and ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 53, while its predecessor scored 44. It also took first place on Terminal Bench 4.0 with 67 percent, up from 13 percent for Kimi K3 and ahead of Claude Sonnet 5.5 at 64 percent. The model costs $2 per million input tokens and $10 per million output tokens, and Artificial Analysis put its average cost at $2.11 per task, against $5.98 for Claude Opus 5.5 at maximum reasoning effort.

On responsibility, OpenAI said in a September 30 blog post that it had tied a core part of a distillation campaign, which began in July, to individuals associated with Moonshot AI. Separately, the US government, Anthropic and OpenAI have accused Moonshot AI of unauthorized distillation of their models. Anthropic alleged that Moonshot used fraudulent accounts and proxy networks to gather responses and reasoning traces from its Claude models and used them to train Kimi. Moonshot AI and DeepSeek had not responded to the claims at the time of reporting.

The dispute comes as US-China technology competition intensifies, and leading US firms, including Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, argue that distillation lets rivals reproduce advanced capabilities more quickly and at lower cost. Earlier this month, Anthropic said new measures to stop copying of its Claude models had cut the data harvested in distillation attacks by roughly 90 to 99 percent. Artificial Analysis noted that Kimi K3.1 Pro offers top-tier performance at a reasonable price, but runs slower than average at 73 tokens per second against 81, and produces very long responses, using 150 million tokens in its evaluation against a median of 87 million. The articles do not say what steps may follow.

stories.Headline: CoreWeave Stocks Rebound 5.6% as AI Financing Faces Scrutiny
stories.Summary:
CoreWeave's stock bounced back sharply this week after a rough stretch for AI infrastructure companies. Shares rose about 6.8% to $58.95 around midday on October 27, the day the company said it had brought most of a new Copenhagen data center online. On Tuesday, the stock climbed almost 8%, gaining $4.38 to close at $59.57, while the Nasdaq-100 rose just over 1%. Other neocloud and AI infrastructure names also advanced as investors rotated back into the sector.

The Copenhagen site, its first deployment in Denmark, is operated by atNorth and is designed to provide 22.5 megawatts of IT capacity. It runs NVIDIA Blackwell systems linked by Quantum-X800 InfiniBand networking, and it brings CoreWeave's European footprint to nine data centers across five markets, including the U.K., Spain, Sweden and Norway. CoreWeave also plans to extend its network into the United Arab Emirates, India, Indonesia, Singapore, Australia, South Korea and Japan, with rollout starting in late 2026 and a network spanning four continents targeted for mid-2027. As of June 30, the company operated 51 data centers with more than 1.5 gigawatts of active power, and it reported about 4.2 gigawatts of contracted power on its Aug. 11 earnings call.

The rebound followed weeks of pressure over how heavily indebted AI infrastructure firms can keep financing their expansion. CoreWeave lost roughly a quarter of its value in one recent week amid worries about its debt load of about $50 billion and higher borrowing costs. A GuruFocus analyst described the rally as a recovery in sentiment rather than proof that the financing problem is solved, and said the company must show its balance sheet can support demand. A separate GuruFocus piece noted that CoreWeave is loss-making, with a market value of $32.51 billion, an enterprise value of $77.71 billion and a GF Score of 15 out of 100. It also pointed out that the Denmark announcement brought no new contracted revenue and no utilization figure for the site.

Tuesday's lift came as Anthropic's IPO filing showed strong demand for computing power, with $16.3 billion in first-half revenue, nearly 14 times the year-earlier figure, along with large long-term compute commitments. Tech Contrarians' Sara Awad, speaking on an Investing Experts podcast published Tuesday, took a more cautious view. She expects a potential bubble burst in 2027 driven more by funding pressure than weak demand, and she favors chip equipment and optical-networking firms such as ASML over capital-intensive operators like CoreWeave, IREN and Hut 8. She said CoreWeave has fallen more than 50% from its highs. Analysts say investors will watch bond yields, funding costs, new capacity, backlog conversion and whether revenue growth turns into stronger free cash flow.

stories.Headline: IBM Introduces Identity and Control for AI Agents, Securing Frontier Intelligence for the Enterprise
stories.Summary:
IBM announced on October 27, 2026, at its TechXchange 2026 conference in Atlanta, a set of new identity, credential, discovery, containment and evaluation capabilities for enterprise AI agents. The package includes the general availability of IBM Agent Identity and HashiCorp Vault 2.2. IBM said the tools are meant for developers, IT and security teams that run agents across business systems with defined authority and accountability. It framed the rollout around a gap in current deployments, citing a Gartner prediction that by 2028 the average Fortune 500 enterprise will use more than 150,000 agents, up from fewer than 15 in 2025, while only 13% of organizations believe they have the right governance in place.

Agent Identity registers each agent in a central inventory that records its owner, metadata, risk classification, approved tool connections and lifecycle state. It issues short-lived, task-scoped OAuth tokens, preserves delegation so an action can be traced back to a person or upstream system, and keeps structured audit trails for compliance and incident investigation. Vault brokers just-in-time credentials for systems that cannot use delegated tokens, enforces least-privilege access and allows real-time revocation when an agent attempts something unauthorized. Vault 2.2 gives agents their own secured accounts, renews their credentials automatically and adds post-quantum encryption, along with vTPM support for Linux virtual machines. IBM added that Vault already secures non-human identities at organizations including ABN AMRO, Adobe, athenahealth, BBVA, BlackRock, Canva, Duke Energy, Expedia, London Stock Exchange, Starbucks, Swiss Federal Railways and Target.

In watsonx Orchestrate, IBM introduced an AI Gateway that discovers third-party agents, models and MCP servers on platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Microsoft Foundry and Google Gemini, a capability currently in tech preview. A containment feature, also in tech preview, runs agents in isolated sandboxes and gives teams a kill switch, while evaluation tools, which are generally available, let teams test agents, models and MCP servers before deployment and monitor them in production with cost tracking. Two Vault previews are also public: Secure Hub, for visibility across distributed Vault environments, and Vault Arc, which adds scoped and ephemeral authorization and agent governance. HashiCorp Boundary 1.1 is available with a public-preview MCP server, and IBM said Agent Identity and Vault integrate with NVIDIA OpenShell secure runtime software.

Dinesh Nirmal, Senior Vice President of IBM Software, said the winners in enterprise AI will be those who change how their business runs rather than simply adding more AI. He said agents doing real work need an AI operating model that connects them to a company's data, applications and infrastructure and runs them with the discipline applied to critical systems. John Fanelli, NVIDIA's vice president of enterprise software, said the work pairs OpenShell's policy-governed runtime with Agent Identity and Vault to support secure execution and tightly scoped access. Shailesh M. Shenoy, Assistant Dean for Information Technology at Albert Einstein College of Medicine, said tools such as IBM Verify and HashiCorp Vault can help organizations set up the identity, access and security controls needed to innovate with confidence.

IBM said this year's TechXchange, which incorporates HashiConf, draws nearly 6,500 attendees from 85 countries, with more than 1,000 sessions, 180 hands-on labs, 260 client-led sessions and over 50 certification exams. Client speakers include athenahealth, Albert Einstein College of Medicine, Optum, Seven-Eleven Japan and Yum! Brands. On availability, Vault 2.2, Agent Identity and the Orchestrate evaluation capabilities are generally available, while Secure Hub is in public preview and the Orchestrate discover and contain capabilities remain in tech preview.

stories.Headline: Former Meta AI director Rohit Patel launches Ndoc to challenge Microsoft Office and Google Workspace
stories.Summary:
Rohit Patel, who spent eight years working on AI at Meta, has left the company to launch a startup called Ndoc, according to reports based on a TechCrunch story published on October 27, 2026. At Meta he was a director at Meta Superintelligence Labs, and his work covered reinforcement learning and evaluating whether AI outputs can be trusted. He describes Ndoc as an AI-native alternative to Microsoft Office and Google Workspace. His exit follows other recent departures from Meta, including Chief Global Affairs Officer Joel Kaplan, AI researcher Andrew Tulloch and Emily Dalton Smith, the company's Head of Product for AI-for-Work.

Ndoc is meant to pull work that is now scattered across tools such as Excel, Word, PowerPoint, Tableau, Replit and ChatGPT into a single shared workspace. Colleagues can open that workspace even if they have not signed up. The interface has three sections: Stage for presentations, dashboards, simulations and mini apps, Narrative for analyses with numbered citations and generated figures, and Model for the underlying datasets and Python scripts. Files can be exported as a single .ndoc.html file that opens in any browser, and Patel plans to make that format open source so developers can build compatible apps without depending on Ndoc, Microsoft or Google. He says the product is built and fine-tuned with a mix of open-source models, which costs far less to run than tools based on frontier AI models, though early trial users cared more about having the whole workflow in one place.

Patel says people should be able to inspect the work behind AI-generated spreadsheets and presentations that feed business decisions, and that users can ask the chat to explain any script or point to a formula. He says he left Meta partly because he wanted to move faster than a large company's process for agreeing on an open format would allow. He acknowledges that OpenAI's Space, a shared workspace inside ChatGPT launched in September 2026, could be a threat, but argues that simply adding AI to spreadsheets is too limited an approach. He also says he will seek funding only after seeing proof that customers love the product, and that he will not release a tool he would not want to use himself.

The ambition is a large bet for a three-person team with no funding. OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta, SpaceXAI and Google have all introduced enterprise AI tools that connect to Google Workspace, Microsoft 365 and other workplace apps. One report pointed to the scale of the incumbents, saying Microsoft Office has more than 345 million paid subscribers and Google Workspace serves over 9 million paying businesses. As of Tuesday, Ndoc was running an enterprise pilot and offering an alpha to a limited number of customers on its waitlist. Signing up is free, but customers pay for usage and tokens, and Patel hopes to release a beta in the coming weeks and to launch fully in 2027.

stories.Headline: Alphabet Loses $500 Billion in Market Value as AI Threatens Google Search
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, the parent company of Google, saw its stock fall 13% on Thursday, October 29, 2026, erasing about $500 billion in market value and marking the worst single day in the stock's history, according to the Wall Street Journal. The drop came after the company released its third-quarter results on Wednesday, October 28, which stoked investor fears about how the rise of artificial intelligence is affecting its core business. Shares of the Class A stock closed at $283.82, down $41.07, leaving the company's market value at roughly $3.97 trillion. Reuters reported that the three major U.S. equity indexes lost ground in the wake of the report, with the tech-focused Nasdaq falling the most.

The numbers behind the selloff were mixed. Total revenue rose 25% to $127.6 billion, but analysts had expected $128.2 billion, and Bloomberg noted that ad sales grew at the slowest pace in five quarters. Google Search revenue climbed 12% to $63.4 billion, down from 17% growth in the prior quarter, which fed the idea that consumers are turning to AI chatbots instead of Google's search engine. Operating income rose 30% to $40.6 billion, while earnings per share fell to $2.12 from $2.87 a year earlier, partly because of an unrealized investment loss tied to Space Exploration Technologies. Spending was the other worry: capital investments reached $51.4 billion against $42.3 billion in operating cash flow, leaving negative free cash flow of $9.1 billion, the second negative quarter in a row after none since the company went public.

The company's own filings and statements explain much of the pressure. Management raised its 2026 capital spending budget to between $195 billion and $205 billion and said spending is expected to rise significantly next year. To help pay for it, Alphabet raised about $12.4 billion through stock issuance and another $28.7 billion through debt in the quarter, and Bloomberg reported that its future commitments to buy data centers, computing power and energy have passed $1 trillion. On the positive side, Google Cloud revenue surged 103% to $30.7 billion, with operating income of $11.1 billion and a margin of 36.2%, up from 23.7% a year earlier. Management also pointed to interest in its custom Tensor Processing Units from Anthropic, Apple, Meta Platforms and Oracle, among others, and said the Gemini app now reaches 1 billion users.

Some analysts see a buying opportunity, with Motley Fool contributor Adam Spatacco arguing that Wall Street is overlooking Alphabet's combination of custom chips, cloud and DeepMind research, and noting a Google Cloud backlog of about $561 billion. Others raised caution about the cloud figures, since a filing showed that upward of a third of the quarter's cloud growth came from a joint venture Alphabet partly owns. PYMNTS said the results returned attention to concerns that Big Tech's AI spending could outrun the earnings and cash needed to justify it. The articles do not say what happens next, though investors will be watching whether Search growth stabilizes and whether cash flow recovers as spending climbs.

stories.Headline: PA Senator's Bill Would Ban AI for Student Mental Health
stories.Summary:
Pennsylvania state Sen. Nick Miller, a Democrat who represents parts of Lehigh and Northampton Counties, has introduced a bill that would stop schools from using artificial intelligence for student mental health services. The measure, Senate Bill 1505, was reported on October 27 and 28, 2026. Miller circulated a memo explaining his reasoning, and the bill now awaits deliberation in the Senate Education Committee. It is meant as a companion to upcoming House legislation from Rep. Melissa L. Shusterman, whose proposal carries the same title, Prohibiting Artificial Intelligence for Student Mental Health Services.

Under the bill, schools could not use AI to provide mental or behavioral health services that are otherwise handled by mental health professionals. The ban would not reach administrative work, so those professionals could still use AI for scheduling, organizing records and managing files. Miller argues that AI can produce inaccurate or unsafe advice and lacks the professional judgment needed to recognize and respond to a student in crisis. He has also said that struggling students should be able to rely on trusted adults at school, and that technology should support those relationships rather than replace them.

The push comes as teen mental health remains a serious concern and counselors are in short supply. Citing CDC figures, EdSource reported that about 40% of high school students experienced persistent sadness or hopelessness, and roughly 20% had seriously considered suicide in 2023. RAND researchers found that about one in five adolescents already turn to AI chatbots for mental health advice. At least 200 schools in 19 states have partnered with a company called Alongside to offer its Kiwi chatbot to students in grades four through 12, with counselors alerted within five minutes when a serious topic such as suicide is flagged. The Guardian reported that the tool starts at around $10 per student a year.

Other states have taken varied approaches. Nevada generally bars psychotherapists from using AI beyond administrative tasks, while Colorado and Maine prohibit clinicians from letting AI make independent clinical decisions but allow certain uses when a clinician reviews and approves the output. At least 35 states have published guidance on AI in education, but Pennsylvania has not yet issued its own. Members of the House Education Committee traveled to Pittsburgh to gather input on possible AI legislation, and committee Chair Pete Schweyer said people are generally concerned about ethical use, student privacy and student data. Teachers unions have also urged lawmakers to ensure new rules prevent educators from being replaced by AI, and what happens next with Miller's bill rests with the Senate Education Committee.

stories.Headline: The Privacy Commissioner is telling organisations handling private data to take note - as he releases his final findings into the Manage My Health data breach - 30-Oct-2026
stories.Summary:
New Zealand's Privacy Commissioner, Michael Webster, has released his final findings into the Manage My Health data breach and used the occasion to tell organisations that handle private data to take note. The breach happened in December, when the Manage My Health portal was hacked. The information of 100-thousand people was leaked as a result. The findings were reported on 30 October 2026, and the account of them comes from Newstalk ZB and NZCity.

Webster's findings point to two main problems. He says the breach made existing distrust in health and government systems worse. He also says it took too long for the people affected to be told that their information had been exposed. The articles do not give a specific figure for how long the delay lasted, and they do not list any penalty or formal order attached to the findings.

The main message from the Commissioner is aimed at the wider sector rather than a single company. He says his office wants every organisation to have a plan in place for the event of a cyber breach. In his view, a ready plan should help organisations respond faster, including by notifying affected people sooner. The articles describe this as a call for preparation, and they do not say whether any new rule or legal requirement will follow.

On the question of what happens next, one related item says Assurance Health New Zealand is making changes since last year's Manage My Health hack. The articles do not explain what those changes are. They also do not say whether further action is planned against any party involved in the breach. For now, the Commissioner's findings stand as a warning to organisations across the country about how they prepare for and respond to cyber attacks.

stories.Headline: Airship Announces Next-Generation AI Capabilities to Deliver the Right Customer Experience in the Moment
stories.Summary:
On October 27, 2026, Airship, the mobile-first customer experience company, announced new AI capabilities built to deliver personalized mobile interactions at the moment a customer shows intent. The headline additions are on-device decisioning AI and zero-copy integrations with leading data warehouses, which let the platform combine stored customer profile data with live context from the app. Two days later, on October 29, Toronto-based Cohere said it had reached the initial close of its Series E round, which targets up to CAD $7 billion at a valuation of CAD $35.7 billion. Cohere describes itself as a provider of sovereign AI for regulated industries and governments, and calls the round the largest private raise ever by a Canadian technology company.

Airship's decisioning AI runs locally on the user's device when a screen loads, using signals such as the current screen, cart status and in-app behavior, which removes server delays and keeps customer data secure. Zero copy reads profile data straight from data warehouses without duplicating it, and external feeds, such as weather or store inventory, can pull live information into messages as they render. Data Branching routes each user down the best path without developer resources, and automated triggers can act on insights, for instance by helping customers finish abandoned carts. The company also certified its approach under ISO 42001, the global standard for AI management systems, and will demonstrate the tools as lead sponsor of Elevate'26 in London on November 4 and 5. At Cohere, commitments so far include Schwarz Group as lead investor, joined by new backers Bell Ventures, Bullhound Capital and the Government of Canada, with Inovia Capital, NVIDIA and Prosperity7 Ventures returning.

Airship CEO Brett Caine said relevance at scale is now the standard for enterprise brands, and pointed to the company's more than 15 years of mobile experience and its Results Guarantee tying value to business outcomes. CTO Mike Herrick said the key moment is the instant a screen loads, so the decision was moved onto the device, and that customer data stays secure because decisions happen in the app. David LoPresti, U-Haul's Director of Mobile Experience, said that working with Airship lets his team add real nuance, and that technology is no longer the challenge. At Cohere, CEO Aidan Gomez called the round a historic honour for the company and for Canada, while CFO Francois Chadwick said the money will go to the model and product roadmap, vertical AI solutions for regulated industries, and long-term compute for training frontier enterprise models. Schwarz Digits CEO Christian Müller said digital sovereignty means strategic choice and holding the keys to your own data, and that the goal is to anchor Cohere's capabilities in the sovereign STACKIT cloud.

Prime Minister Mark Carney said Canada's equity stake is an investment in choice and security, and that all Canadians will now share in Cohere's success, while AI Minister Evan Solomon said companies should be able to grow and create jobs in Canada. Germany's Digital Minister Karsten Wildberger praised the round as a sign of confidence in sovereign AI and German-Canadian cooperation. Cohere said it ended the third quarter of 2026 with 165% year-over-year ARR growth after launching its North agentic platform, and grew its customer base twentyfold to 300 customers. This year it also completed transactions involving Aleph Alpha, Reliant AI and AISLE, and released new models including Command A+ and Embed 5 alongside North 2. Cohere cites a McKinsey projection that the sovereign AI market will reach $600 billion, and says it will keep expanding across North America, EMEA and APAC.

stories.Headline: Ottawa investing up to $1.6B in Canadian AI company Cohere
stories.Summary:
Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on Thursday that his government will invest up to $1.6 billion in Canadian artificial intelligence company Cohere. He made the announcement in Montreal while welcoming European Union leaders to a summit aimed at building closer ties. Carney said Canada is not willing to wait while the future of AI is decided elsewhere by people it does not know or trust. He said the country is building that future at home, in the right way.

The government said the money will arrive in stages, with regular reporting on the commitments the company has made. Those commitments include creating at least 1,000 new high-paying technical jobs in Canada and putting at least $1.7 billion toward more computing infrastructure by 2030. Cohere must also keep its Canadian headquarters and incorporation, invest in research partnerships, create opportunities for students and graduates, and keep working with the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Carney said the investment is being made on a commercial basis, alongside private investors including Nvidia, Bell and Germany's Schwarz Group. The government's press release said the funding will let Cohere build far more advanced models and products, expand its computing capacity and grow its Canadian workforce.

Cohere CEO Aidan Gomez said the company, founded seven years ago, is now one of the very few in the world building frontier AI technology at a global scale. He added that it is the largest AI company outside the United States and China. Artificial Intelligence Minister Evan Solomon said the aim is to make sure Canadian companies are built in Canada and do not move elsewhere once they have grown. He compared the approach to planting and tending a crop and then letting someone else harvest it. Solomon did not directly answer questions from The Canadian Press about whether Cohere could leave the country, or whether Carney's remarks about trust meant some U.S. giants could not be trusted.

The announcement builds on earlier support and on a European tie-up. In April, Cohere said it would merge with Germany's Aleph Alpha and that the combined company would be anchored in both Germany and Canada. Carney called that partnership a concrete example of what Canada and Europe can build together, and said Cohere will remain Canadian under the agreement. In 2024, Ottawa announced up to $240 million to boost Cohere's computing capacity, and in 2025 it signed an agreement with the company to find ways AI can improve public service operations. Solomon said that if Canada does not build the technology it must buy it, and that the investment gives Canadians a seat at the table in shaping the future of AI.

stories.Headline: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe and Granary v2: Intelligent Multilingual Transcription You Can Prompt and Adapt
stories.Summary:
Nvidia released Nemotron 3.5 Transcribe on October 28, 2026, an open-weight model that handles transcription, speaker labeling, translation and audio question answering in a single pass. It is a 30-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts model with about 4 billion parameters active at a time, and it is available on Hugging Face and ModelScope. Alongside it, Nvidia put out Granary v2, an open-source multilingual speech dataset and curation pipeline built with NeMo Curator. Developers can download a checkpoint, adapt it for a specific field through fine-tuning, and try it in a Hugging Face demo.

The model transcribes 40 languages, translates 31 of them to or from English, and attributes speakers in 13. It handles recordings up to an hour long and labels up to eight speakers, while one SiliconANGLE report says it can take in 100 hours of audio. Nvidia said one Blackwell Server Edition GPU running a forthcoming NVFP4 quantized version processed 100 hours of audio in under three minutes, measured on 30-second clips at high concurrency. Granary v2's public manifest covers 463,062 hours across 48 languages and 16 source corpora, up from 25 languages in the first version, and it provides three transcript styles that can be requested by prompt: verbatim with fillers, written-form with numbers as figures, and a version with filler words removed. Quantized versions are due soon so the model can run on an RTX Spark, DGX Spark or Jetson AGX Thor, and the available checkpoint can already be served with vLLM.

Nvidia, through its Hugging Face post, said the model leads open-weight systems on several benchmarks. It ranks first among open-weight models on the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard for English at 5.33% average word error rate, and it ties for first among open-weight models on the Artificial Analysis index at 2.8%, using about 4 billion active parameters against 24 billion for the model it ties. On David AI's 21-language diarization leaderboard it posts an 18.26% error rate, just ahead of Nvidia's own Nemotron 3 Diarization at 18.38%, and on VoiceArena it leads 14 systems at 32.4% cpWER. SiliconANGLE reported out-of-the-box word error of 30.8%, cut to 20.8% with careful prompting, and 11.8% after fine-tuning on the Eka Care Indian medical speech benchmark. Nvidia's own medical case study said fine-tuning cut word error on held-out speakers by 45.8% relative to the best prompt.

Users steer the model with plain-language prompts, so one recording can yield a labeled transcript, an English translation or answers about decisions made in a meeting. They can also supply expected jargon, such as medical terms, to improve accuracy. Nvidia advised spot-checking names, speaker changes and answers against the recording, and noted that language support varies by task and that audio question answering is trained in English. As an early use, Agora built a classroom demo using the model's word-level timestamps to show a transcript beside a lesson replay.
