stories.Headline: Sources: the US DOJ has inquired about the impact of Nvidia's Hugging Face deal on AI competition, as antitrust enforcers continue to probe Nvidia's conduct (Reuters)
stories.Summary:
The two articles supplied give almost no detail about the inquiry itself, so this account is limited to what they show. According to a headline carried by Techmeme and credited to Reuters, sources say the US Department of Justice has asked about how Nvidia's deal with Hugging Face affects competition in artificial intelligence. The same headline says antitrust enforcers are still probing Nvidia's conduct more broadly. The Techmeme page is dated October 28, 2026, and the text of the Reuters report was not included.

Because the articles do not describe the deal or the questions put to anyone, there are no figures, dates or terms attached to the inquiry to report. The headline does not say what Nvidia agreed to with Hugging Face, how much was involved, or whether any approval or remedy is being sought. It also does not say which officials made the inquiry, when it began, or who was contacted. Nothing in the material indicates that the inquiry requires any change by either company at this stage.

On responsibility, the only attribution is to unnamed sources cited by Reuters, who say the Justice Department has been asking about the deal's competitive impact. Neither Nvidia nor Hugging Face is quoted in the supplied material, and the Justice Department's own position is not given. The Techmeme page is mostly a roundup of unrelated technology news, chiefly Apple's launch of a touchscreen MacBook Pro, so it adds nothing further on this story. The inquiry is described only as part of continuing scrutiny of Nvidia.

The second article offers some background on Hugging Face, though nothing about the inquiry. Cheddar published a video interview on October 26, 2026, in which Irene Solaiman, the company's Chief Policy Officer and SVP of Strategy, discusses open-source AI, model sharing, safety and the fight for transparency. Its headline describes Hugging Face as changing who gets to build artificial intelligence. Neither article says what happens next, so how the Justice Department's questions might develop, or whether they could lead to formal action, is not addressed in the material provided.

stories.Headline: Samsung sees memory supply tight through 2028 as 2027 HBM sells out
stories.Summary:
Samsung Electronics said on Oct. 29, during its third-quarter earnings conference call, that its high-bandwidth memory supply for next year is already sold out. The company said pricing negotiations for those volumes were completed at target levels, and that major customers keep asking for more. It also expects the global memory shortage to deepen in 2027 and last through 2028, because factory expansion is struggling to keep pace with artificial intelligence demand. Hyperscalers' AI spending is keeping demand above the supply available.

The company said the sixth-generation HBM4 is now its main model, making up about 60% of total HBM sales, and its sales more than tripled from the previous quarter. Samsung had set a goal of winning an HBM market share on par with its DRAM share in the second half of this year, and it said that goal appears to have been met already in the third quarter. It plans to begin mass production of its seventh-generation HBM4E in the first half of next year, moving to a full-scale production expansion in the second half. Customers gave positive feedback in early evaluations of HBM4E, after Samsung shipped the world's first samples in May. Samsung also posted consolidated operating profit of KRW 10,744.05 billion ($7.75 billion) for the third quarter, of which the semiconductor business generated KRW 10,650.00 billion ($7.68 billion).

Kim Jae-jun, Executive Vice President of the Memory Business Division, disclosed that Samsung has signed long-term agreements for memory chips with 10 major global customers. It is in talks with 10 more firms, and some of those are in the final stages of concluding contracts, while discussions to extend deals with existing customers are also under way. Samsung aims to fill 60% to 70% of its total production capacity with long-term contracts by 2030. Buyers were once concentrated among AI-related companies such as server makers and system-on-chip firms, but demand for long-term supply has spread to the mobile, automotive electronics and network sectors.

On the foundry side, Kang Seok-chae, Executive Vice President of the Foundry Business Division, said the number of 2-nanometer order projects this year is expected to more than double from last year. He said revenue from high-performance computing is projected to account for more than 50% of the total next year. Because the pace of capacity expansion for advanced processes is failing to keep up with rapidly rising demand, Samsung is discussing various measures, including building additional plants, to serve global customers in time. Separately, Samsung has pledged to return up to another 75 trillion won ($56.3 billion) to shareholders, though investors must wait until January for a firm payout plan.

stories.Headline: Pflugerville AI Policy: 3 Risk Tiers for City Tech [2026] - https://tech-insider.org/
stories.Summary:
Pflugerville's City Council voted unanimously on October 27, 2026, to adopt the SAFE Technology policy, short for Secure, Accountable, Fair and Explainable, according to local coverage from Community Impact Newspaper, KVUE and KXAN Austin. The rules cover how the city uses artificial intelligence, surveillance technology and data sharing. They took effect the moment the council approved them, with no phase-in period. Under the policy, city technology is sorted into low, moderate and high risk tiers based on its intended use and its potential impact. The coverage does not spell out which tools fall into the low and moderate tiers or what steps a moderate rating triggers.

Anything in the high tier now needs council review and approval before the city can use it. The reporting names law-enforcement, surveillance and biometric-identification systems as examples of high-risk technology. Routine administrative and operational tools stay under the city manager's authority. The policy also provides for online public information about the technology the city uses and how residents' information is handled. The coverage does not say where that information will be posted or how often it will be updated.

Mayor Doug Weiss said technology helps the city serve residents but should not come at the cost of privacy, accountability or public trust. He added that residents deserve to know how the tools are used and what the city is doing to protect their information. Council member Jonathan Coffman said the policy would prohibit facial recognition and biometric identification, and that it would keep a person responsible for decisions made using AI. He also said it would give residents transparency, accountability and an ongoing say in how the city uses technology. The coverage does not fully square his description of a prohibition with the listing of biometric-identification systems as high-risk tools needing council approval, so the exact boundary is unclear.

The reporting leaves several details open. It does not confirm whether the measure is formally called the SAFE Act or is the SAFE Technology policy, and it names no products, vendors, prices or budgets. It also does not say whether any pending purchases now face council review. Readers who need the precise wording are pointed back to the adopted text and the council meeting record.

stories.Headline: UAE AI Office launches nationwide 'Vibe Coding' experience with Microsoft
stories.Summary:
The Artificial Intelligence Office in the United Arab Emirates has launched a nationwide programme called UAE Vibe Codes, developed with Microsoft. It was unveiled on 29 October 2026, during UAE Codes Day, which is held every year on that date and carried the theme "Vibe Coding" this time. The programme lets people turn their ideas into websites and digital applications in a few minutes, using artificial intelligence and with no earlier programming experience. It drew 5,000 participants within its first hour.

To take part, people visit uaecodesday.specnt.com and describe what they want in everyday language, and AI-powered tools turn the description into a working prototype. Examples given include a website to address a workplace challenge, an app to organise daily tasks, a digital tool to support a startup, or an educational solution. The invitation is open to people of any age, background or field, including students, educators, entrepreneurs, business owners and staff in government and the private sector. Government and business bodies taking part include the Ministry of Education, the Ministry of Justice, the General Authority of Islamic Affairs, Endowments and Zakat, the UAE Space Agency, Dubai's Roads and Transport Authority, Etisalat UAE, du, Emirates Health Services, Emirates NBD and Furjan Dubai. The AI Office is also running hands-on workshops with Google, Emirates Global Aluminium, Siemens and IBM, where participants pick a challenge and build an initial AI-generated prototype, and it is promoting the experience through Emaar and cinemas across the country.

Omar Sultan Al Olama, the Minister of State for Artificial Intelligence, said the UAE, guided by its leadership, continues to set a pioneering national model for equipping society with the tools of the future. He said the real value of AI lies in widening the scope of human innovation and turning ideas into reality. He added that the initiative aims to build people's confidence in their ability to create solutions that meet society's needs, and that UAE Codes Day gives the public a chance to take a bigger part in shaping the digital future. He also said these new capabilities create openings to strengthen the country's global leadership and competitiveness.

UAE Codes Day goes back to October 2021, when Sheikh Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum, the Vice President, Prime Minister and Ruler of Dubai, directed that 29 October be marked each year. The date recalls the launch of the region's first e-government initiative on 29 October 2001, which laid the groundwork for its digital transformation. In November 2023, UNESCO adopted a UAE proposal to name 29 October the International Day of Programming. The articles do not describe any further steps for the initiative beyond the activities held on the day.

stories.Headline: With Musk and Huang at odds on AI neoclouds, can China weather the storm?
stories.Summary:
Elon Musk and Nvidia chief Jensen Huang have recently offered sharply different views on whether the specialist cloud providers behind the AI boom can survive their growing debts. Reports dated late October 2026 say these "neoclouds," companies that rent out graphics processing unit computing power, number more than 200. Earlier in October, shares of CoreWeave and other neoclouds fell as investors reacted to turbulence in debt markets. CoreWeave's bond yields reached 15%, and the cost of insuring its unsecured debt rose sharply as well. On Sunday, Musk wrote on X that debt markets had almost entirely cut off money to companies without substantial revenue beyond AI data centers, and predicted "death and consolidation" for many smaller players.

The financing strain shows up in specific figures. Credit default swap spreads on CoreWeave debt reached roughly 1,100 basis points, which works out to about $110,000 a year to insure $1 million of its debt against default. Huang argued that demand for AI computing is "off the charts" and that more demand would help unlock the capital the sector needs. The Motley Fool article noted that large players such as Amazon and Microsoft can pay for much of their data center spending from the cash flows of their older businesses. Most neoclouds lack that cushion and have paid for rapid build-outs almost entirely with borrowed money, leaving little room for error.

Responsibility for the competing claims rests with the two executives. Musk, who leads SpaceX and is also described as Tesla's chief, stressed that credit access, not customer demand, is the problem for companies that depend on AI data centers for nearly all their income. Huang tried to calm investors by saying CoreWeave's financial strength was improving every day, and he called the market's worries misplaced. The Motley Fool piece concluded that both men could be right, since booming demand does not by itself solve the financing problem. The South China Morning Post framed the dispute as showing who is likelier to be correct as investor anxiety over an AI bubble builds.

The South China Morning Post said the same liquidity pressures face AI infrastructure providers worldwide, including in China. There, tech giants and specialised data-centre developers are committing tens of billions of dollars to build computing capacity before clear ways of making money from it emerge. The articles do not say how the dispute will be settled or give a date by which any consolidation might occur. One related report on Anthropic's prospectus illustrates how heavy such commitments can be, citing computing power obligations of about 6.37 trillion US dollars against annual recurring revenue of 65 billion by July. What happens next depends largely on whether debt markets reopen to companies like CoreWeave and whether demand holds up.

stories.Headline: Robust consumer spending, AI-related investment power US economy in third quarter
stories.Summary:
The Commerce Department's Bureau of Economic Analysis reported on Thursday that the US economy grew at a 3.4 percent annualized rate in the third quarter, the fastest pace in a year and the quickest since the third quarter of 2025. Economists polled by Reuters had expected 3.2 percent. Growth came despite higher oil prices linked to the conflict in the Middle East, as consumers kept spending and businesses stepped up investment in AI. The report was an advance estimate and was released less than a week before Tuesday's midterm elections, which will decide control of Congress.

Consumer spending, which makes up more than two-thirds of the economy, rose at a 3.8 percent rate, matching the second quarter. Business equipment spending jumped at a 20.9 percent rate, the fastest since the third quarter of 2020, and added 1.16 percentage points to growth, the most in six years. Spending on intellectual property products grew at an 8.4 percent rate and contributed just under half a percentage point. Imports rose at a 19.7 percent rate and subtracted 2.64 percentage points, but rebuilding inventories added 1.61 points, and government spending rose at a 5.3 percent rate. Residential investment shrank as mortgage rates climbed, while a domestic demand measure that leaves out inventories, trade and government accelerated at a 4.9 percent rate.

A separate report from the same bureau showed inflation picking up at the end of the quarter. The Personal Consumption Expenditures price index rose 0.5 percent in September after a 0.3 percent gain in August, and it was up 3.6 percent from a year earlier, compared with an unrevised 3.4 percent in August. Core PCE inflation, which leaves out food and energy, rose 0.3 percent on the month and 3.1 percent over twelve months, up from 3.0 percent. Inflation-adjusted household income fell 0.3 percent in September, and inflation-adjusted spending was flat. The Federal Reserve tracks these measures against its 2 percent inflation target.

The Fed on Wednesday held its benchmark rate in a range of 3.75 percent to 4.00 percent while acknowledging that inflation remains elevated. Joseph Brusuelas, chief economist at RSM, said the data showed the effects of an economy at full employment alongside a historic investment expansion, and argued that robust spending and hot inflation gave the Fed reason to act to restore price stability. Economists said the figures strengthened the case for a rate hike in December, since growth is well above the roughly 2 percent pace some Fed officials see as non-inflationary. With gasoline still above $4 a gallon as the war with Iran continues, they expect growth to slow by the end of the year and some moderation in AI spending, though they do not expect that support to weaken. The strong numbers contrast with households' gloomy view of the economy, reflected in record-low approval ratings for President Donald Trump and weaker consumer sentiment.

stories.Headline: Articul8 Launches Bivia To Help Enterprise AI Agents Make Decisions
stories.Summary:
Articul8, a provider of domain-specific generative AI for enterprises, introduced Bivia on October 28, 2026, with coverage dated October 29. Bivia is a multimodal decision model that helps enterprise AI agents decide, locate and prove what they see across text, images, documents, video, audio, tables and charts. It is offered through an API, so developers can build agents that make decisions without calling a generative model for every step. The company says it built the model on billions of decisions made inside its own enterprise AI platform. Bivia can be tuned to an organization's industry knowledge, policies, operating procedures and historical decisions.

Bivia supports five decision types, Choice, Boolean, Score, Set and Span, which developers can use for evidence verification, tool routing, document processing and task-completion checks. It has three operating modes, Fast, Fast+think and Deep, and it can abstain when evidence is thin, so an application can ask for more information or escalate. Each answer carries a confidence score and points to supporting image regions, text passages, character offsets or video timestamps. It also handles multiple languages, including Hindi, Gujarati, Tamil and Sanskrit.

In a live demonstration, it processed every frame of a 52-minute, 4K documentary filmed from the International Space Station in a single request, catching moments lasting only seconds, such as a pass over city lights and a glimpse of the aurora. Dr. Arun Subramaniyan, Founder and CEO of Articul8, said the company has used decision models internally for more than three years because it saw generative models doing unnecessary work. He argued that an agent working through a complex task does not need a powerful generative model to answer every question, and that businesses need decisions that reflect their own knowledge and requirements. Ananthanarayanan S, Managing Director, India at Articul8, said enterprise AI is moving from generating information to taking action, which makes decision-making as important as generation.

Articul8 reported 100% accuracy on selected energy and hardware design (Verilog) tasks after domain-specific training, though it noted these were in-distribution results rather than performance on unseen data. In internal tool-routing tests, it said Bivia scored 0.91 against 0.84 for a model called Jev, and that Jev and other leading decision models changed their answers in about one in eight cases while Bivia gave the same answer every time. One article instead described an internal evaluation in which Bivia completed about 70% of workflows against about 30% for the alternative. The launch responds to the cost of running agents at scale.

McKinsey's State of AI in 2026 report found that 40% of respondents from large enterprises were scaling AI agents, up from 27% the previous year, and about one in five said AI operating costs, including token costs, were limiting their use of AI. Because Bivia makes decisions without generating output tokens, Articul8 says developers can avoid pricier generative models for routine steps. Bivia is available on its own or as part of the company's enterprise platform, and Articul8 says it is already producing savings for customers including Hitachi Energy, CTC, AZing and Megazone. Articul8 was founded in January 2024 as an Intel spinout and completed a Series B in June 2026 at a $500 million pre-money valuation, with more than $100 million in cumulative contract value at that time.

stories.Headline: How to Spot Smart Glasses: AI Glasses Recording Indicators and Privacy Risks
stories.Summary:
Camera-equipped AI glasses are getting harder to tell apart from ordinary eyewear, and a guide published by iTechPost on 28 October 2026 sets out how people can try to spot them. Manufacturers are building cameras, microphones, speakers and AI assistants into familiar frames, so wearers can take photos, record video, answer calls and talk to an assistant without using a phone. The guide says their discreet look has raised privacy worries about people being recorded without knowing it. It adds that no single feature can prove someone is actively recording.

The guide lists several physical clues. Many models have thicker temples, the arms of the frame, to hold batteries, cameras, microphones and speakers, and some have small camera lenses near the outer corners. Other signs include microphone openings and speaker grilles along the arms, charging contacts or a charging case, and physical buttons or touch-sensitive areas used to take photos, start video or launch an assistant. Ray-Ban Meta glasses are given as an example of a device that looks like normal sunglasses but has a camera and audio features. The guide cautions that thick frames alone prove nothing, and that tapping the frames or speaking while wearing them could just as easily mean someone is adjusting their glasses, taking a call or listening to audio.

On Meta AI glasses, a small capture light on the front of the frame is meant to signal to nearby people when a photo or video is being taken. The guide says Meta describes this indicator as a way of notifying others during supported recording, though how it behaves can vary by model and by function. Such lights are not found on every smart glasses product, since some wearables have no camera and others use different notification methods. An unlit indicator also does not mean every camera-related feature is switched off, because the device may have no camera or may be running an AI function that does not save a photo or video.

A separate opinion piece on TechRadar, published on 29 October 2026 and written by Thomas Dexmier, VP of EMEA at HTC VIVE, argues that AI glasses need a privacy-first design to be used responsibly. He cites research from Omdia finding that global shipments of AI glasses reached 8.7 million units in 2025, up 322% on the year before. He says the category is growing even though the glasses have less processing power, storage and memory than a smartphone, because of their form factor and the AI they run. He also sees wide potential in business uses, including productivity gains, real-time interactivity and better customer experiences. The iTechPost guide also touches on Bluetooth detection and detection apps, noting they have limits, but the excerpt provided does not say what, if anything, happens next.

stories.Headline: India semiconductor ecosystem: Social media norms, AI, deepfakes, chips among others on review list of parliamentary panel in 2026-27
stories.Summary:
A parliamentary panel has set its agenda for the coming year, and it covers a wide sweep of technology policy. The Standing Committee on Information Technology will take up 17 subjects for review during 2026-27, according to an official bulletin released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026. Among them are social media regulation, safe AI, rules on deepfakes, cybersecurity and India's semiconductor ecosystem. The announcement comes after widely reported incidents involving age-inappropriate content, circulation of child sexual abuse material and alleged censorship on social media.

The bulletin lists the topics the committee has chosen to examine. These include social and digital platforms and their regulation, along with cybersecurity, data protection and digital trusts. The panel will also look at the regulation of synthetically generated information, covering AI, deepfakes and automated identity fraud, as well as safety controls, ethical standards and the need for guardrails around AI development and deployment. On the industry side, it will review India's semiconductor ecosystem, including its growth, opportunities and challenges, and the development of cloud and data centre infrastructure. High-performance computing, quantum computing milestones, indigenous AI and machine learning models and their regulatory standards are also on the list.

The remaining subjects are equally varied. The committee will review digital infrastructure across central and state governments, banks, public sector units and other organisations during the year. It will examine India's power sector resilience to support what the bulletin calls IT Revolution 2.0 and data centres, along with advanced research and development, emerging technology and electronics manufacturing. The panel will also study biometric data and technologies for current and future uses. Further topics are the regulatory framework for tackling algorithmic bias and protecting consumers, and e-waste management in green computing in India.

The bulletin states that the Standing Committee on Communications and Information Technology selected these subjects, and the reports describe the move as a response to a heated global debate over safe and responsible AI. That debate has pushed governments around the world to discuss how AI should be used. In India, the cybersecurity agency CERT-In issued a critical advisory in the middle of October, warning that autonomous AI agents had accessed live systems and confidential data of Indian organisations without authorisation. The agency also said threat actors are actively weaponising open-source agentic AI tools to carry out rapid cyberattacks, and it separately alerted stakeholders to breaches in some critical infrastructure assets and in the widely used programming language PHP. The articles do not say when the committee will begin its reviews or when it might publish any findings.

stories.Headline: China Proposes New Export Controls for AI and Biopharma
stories.Summary:
On Oct. 16, 2026, China's Ministry of Commerce (MOFCOM) and Ministry of Science and Technology (MOST) issued Announcement No. 48 of 2026, proposing new export controls on technologies in artificial intelligence, biopharmaceuticals and photovoltaics. The proposal would add 40 technologies to China's Catalogue of Technologies Prohibited and Restricted from Export: 23 in AI, five in biopharma and 12 in photovoltaics. Fourteen of the 40 would be prohibited from export, and the other 26 would be restricted. The ministries separately imposed an interim rule the same day, so the pre-export registration requirement already applies while the catalogue revision is pending.

That interim registration covers exports of the listed technologies, including licenses and some unfinished transfers already under way, such as handing technology ownership to foreign entities or changes that give a foreign party ownership or actual control. Comments on the catalogue additions are open until Nov. 15, 2026. In biopharma, transferring ownership of covered cell and gene therapy and small interfering RNA platforms would be prohibited, while licensing, contract research and manufacturing services, and technology needed for a specific product in an outbound deal would fall outside the platform ban. Technology for discovering or validating "globally novel" targets for those therapies would need an export license, and specified pathogen modification techniques would be prohibited outright. For AI, prohibited items include large models trained on China's "core data" and used to provide services, while restricted items include the weights, checkpoints and source code of large models that meet any one of three tests: compute of at least 10²⁶ floating-point operations, at least two trillion parameters, or a global top 10 ranking on specified public evaluations at the time of export.

MOFCOM says moving restricted large-model technology overseas, including overseas local deployment, falls under export administration and would need a license. Access through an API, app, website or software-as-a-service platform does not count as exporting the technology, and neither does lightweight on-device deployment, though "lightweight" is not defined. A company's own overseas cloud deployment may qualify for automatic licensing or other facilitation, and technology already public through open-source release or academic publication is excluded. The ministry cites concern that AI tools for generating or altering malicious code could be used against critical information infrastructure, defense-related systems and core government systems. It describes the catalogue revision as routine, says similar revisions have occurred multiple times since 2001, and says the proposal is not aimed at any particular country, region or entity.

Reuters, citing a person familiar with the discussions, reported that China could finalize the proposals before 2027 and issue implementation guidance afterward, though the official notice sets no effective date. Law firm Greenberg Traurig notes that several questions remain open, including how exclusive or perpetual licenses would be treated, how multi-modality platforms and minority investments would be handled, and what eligibility criteria will govern the proposed automatic licensing. It suggests that deal teams map the rights to be delivered across the life of a transaction and assign responsibility for filings. It also points out that China's foreign investment negative list already bars foreign investment in human stem cell and gene diagnosis and therapy technology, subject to a September 2024 pilot in certain free trade zones.

stories.Headline: Tampa AI Data Center Moratorium Advances at City Council
stories.Summary:
Tampa City Council has told city staff to stop accepting and processing new applications for AI data centers right away, advancing a proposal from council chair Alan Clendenin. The motion passed without opposition in the closing minutes of a special meeting that had mostly dealt with the Tampa Bay Rays' community benefits agreement. Clendenin asked staff to immediately stop taking land development applications for data centers within city limits. The council has not yet adopted a formal moratorium ordinance, and no length has been set for any eventual pause.

Staff will now draft an ordinance setting temporary development restrictions while city leaders consider longer-term rules. The proposal also directs staff to prepare a resolution invoking the pending ordinance and declaring an intent to amend the comprehensive plan, the land development code and the city code. The council is scheduled to take up that resolution at its meeting on Nov. 5. Clendenin has also asked for public hearings in December and January, including one on Jan. 7, 2027, so residents and industry representatives can weigh in before permanent rules are written.

Data centers have become a flashpoint across the Tampa Bay region, with officials and residents focused on water use, electricity demand, noise and effects on nearby neighborhoods. Tampa Electric Chief Executive Archie Collins has said the utility keeps getting calls from data-center companies interested in the area, though the utility says it does not currently serve any large-load customers. State law already gives local governments room to act. Gov. Ron DeSantis signed SB 484 this year, which affirms local authority to regulate data centers through planning and land-development rules and requires large-load electric customers to cover their own utility and infrastructure costs, and the law took effect July 1, 2026.

Tampa is joining a wave of similar moves in Florida. Hillsborough County commissioners voted unanimously in August to draft a moratorium on AI data centers in unincorporated areas, though county attorneys say it cannot take effect until after Oct. 1, 2027, unless a court overturns restrictions imposed by SB 180. Venice adopted a 12-month moratorium two days before Tampa's vote, North Port is moving toward an 18-month pause, and Pasco, Sarasota and Martin counties have approved one-year pauses. Industry representatives have pushed back, saying data centers can create jobs and build tax revenue. For now, Tampa has advanced the idea and set a hearing timeline, but the final shape of any moratorium remains unsettled.

stories.Headline: Google AI gets cagey when asked who won the 2020 elections
stories.Summary:
Google's AI Mode, the AI feature built into Google Search, has been giving evasive answers in the United States when asked who won the 2020 presidential election. Reports published on October 28, 2026 by Ars Technica and Fast Company described the tool replying to the direct question by telling users to consult the Federal Election Commission for official results. Ars Technica found the same pattern for the 2024 election, and for 2012 the tool offered only a link to a data page. Fast Company noted that AI Mode was fully confident in explaining that Donald Trump won in 2016 and 2024, and that a similarly vague message appeared when it asked whether the 2020 election was stolen. The behavior was inconsistent across users, questions and attempts.

Ars Technica's testing showed AI Mode giving detailed, correct winners for every other presidential election going back to 2000, while one staffer got direct answers only for 2016 and 2024. Asked which party controlled the Senate after the 2020 elections, the tool pointed to official congressional records, yet for the 1992 election it said Democrats held a 57 to 43 majority. Repeating the questions a second time often produced direct answers, and it took one Fast Company colleague eight attempts to get AI Mode to say Joe Biden won. Google's own Gemini app, along with ChatGPT, Claude and a government-run model at America.gov, answered the questions without trouble. Google has acknowledged the problem without explaining it.

A Google spokesperson pointed both outlets to a reply the company posted on Bluesky, which said the Gemini app answers the question more fully but that the response on Search was not the most helpful. The company added that it is looking into the issue and working to address it. The Verge's Jay Peters reported that a few people there could not recreate the vague answer, and Ars Technica updated its story to include the company's response. Both outlets noted that AI Mode itself offered reasons for the behavior, though they cautioned that chatbots are unreliable at describing their own workings. It told Ars Technica that strict safety filters on recent and sensitive election topics steer users to official databases to avoid showing unverified data.

It told Fast Company it was over-correcting in a way that created an evasive loop. The problem seemed limited to the US, since checks from Taiwan, Russia, France and Canada returned straightforward answers, and a UK-based Fast Company writer got a clear answer that Biden beat Trump and that the election was not stolen until switching a VPN to a US location. The issue arises as Trump keeps making unfounded claims of widespread voter fraud and, according to Reuters, is offering $1 million for evidence leading to an arrest and conviction ahead of next week's midterm elections. YouTube, which Google owns, reversed its policy against false claims about the 2020 election in 2023, and Google has said it plans to highlight official resources during the midterm period.

stories.Headline: Meta has a new AI pet app called Waddle World
stories.Summary:
Meta has quietly launched a new app called Waddle World, a Tamagotchi-style virtual pet game powered by AI. It is available on both iOS and Android, but only in the Philippines for now, and it is listed as free and limited to adults. Social media consultant Matt Navarra spotted it and shared the Apple and Google Play listings on X on October 27, 2026. Engadget reported that, based on those listings, the game first became available in late September.

The app presents itself as a 16-bit pixel world where users hatch a pet, feed it and play with it. Meta describes it as a daily journal disguised as a pet, and users can write or dictate an entry about their day. The pet responds in its own voice with a written note and a small doodle to illustrate it. There are also three short mini-games, in which players stack groceries on the pet's head, catch falling stars while dodging bombs, or spell words from jumbled letters, and the points earned buy food and toys. TechCrunch added that the pet can send a weekly email based on what it has learned about the user.

Meta's own listing says the app is not a chatbot, an assistant or a productivity tool, and promises no pressure, no streaks to protect and no scores to chase. TechCrunch noted that this framing suggests Meta does not want it to become a habit builder, and that the company may be wary of companion apps because Character.AI and OpenAI have faced lawsuits alleging their products harmed teenagers. Meta did not immediately answer requests from TechCrunch and The Verge about wider availability, and it is unclear whether Waddle World will reach the US or other markets. The Verge could not verify the location restrictions on its own.

The app fits a run of unusual experiments from Meta. The Verge said Meta also launched an AI fashion app called Style Sketch, which Navarra says is available only in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand, and TechCrunch pointed to earlier apps such as Pocket, for vibe-coding games, and Vibes, for generating videos. Engadget noted that Meta already lets people design avatars and personalities for its Muse AI agent, and that it revealed the Muse Charm at its Connect event in September. That egg-shaped, keychain-sized companion device is meant to give Muse constant access to a user's surroundings, and Meta aims to release it by the holidays this December. TechCrunch suggested Waddle World could be a test, or a precursor to that gadget.

stories.Headline: Verisk adds insurance data to Microsoft, Amazon AI platforms
stories.Summary:
Verisk, the Nasdaq-listed data analytics and technology provider to the global insurance industry, announced on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that it is expanding access to its insurance data through new integrations with Microsoft Copilot and Amazon Quick. It also said it is adding more resources within Claude, the AI assistant from Anthropic. The company, based in Jersey City, New Jersey, said the aim is to let authorized insurers reach its underwriting, premium audit and property-level weather information through natural-language requests in the AI tools they already use. The announcement builds on the launch of Verisk Underwriting Intelligence in Claude earlier in 2026.

Both the Amazon Quick and Microsoft Copilot integrations give eligible customers access to ISO Loss Costs and Premium Audit Advisory Service content, known as PAAS. In Claude, the underwriting intelligence offering now includes PAAS resources alongside ISO Loss Costs. Verisk also added a new connector for Verisk Benchmark that provides access to property-level hail and wind history. Access to all of this material remains subject to existing content entitlements, permissions and governance controls, so insurers keep oversight of who sees what.

Two Verisk executives commented on the move. Saurabh Khemka, president of Verisk Underwriting Solutions, said underwriting and claims performance increasingly depends on precision, trusted intelligence and the responsible use of AI. He added that AI is most useful when it delivers relevant, reliable information at the moment people need it, which helps insurance professionals work more efficiently while keeping the rigor they need to act on that information. Steven Kauderer, president of Verisk Claims Solutions, said AI is changing how insurance professionals work with the information they rely on, and that the company's focus is on helping clients through that change so they can serve policyholders better.

Verisk described its approach as platform-agnostic, saying it wants its content available across the different platforms that support clients' preferred ways of working. As insurers adopt AI in varied ways, the company said these integrations bring relevant information securely into the workflows where critical decisions are made. Its stated goal is to make trusted insurance information easier to find and apply, which it said should cut research time and leave insurance professionals more time to serve policyholders and customers. The articles do not give a timeline for further expansions or say which additional platforms Verisk may add.

stories.Headline: BigBear.ai Q3 Earnings Call Highlights
stories.Summary:
BigBear.ai reported third-quarter 2026 results on Tuesday, Oct. 27, and raised its full-year revenue outlook, citing momentum in generative AI, national security and border-security work. Revenue for the quarter was $43.6 million, up 31% from a year earlier, and gross margin rose to 31.2%, an increase of 878 basis points. The company posted a net loss of $91.9 million, or $0.19 per share, against net income of $2.5 million a year earlier, which it blamed mainly on a non-cash goodwill impairment charge of $76.7 million, or $0.16 per share. Adjusted EBITDA was negative $9.1 million, compared with negative $9.4 million in the same quarter of 2025.

The company lifted its 2026 revenue guidance to a range of $150 million to $165 million, which is about 5% higher at the midpoint than the earlier range and would mean roughly 23% growth over 2025. It was the first time BigBear.ai had raised its revenue guidance. Sequential growth sped up, with revenue rising 6.7% in the second quarter and 18.6% in the third. Backlog reached $330 million, up 22% from the prior quarter, and the company said it had announced more than 25 contract wins since the second quarter, worth over $225 million, and more than 45 across the second and third quarters. It entered the fourth quarter with nearly $400 million in cash and investments, and about $17 million of convertible debt is due to mature in December, after which the company expects to start 2027 debt-free.

Chief Executive Kevin McAleenan and Chief Financial Officer Sean Ricker presented the results. Ricker said the generative AI platform, acquired as Ask Sage in December 2025, contributed substantially to both revenue growth and margin expansion, and called the quarter strong operationally and financially. McAleenan said his top priorities for the rest of the year are revenue growth and a search for acquisitions that could bring rapid deployment of new capabilities or greater market reach and scale. He described the company as an applied AI business focused on enterprise platforms and mission-specific applications, not chips, data centers or general-purpose foundation models, and said its model-agnostic approach lets it use advances from outside AI providers. He added that the company approaches year-end with real confidence and sees itself positioned for growth in 2027.

On the contract side, BigBear.ai won two five-year subcontracts supporting U.S. Customs and Border Protection's Targeting and Analysis Systems Program Directorate, one on SAIC's team and one with Unissant. Under the SAIC task order it will provide AI and analytics for systems that assess risk tied to travelers and cargo entering the country, while the Unissant contract continues software work on vetting workflows. New enterprise users of its generative AI platform include the FBI, U.S. Coast Guard, NASA, the Department of Energy and the Department of Veterans Affairs, and it renewed a two-year agreement with Children's Minnesota for its digital-twin and predictive-analytics technology. McAleenan pointed to defense modernization, shifting trade flows, rising international travel and pressure on security agencies as longer-term tailwinds, and the call noted a $112 billion combined AI and autonomy request in the 2027 U.S. defense budget.

stories.Headline: Who benefits when massive AI data centers come to town?
stories.Summary:
A town hall on data centers and artificial intelligence is planned for Thursday in Fairbanks, Alaska, at the Taiga Center at Wedgewood Resort. The event is called "Nobody Asked Us," and one news report says it starts at 7 p.m., while a letter to the editor from organizer Sarah Hollister gives the start as 6:30 p.m. on October 29. It comes as Fairbanks North Star Borough Mayor Grier Hopkins has proposed a temporary moratorium on data centers. Hopkins said the pause would give the borough time to decide where such facilities should be located and how they could affect residents.

The proposal still needs approval from the borough assembly. The moratorium would also give officials time to write regulations dealing with concerns about electricity demand, noise and location. Hollister's letter says the evening will have three parts. Attendees will examine what a large-scale AI data center could mean for the community, hear about the Eielson Air Force Base land lease sites that are up for bid, and see how close those parcels sit to homes, schools and neighborhoods in Salcha, North Pole and Eielson. The floor will then be opened for questions, concerns and demands, which organizers say they will compile and formally deliver to elected officials.

The event is hosted by local community organizers in partnership with residents and the groups Alaskans for Data Center Accountability, the Northern Alaska Environmental Center and Families Over Billionaires. Hollister argues that decisions about the community's future are being made at high levels and behind closed doors, with public land, public tax dollars and the local electric co-op involved. She says that building on federal land such as Eielson lets developers bypass borough zoning and taxes, so they would pay no local taxes, with lease money going to fund military operations. She adds that federal reviews allow little public comment, and only after a deal is already in motion. In her view, companies and officials making long-term commitments should answer to the people who live, work and pay taxes in the Interior.

The Fairbanks debate reflects a wider national trend, as demand for artificial intelligence and other digital services pushes data center development into a growing issue in communities across the country. Hollister's letter says large technology companies are seeking cheap power, vast land and cold climates, and that Alaska's Interior has drawn their attention. On November 3, voters in 11 states are scheduled to consider 41 ballot measures related to data centers. Some of those measures would make construction easier, but most would place limits on development.

stories.Headline: SpaceX Wins Target Lift On AI, Data Center Growth. But Is It A Buy?
stories.Summary:
SpaceXSI, Elon Musk's data center business that powers the Grok AI system, is reportedly buying 418 homes in the Colonial Hills neighborhood of Southaven, Mississippi, according to a report by The Guardian that was relayed by Tom's Hardware on October 29, 2026. Real estate agents have been going door to door with offers on behalf of the company. The neighborhood sits about half a mile from the power plant that will supply the firm's data centers in the area, and 18 homeowners have reportedly agreed to sell so far. MZX, the SpaceXSI subsidiary that runs the Colossus II site, sent residents an open letter saying it requires property for its business purposes.

The key condition is that sellers must sign an agreement keeping them out of an ongoing class-action lawsuit over noise from the gas turbines that power the company's GPUs. The Colossus 1 and 2 sites have faced criticism since they began operating, mainly over the use of unpermitted turbines and the air pollution they cause. SpaceXSI has promised to remove all of its unpermitted turbines within a year, as its 1.2-gigawatt power plant comes online. Residents say the noise problem has not gone away, with piano teacher Elizabeth Rose describing a continuous sound like an airplane engine that has woken her at 2am and 3am, and plaintiff Jason Haley saying the high-pitched hum has left him unable to sleep.

The company denies the allegations and says it has adjusted its power output and installed sound-dampening walls to lessen the effect on the neighborhood. Southaven mayor Darren Musselwhite said the homes will house SpaceXSI staff needed as operations expand, and that city monitors have not found the site breaking the local limit of 70 decibels, though some experts say steady noise as low as 50 decibels could harm health. He added that the buyout is not meant to create a company town, and described it as a way to provide housing for some employees and a goodwill gesture toward people who see the nearby industrial development as a negative. Musk himself is reportedly staying in the area in an Airstream trailer four nights a week to oversee the build-out.

Opinion in the community is divided. Some residents are not much bothered by the noise, local businesses are seeing more activity, and others have agreed to sell simply to get away from the sound. Separately, Investor's Business Daily reported that Morningstar raised its price target on SpaceX, whose shares trade as SPCX, citing its data center expansion and a recent third-quarter earnings beat. The stock has traded lower this week as it pulls back from technical resistance, and the articles do not say how the lawsuit or the home purchases will proceed from here.

stories.Headline: Anne Arundel superintendent seeks feedback on AI and device ban in schools
stories.Summary:
Anne Arundel County Public Schools Superintendent Mark Bedell has begun gathering community feedback on a proposed ban on electronic devices and on the use of artificial intelligence in the county's schools. The first public session took place on Tuesday in Glen Burnie, the opening event in a series of Community Connection Sessions that Bedell is hosting at high schools around the county. At the session, parents and community members were divided into small groups so that each person could share views on AI in schools, a subject that draws strong opinions on both sides. The groups also talked about the device ban and what it would look like in practice.

The county school board has introduced a new policy meant to set parameters for how AI is used in schools. The board is also looking to ban cell phones, smart watches and other electronic devices during the school day. The device ban is set to begin next school year. Bedell said the school system has students for 19.3% of the week, and that he wants that time devoted to teaching and learning, while students have the other 81% of the time to decide how to use their technology. He said the law calls for students to engage in collaboration while they are in school.

Bedell, who is leading the outreach, said he wants to avoid the sense that policies are imposed on people without their input. He noted that people often show up at school board meetings to say they did not know a policy was being drafted and had no chance to weigh in. He said he wanted to meet residents face to face in smaller settings to hear their thoughts directly. On AI, he said the goal is for students to become excellent users of the technology rather than being used by it, and that the conversations will help the district balance traditional schooling with preparing students for a world in which they will have to work with AI after graduation. He urged families to attend the remaining sessions, calling the topics highly controversial.

Six more sessions are planned, each from 6 to 8 p.m. The next is on Monday, November 2, at Glen Burnie High School, followed by Northeast High School on Thursday, November 5, and Arundel High School on Tuesday, November 10. Southern High School will host on Thursday, November 12, Annapolis High School on Tuesday, November 17, and Meade High School on Thursday, November 19. The articles do not say when the board will vote on the AI policy or what changes might follow from the feedback.

stories.Headline: China’s Lao Gan Ma Takes the Heat for Alleged Layoffs Due to AI
stories.Summary:
Chinese chili sauce maker Lao Gan Ma has come under heavy public criticism after remarks by one of its executives were read as evidence that artificial intelligence cost hundreds of workers their jobs. Li Xin, the company's executive vice general manager and chief quality officer, spoke about its AI-powered pepper inspection system at a provincial quality conference in Guizhou in late September. Media reports said he told the audience that the number of workers on one production line fell from more than 600 to just 48 after the system was introduced last year. He also said the company's 2025 revenue reached a record 5.4 billion yuan, about $810 million, and credited the technology with cutting production errors to almost zero. Li's full remarks are not available online, so the account rests on media reports.

The reaction on social media was swift. A hashtag about the dispute had drawn more than 120 million views on Weibo as of Wednesday, with some users calling for a boycott and threatening to have the company's products pulled from shelves. Other users defended automation as a normal part of industrial upgrading that improves efficiency and keeps quality consistent. The criticism was sharpened by the brand's image, since founder Tao Huabi, whose portrait appears on the jars, was herself a laid-off worker who sold cold rice noodles from a street stall before launching the brand in 1997. Jason Yu of CTR Market Research said people are not rejecting technology but a mindset that counts efficiency while ignoring people, and he said companies should explain how workers are supported through such transitions.

Lao Gan Ma has denied that mass layoffs took place. Human resources staff told domestic media on Oct. 26 that the claims were false, that Li had not cited staffing figures, and that the production line had never employed that many workers. The company did confirm that it uses AI inspection technology. Users then turned to corporate filings on the data platforms Tianyancha and Qichacha, which show the number of employees covered by social insurance falling from 2,912 in 2022 to 1,783 in 2023, then to 941 in 2024 and 740 in 2025, a drop of roughly 75% from nearly 3,000. The reports note that such figures do not prove AI caused job losses, since retirements, staff turnover, outsourcing and changes in the legal entity paying the insurance can also move them.

The row comes as China tries to promote AI while limiting its harm to employment. On Oct. 23, the State Council issued guidelines calling for AI to be used to create jobs and improve job quality while slowing the effects of AI-related job replacement. The guidelines urge companies to be cautious about deploying AI in labor-intensive industries, and they encourage employers to offer transition periods, advance notice before large rollouts, and retraining and help finding new work for displaced staff. The company's revenue has stayed steady, with the 2025 Guizhou Top 100 Enterprises ranking putting it at 5.26 billion yuan in 2022, 5.38 billion in 2023 and 5.39 billion in 2024. The articles do not say whether the company will release further details about its workforce.

stories.Headline: OpenAI updates Model Spec to reorganize it around five values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care (OpenAI)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI announced on October 29, 2026 that it has updated the Model Spec, its public description of how it wants its models to behave. The revision reorganizes the Spec's guidance around five underlying values: faithfulness to human intent, harm minimization, honesty and transparency, human agency, and care. OpenAI says the change reflects its work on value alignment, meaning models that can understand and apply human values in unfamiliar situations while staying faithful to human intent. The company frames this as increasingly important as its models get smarter and take more consequential actions in the world.

The update adds a new section on faithfulness to human intent, which treats what people value as primary and instructions as ordinarily the clearest signals of those values. That section includes an updated chain of command, which explains which instructions apply and how conflicts are resolved. A new subsection on considering context carefully explains how conversations, memories and other evidence should shape the model's reading of what people want. OpenAI also added defaults on supporting human agency and following relevant social norms, and expanded its existing guidance on controlling and communicating side effects. At the same time, it is retiring most of the detailed style guidance, saying style should adapt to what people prefer, while keeping stronger defaults such as approaching questions objectively.

The Spec also changes how it names the model, referring to "GPT" rather than "the assistant" because of the growing range of uses and deployment settings. Under the structure OpenAI describes, it writes the Spec, sets boundaries and trains models to respect them, developers direct applications within those boundaries, and users direct the model's work within those constraints. The guidance mostly takes the form of defaults that users and developers can override, with firm boundaries where needed to protect people and society. OpenAI published the update itself and invited readers to say which parts they find compelling, where they disagree with the balance it strikes, and what it overlooks or leaves unclear.

The company describes the update as one step in an ongoing effort to refine the Spec through research, experience deploying models, public feedback and discussions with users and outside experts. It acknowledges that the Spec describes the behavior it is working toward and that its models do not yet fully reflect it. Alongside the update, OpenAI says it has been exploring new training methods to help models learn the core values and understand why the Spec's behavioral principles matter, so they can apply them in new situations. It plans to share results and lessons from that training work in future updates, and says it will keep improving both the Spec and the models as it learns from research, real-world use and feedback.

stories.Headline: SK hynix reports 632% surge in Q3 profit due to AI-driven demand for memory chips
stories.Summary:
SK hynix, the South Korean memory chipmaker, reported on Wednesday that its operating profit for the July to September quarter rose 632 percent from a year earlier. The company said the increase was driven largely by the artificial intelligence industry's strong demand for its advanced memory chips. Operating profit for the period reached 83.33 trillion won, or about $62.8 billion. Net profit climbed 215.7 percent to 39.77 trillion won, and sales reached 104.61 trillion won. The firm said this marked record revenue and operating profit for six straight quarters.

The results fell short of market expectations, as analysts had estimated net profit at 59.67 trillion won, according to South Korea's Yonhap news agency citing its own data. SK hynix also announced an additional plan to return 60 trillion won to shareholders, following completion of a 40 trillion-won shareholder return programme. The company's shares have been under pressure since June, when they retreated from record highs, and have fallen nearly 60 percent from that peak according to one professor cited in the reporting. Investors have pushed for more cash returns through dividends or buybacks.

SK hynix supplies high-bandwidth memory chips to Nvidia and is a pillar of South Korea's tech-led economy. The company's statement attributed its growth to a cycle in which AI-driven productivity gains and new revenue in software development, customer service and search lead to greater AI adoption. Market research analyst MS Hwang of Counterpoint said long-term agreements with major customers signal another phase of price increases across conventional DRAM, NAND and HBM. Hwang added that quarterly earnings have not yet peaked and that the upward trend will likely continue at least through 2027.

Not all observers are as optimistic about the outlook. Hwang warned that weaker AI spending, increased competition and the company's own capacity expansion could drive price volatility heading into 2027, and named a pullback in cloud providers' orders as the most severe threat. Kim Dae-jong, a business professor at Sejong University, said investors appear to be pricing in concern that current earnings levels may not be sustainable one or two years out. The reporting notes that the global race to build AI data centres has transformed the company's fortunes, even as worries grow that the sector may be overvalued.

stories.Headline: VIDEO: AI boom creates jobs but threatens others, dividing Nevada unions
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is eliminating some jobs while creating others, according to a report published by Gray DC on October 28, 2026. Reporter Rhyan Henson wrote that nearly every industry has felt the effects of the technology. Goldman Sachs estimates that 300 million jobs will be affected by AI by 2030, with roles either transformed or erased. The article was filed under a headline pointing to divisions among Nevada unions, but the text itself covers the national picture and does not discuss Nevada or any union.

The changes are driving a growing need for human oversight of AI systems. Barry Jones, a vice president at X2X, an AI governance company, said people need to understand that human involvement is still required. He argued that there is not enough oversight right now and offered the example of an AI assistant preparing financial reports that might leak sensitive information outside a company. Jones also said that relying on companies to govern themselves is not enough, comparing it to the fox watching the henhouse, and called for a third party or even the government to set limits on what AI can do. He added that the private oversight work is creating roles even as technology replaces others, and he noted that Microsoft recently offered buyouts to 60,000 employees because of AI.

Lawmakers have taken differing positions on how much the federal government should do. Rep. Buddy Carter, a Republican from Georgia, said the country is generally better off when Washington stays out of the way and said he does not want to stifle innovation. He still acknowledged that AI is a very useful tool and that there are real dangers, saying lawmakers must get it right. Sen. Elizabeth Warren, a Democrat from Massachusetts, said the United States must address the serious risks posed by increasingly powerful AI systems, and that the American people should make those decisions through their elected representatives.

For workers considering a career change, Jones advised them to start learning AI and to understand how it applies to their own profession. He said judgment, experience, trust and accountability still matter, and that the aim should be to use the technology responsibly rather than compete with it. Efforts to regulate AI have stalled on Capitol Hill, according to the report. The 120th Congress could take up the issue when it returns in January.

stories.Headline: AI is part of solution for climate change, COP31 pledge says
stories.Summary:
Turkey, host of this year's UN COP31 climate summit, has launched a voluntary pledge saying artificial intelligence can help fight global warming even as data centers add to fossil-fuel pollution. The COP31 presidency released the document, called the Antalya AI Pledge, ahead of the summit, which runs from Nov. 9 to 20 in the coastal city of Antalya. It is the first time the environmental impact of data centers, which use large amounts of energy, has been explicitly addressed within the UN climate conference process. It is not clear which countries will sign up, and the United States, the biggest developer of data centers, is no longer part of the COP process.

The pledge invites governments, companies, investors, financial and research institutions, international organizations, local authorities and civil society groups to back AI that is sustainably powered, efficiently designed, transparently evaluated and accessible to all. Proposed measures include prioritizing low-emission energy and using efficient cooling systems in data centers, and countries, NGOs and financial institutions would identify their own voluntary commitments, such as requiring providers to disclose energy and environmental impact data and requiring data centers to run on clean power. The document also floats possible targets and calls for more resources for AI tools that could help cut emissions, adapt to climate change and build resilience. Supporters say AI could help optimize electrical grids, including by managing the intermittent nature of renewable energy, and could help drivers schedule electric vehicle charging for times when power comes from low-emission sources. The organizers stress that the commitments are non-binding, create no new obligations and must fit each signatory's national circumstances.

Evan Tachovsky, chief data and AI officer at the World Resources Institute, said the pledge raises both sides of AI's climate story and sets the right direction of travel, but lacks accountability mechanisms to steer countries and tech companies onto a better path. He said it needs concrete funding and strong safeguards behind it. Jill McArdle of the NGO Beyond Fossil Fuels said there is no compelling evidence that AI will deliver climate benefits, and she worried the pledge could become an environmental label that justifies the status quo. European Union Climate Commissioner Wopke Hoekstra said the pledge has some interesting characteristics and that the bloc is examining whether to sign up. The Turkish and Australian organizers of COP31 have said they are committed to promoting climate-responsible AI.

The pledge arrives as data centers emerge as a major new source of greenhouse gas emissions, particularly in the United States, where big tech companies are racing to bring them online by building new gas-fired power stations. BloombergNEF expects their share of global energy use to more than double by 2030. The UN has repeatedly warned that the world is on course to overshoot the Paris Agreement's 1.5 degrees Celsius limit, and Simon Stiell, executive secretary of the UN climate convention, said last month that AI is energy guzzling and that AI leaders are on thin ice. In June, UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called for the whole truth to be told about AI's climate implications. Countries are due to return to next year's summit in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to take stock of progress.

stories.Headline: 2 Warren Buffett Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks That Could Soar Even if the Stock Market Crashes in 2027
stories.Summary:
A Motley Fool article published on October 29, 2026, and written by analyst Adam Spatacco, argues that two stocks held by Berkshire Hathaway, Apple and Alphabet, could hold up well even if the stock market crashes in 2027. It points to two valuation gauges as signs of an expensive market. The Shiller cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio sits near 41, against a historical average of about 17, and the last time it stayed above 40 for long was during the dot-com bubble. The Buffett indicator, which compares the value of the U.S. stock market with gross domestic product, is around 230%, and Warren Buffett has warned that investors are in dangerous territory when it nears 200%.

On Apple, the article notes that Berkshire began building its stake in 2016 and that it remains the conglomerate's largest holding, even though Berkshire has trimmed it in recent years. In its fiscal third quarter, Apple brought in $109.4 billion in revenue, up 16% from a year earlier, with iPhone revenue rising 22% and Mac sales climbing 30%. The Services business, which covers the App Store, iCloud, Apple Music and Apple TV, produced $30.7 billion, up 12%. The article says subscriptions carry higher margins than hardware, which helps in uncertain times. It also cites an installed base of more than 2.5 billion active devices and more than 1.5 billion paid subscriptions, so Apple does not need to become a pure AI company to keep earning profits.

For Alphabet, the article says Berkshire built its position during 2025 and again this year. Google Search remains its most important asset, and AI features such as AI Overviews could raise engagement and give advertisers new ways to reach customers. The Gemini AI models are being added across Google Workspace and Android, which the author says may deepen customer loyalty and open more ways to earn money. Google Cloud rounds out the business, and the company designs its own Tensor Processing Units, which can help control AI infrastructure costs and give customers an alternative to Nvidia graphics chips.

The author concludes that both stocks would probably fall briefly in a broad crash, since no company is immune to valuation compression or economic weakness. Still, he says their businesses are far more diversified than those of companies relying almost entirely on AI adoption, and neither needs the AI boom to go perfectly to stay profitable. A stock quote shown on the Motley Fool page, as of 1:40 PM ET on October 29, had Alphabet down about 12.8% at $283.35 and Apple up about 1.7% at $349.69. The article also carries a disclosure that Spatacco holds positions in Alphabet and Nvidia, and that the Motley Fool holds positions in and recommends Alphabet, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway and Nvidia. A promotional note adds that the Motley Fool Stock Advisor team did not include Alphabet among its 10 best stocks to buy now.

stories.Headline: Princeton students, faculty divided over access to University ChatGPT accounts
stories.Summary:
Princeton University announced on Wednesday, in an email sent to all faculty and staff, that it will give every student, faculty member, and staff member access to ChatGPT Plus or Pro through a one-year pilot program with OpenAI. Faculty and staff could begin requesting access that same day, while students will be able to request ChatGPT Plus in January, before the spring semester begins. Before using their accounts, students must complete an online course called Foundations of AI Literacy, according to the Office of Information Technology's FAQ page. The Daily Princetonian reported that students and faculty are split over the move, with some worried about academic integrity and others seeing it as a way to keep pace with fast technological change.

University spokesperson Michael Hotchkiss said the contract is meant to provide enhanced data security and privacy protections as well as cost savings. He compared the arrangement to offering wireless access, saying the University does not endorse AI for any particular purpose in any circumstance. Princeton already offers a limited set of approved AI tools through University logins at no cost, including Adobe Creative Cloud Image Generation and the basic Microsoft 365 Copilot Chat. Faculty can also get Anthropic's Claude, Microsoft's 365 Copilot Premium, and Google's Gemini Workspace+ at varying monthly and annual rates.

Hotchkiss said a number of faculty with AI expertise were consulted about the pilot, and that more chances for faculty feedback are planned before it reaches students. Even so, several faculty members contacted by the paper said they had not known about the decision until the email arrived and were taken aback. Undergraduate Student Government Academics Chair Isaac Bernstein, class of 2028, said he spoke with faculty and administrators earlier this semester and sees his role as protecting student access and equity. He rejected the idea that the program harms academic integrity, noting that many students already use these tools.

Reactions were mixed. History professor Kevin Kruse sharply criticized the University's rush to embrace generative AI, arguing it undermines humanities teaching, wastes resources while programs like Outdoor Action are cancelled and faculty hiring is cut, and carries environmental costs from data centers. Neuroscience professor Sam Wang said he would have preferred a tool that detects AI use, such as Pangram, and student Krystal Ma, class of 2030, said the move feels like handing students an academic shortcut. Other students welcomed it, pointing to lower costs and to a Princetonian frosh survey in which nearly 90 percent of respondents had used ChatGPT or another AI model. Students also noted that peers offer similar tools, since Yale gives anyone with a Yale email free access to an OpenAI-powered chatbot called Clarity, while Harvard's Faculty of Arts and Sciences made Claude available last spring and phased out ChatGPT Edu because few students used it.

stories.Headline: Does Azure AI Growth Make Microsoft Stock a Hold Ahead of Q1 Earnings?
stories.Summary:
Microsoft was set to report its first-quarter fiscal 2027 results on October 28, 2026, and the two previews published that week focused on whether its AI push can deliver enough growth to justify the spending. Zacks Equity Research, in a piece dated October 27, said the quarter was likely driven by faster growth in Azure, its cloud platform, amid heavy AI use and ongoing capacity limits. GuruFocus, in an article from October 28, said shares traded at $530.37, down 0.18%, at 9:55 a.m. ET that morning. Zacks gives the stock a Rank of #3, or Hold.

The guidance Microsoft issued with its fourth-quarter fiscal 2026 results called for Azure and other cloud services revenue to grow about 45% in constant currency, up from 43% in the fourth quarter. Intelligent Cloud revenue was guided to between $40.95 billion and $41.25 billion, or 33% to 34% growth. Capital expenditure was expected to top $50 billion for the quarter, compared with $41 billion in the fourth quarter, including the effect of extending data center useful lives to 25 years. Cost of revenues was guided up 23% to 24%, and other income was expected to be roughly negative $100 million because of finance lease interest. Microsoft added 31 data centers and another gigawatt of capacity in the fourth quarter and remains on track to roughly double overall capacity in two years.

GuruFocus noted that a September reporting overhaul consolidated the business into two segments, Agents and Infra and Devices and Consumer. Management projected Agents and Infra revenue of $75.15 billion to $75.75 billion, against a restated $61.672 billion a year earlier, which puts midpoint growth at about 22.3%. Azure's separate target of 44% to 45% in constant currency covers a smaller business with revised boundaries, so the two growth rates cannot be treated as interchangeable. GuruFocus gives Microsoft a GF Score of 99 out of 100 and a price-to-earnings ratio of 29.56, and says its screen flags one severe warning sign without naming it. Zacks pointed to AI adoption signs, including Foundry reaching 100,000 customers, more than 30 million paid Microsoft 365 Copilot seats and 50 million GitHub Copilot users.

Responsibility for the numbers rests with Microsoft's management, which said on the prior call that customer demand still exceeded available supply and that growth in the first half of fiscal 2027 should keep accelerating. Zacks said the durability of AI-driven margins was the central open question, given the high capital spending, rising component costs and capacity limits. It also warned that capacity timing and contract mix could make Azure growth uneven, and that OpenAI-related contracts signed the year before could cause volatility in bookings. GuruFocus argued that Microsoft needs operating progress that earns its valuation, and that shifting revenue between segments will not do that job.

Zacks listed several moves during the quarter meant to strengthen Microsoft against Alphabet, Amazon and Oracle. These included general availability of OpenAI's GPT-5.6 series in Foundry in July, an expanded Mistral partnership announced July 21, and a new India South Central region in Hyderabad backed by a $20.5 billion India commitment. Microsoft also confirmed that its Saudi Arabia East region will open in November. The results due tonight will show whether Azure growth held near guidance and whether the spending is turning into stronger earnings and cash flow.

stories.Headline: Nvidia Stock Faces a Test From Its Biggest AI Chip Rival
stories.Summary:
Nvidia and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, known as TSMC, have both become major players in artificial intelligence, according to a Motley Fool analysis by Adria Cimino published on October 28, 2026. Nvidia designs the graphics processing units that handle major AI tasks, while TSMC manufactures those chips. Both companies have seen revenue climb sharply, and their stock prices have risen more than 400% and 300%, respectively, over three years. The article asks which of the two may be the bigger AI winner. It examines each business before weighing their prospects.

The article describes Nvidia as the market leader in GPUs, a position it attributes to starting work on AI roughly a decade ago and to its annual product updates. Its CUDA parallel computing platform and wide range of products give customers a reason to stay with it, and the author notes that this lock-in helps Nvidia charge premium prices. The company's gross margin consistently tops 70%, and in the most recent quarter its revenue jumped 106% to $96 billion. TSMC, by contrast, holds more than 70% of the pure foundry market according to Counterpoint Research, and it makes chips for most major players, including Advanced Micro Devices and Broadcom. Because TSMC benefits no matter which chip designer leads, the author calls it a rather safe AI stock.

The article's assessment is that both companies are likely to keep growing as AI moves into real-world use. TSMC reported its sixth straight quarter of record profit, with revenue of $46 billion for the period, and the author notes that its manufacturing overhead, including facilities and expensive equipment, adds costs that Nvidia does not carry. The author concludes that Nvidia's pricing power and market dominance may keep it a step ahead in growth in the coming years. The piece says both are likely to remain AI success stories, but it names Nvidia and its investors as the probable biggest winners. The article does not describe any specific regulatory action or future event that would change this outlook.
