stories.Headline: Navatar Brings Claude-Powered Recommendations and Actions to CRM for Private Equity and M&A Built on Salesforce
stories.Summary:
Navatar, a CRM provider for private equity and M&A firms built on Salesforce, announced on October 29, 2026 that it is bringing Claude, the AI model from Anthropic, into the daily work of its users. The announcement, distributed through GlobeNewswire, says Claude can now recommend next steps inside Navatar and carry out work that users start there, with results returned directly to the product. Navatar also said it will show work done through Claude or Outlook against the relevant deal or relationship, so colleagues can follow developments without digging through individual fields. The release builds on Navatar's earlier bidirectional Salesforce Model Context Protocol connectivity, which let people working in Claude retrieve updated Navatar information and send selected research back into CRM.

The new capabilities let professionals start inside Navatar, receive Claude-generated action suggestions, and process work through Claude without opening a separate conversation in the Claude interface. Routing an action through Claude does not automatically write results into the CRM. Users can verify returned information and choose which content to apply to which fields. Navatar also extended its Salesforce connectivity to information stored in supported documents, which broadens the context available beyond structured CRM fields. Navatar says the Claude-native deal engine is available now to private markets firms, and it directs interested firms to book a demo through its website.

Navatar's stated aim is to connect AI assistance with ongoing origination and execution so professionals do not have to leave the deal environment to decide what to do next. The company describes its platform as serving private markets and investment banking firms, including corporate finance advisors, M&A firms, private equity, venture capital, private credit, and real estate, infrastructure, and secondaries investors. The announcement is a company press release, and the articles do not include independent assessments of how the features perform in practice. A related HubSpot guide, published the same week, describes a similar pattern of connecting Claude to CRM data for sales tasks such as prospecting, call preparation, and pipeline reviews, though it concerns HubSpot's own product.

stories.Headline: Tracking AI adoption in North Korean threat actor tradecraft
stories.Summary:
Microsoft Threat Intelligence reports that North Korean threat actors are expanding their use of generative and agentic AI across their operations, with varying levels of adoption. Jade Sleet launched campaigns through three front companies in a single week, Onyx Sleet produced dozens of tailored lures in minutes, and Coral Sleet quickly built a capability to trojanize private source code repositories. Onyx Sleet and Pearl Sleet have also used the open-source agentic AI penetration testing framework ARTEX in their operations. Microsoft says these operations remain human-directed and have not become fully autonomous.

The adoption is assessed across four stages: emerging, expanding, accelerating, and operationalized. Jade Sleet, Coral Sleet, and Jasper Sleet are rated as operationalized, meaning AI is built into their routine workflows across entire operations. Diamond Sleet, Onyx Sleet, Pearl Sleet, and Sapphire Sleet are rated as accelerating, and Emerald Sleet is rated as expanding. Microsoft has not assessed any North Korean actor as merely emerging. The report also observes that the use of AI supports existing goals, such as revenue generation for the regime and intelligence collection, rather than marking a change in motivation.

The main uses include reconnaissance on target organizations, research into cryptocurrency and blockchain workflows, and the creation of fake digital personas for job-themed social engineering. Microsoft describes a June 8 to June 12, 2026 campaign in which Jade Sleet posed as recruiters for a spoofed AI-powered blockchain intelligence company using tailored domains and social media profiles. Jasper Sleet is described as using AI-assisted resume workflows to scale fake personas, and Diamond Sleet has returned to targeting the oil and gas sector since August 2026 while building fake communications technology companies. Microsoft notes that these shifts suggest AI is improving the efficiency of existing workflows.

A Seoul Economic Daily editorial, dated October 28, 2026, links the threat to a separate wave of suspected North Korean hacking against South Korea. It reports more than 4.4 million attempts to access South Korean financial firms from North Korean IP addresses, following a banking sector breach earlier that month. The editorial argues that individual companies cannot stop sweeping attacks alone and that the response should be framed as a national security matter. It calls for chief executives to take responsibility for security reviews and for the government to reorganize its cybersecurity response around a central control tower. The editorial also states that the lazarus group quickly tried to exploit a PHP vulnerability once it was found.

stories.Headline: AI's data problem is governance in disguise
stories.Summary:
A Workiva survey of Australian finance, risk and sustainability leaders, published as the 2026 Midyear Executive Benchmark Survey, found that 95 per cent of respondents want AI to deliver measurable return on investment within the next year. The article's author, writing for IT Brief Australia on 29 October 2026, says that timeline is ambitious for reporting work, where accuracy and accountability are essential. The survey also found that only 14 per cent of executives said their organisation's data quality was sufficient for AI use in reporting, while 21 per cent said data quality problems had significantly limited their use of AI and blocked deployment in key workflows. A further 44 per cent said they had worked around these issues, though the author notes this slowed progress.

The author argues that these results point to a governance problem rather than a purely data problem. Where the same figure lives in several spreadsheets, a slide deck and an email thread, AI does not fix the inconsistency but spreads it faster and at greater scale, with a confidence that makes errors harder to detect. The survey also found that 79 per cent of respondents were at least somewhat confident in AI outputs without human review, which the author sees as a risk. The article says the gap calls for connected and controlled data infrastructure, built on three elements: a single source of truth, clear control over ownership, permissions and version history, and lineage built in so any figure can be traced to its source. It also says that 39 per cent of Australian executives reported that their most recent AI audit found data lineage gaps or traceability issues.

The article stresses that traceability matters because financial statements, board papers and sustainability disclosures, including the mandatory climate reporting now phasing in across Australia, must withstand auditors, regulators and investors. The author suggests that an AI process that cannot be audited turns a productivity gain into a liability. The 21 per cent of respondents who said they were blocked are described as being in a safer position than those who have normalised manual workarounds, which the author says erode traceability over time. The author proposes a simple test: take one AI-assisted figure from the last board report and try to trace it to its source, and if that takes days or depends on one person's memory, the organisation is not yet AI-ready.

stories.Headline: Google Shares Tumble 10% as a $51bn AI Bill Pushes Cash Flow Into the Red
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, saw its shares fall about 10% after it reported its third-quarter results. The company had spent $51.4bn on capital expenditure in the quarter, more than double the $24bn it spent a year earlier, which pushed its free cash flow to minus $9.1bn. That was deeper in the red than the minus $5.9bn of the previous quarter, according to a report in Fortune cited by European Business Magazine. The Financial Times reported the same drop, linking it to the outlay on artificial intelligence.

The spending is aimed at building out the computing capacity needed for AI, and its effect on cash is the source of investor concern. Alphabet kept its 2026 spending plans unchanged but signalled a significant increase for 2027, CNBC reported. To fund the build-out, the company raised $84.8bn in new equity in June, including $10bn from Berkshire Hathaway. Revenue rose 25% to $127.6bn, and Google Cloud, which sells AI computing to other businesses, brought in $30.7bn, but the cash position has weakened.

Chief executive Sundar Pichai described the cloud business as accelerating, with revenue growing 48% to an annual run rate of more than $70 billion. Investors, according to the coverage, are now focused less on whether AI demand exists and more on whether the spending can eventually pay for itself. Earnings per share fell to $2.12 from $2.87, partly because of an $8.7bn paper loss on equity investments, and adjusted earnings still missed expectations. Microsoft, which reported on the same evening, was rewarded by the market, as it spent less, remained cash-positive with $18.6bn of free cash flow, and was also cutting costs.

The episode is part of a wider pattern in which large technology companies are spending heavily on AI and raising outside money to do so. Meta is committing up to $145bn this year and selling $35bn of shares, and Amazon has sold its AI chips and rented them back. European Business Magazine also cited ECB economists warning that the AI-fuelled stock boom is heading for a correction, with US borrowing costs near 5% making data centre spending more expensive. Coverage suggests the next few quarters will show whether Alphabet's spending turns into profit, with the shares likely to remain volatile until it does.

stories.Headline: Fathom Launches Bipartisan Group of Former Governors, National Security Leaders, and AI Experts to Advance Independent AI Oversight
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Fathom, an independent nonprofit based in San Francisco, announced a new Executive Council made up of former governors from both parties, national security leaders, technology executives, and AI experts. The council is meant to guide Fathom's work on independent verification organizations, a framework in which government-licensed experts evaluate AI models and systems against public standards. Fathom developed that framework and sponsored California's SB 813, which was signed into law in September and created the nation's first such framework. The organization is also backing the bipartisan FRONTIER Act, led by U.S. Representatives Lori Trahan and Jay Obernolte, which would make independent verification a core pillar of federal AI oversight. Fathom's chief executive, Andrew Freedman, said the work requires a broad, cross-partisan approach that spans sectors and borders.

The council's members include Michèle Flournoy, Stephen E. Biegun, Douglas Beck, Jack Shanahan, Steve Bullock, Brian Sandoval, John Giannandrea, Gillian Hadfield, Geoffrey Irving, and Peter L. Levin, with James Adams serving as secretary. Several members argued that AI is a national security matter, that governance must hold up across administrations, and that independent testing is essential before public adoption. Others, including former governors Bullock and Sandoval, said states will play a major role in regulating AI and need policies they can implement and confidence in the technology. Geoffrey Irving warned that AI companies are advancing toward superintelligent systems faster than safety research, and said policy must cover risks that technical measures do not reach. Peter Levin stressed that agencies must know who qualifies to conduct testing, which benchmarks apply, and what happens when a system fails.

In a separate development, on October 27, 2026, Rwandan President Paul Kagame appointed three senior officials to lead operations, delivery, and strategy and partnerships at the National Artificial Intelligence Agency. The appointments followed the Cabinet's June 8 approval to establish the agency to coordinate AI development and adoption. Olivier Twagirayezu was named Chief Operations Officer, Jessica Ingabire became Chief Delivery Officer, and Robert Kayinamura was named Chief Strategy and Partnerships Officer. The agency's mandate covers government transformation, research, skills, AI ethics and safety, industry development, and international partnerships, and it builds on Rwanda's National AI Policy adopted in 2023. Reports indicate the agency will also coordinate AI initiatives, improve access to AI-ready data and computing infrastructure, and support the growth of Rwanda's AI industry.

stories.Headline: Job concerns rise as AI-generated actors take roles
stories.Summary:
AI-generated actors are moving from online short dramas into advertising and other commercial work in China, offering production teams a cheaper and more controllable option than human performers. Li Xiaolong, a young actor and student at the Shanghai Theatre Academy who stars in the short play My Dual Control, said this shift could further narrow job opportunities for human actors as productions face tighter budgets. He recounted that a friend in Hengdian, Zhejiang province, a major film and television hub, reported fewer actors working there, with some leaving the profession or taking costumed jobs at tourist sites. Li described the account as anecdotal, but it reflects the uncertainty some performers feel.

AI performers let producers control expressions and movements through text instructions, and they generally cost less than human actors, Li said. Producers can also revise scenes by changing prompts, which reduces the need for repeated filming. Actors without a strong personal following find work harder to get, and Li said even day-rate jobs that once paid more than 1,000 yuan ($150) have become difficult to secure. Despite these pressures, he believes human performance keeps qualities AI has not fully matched, such as the slow building of a character through research and emotional exploration. Some viewers, he noted, still prefer the realism and nuance of human acting.

The commercial rise of AI actors is visible in Fang Taozi, an AI-generated actress whose recognizable look and growing following have made her a fixture of AI short dramas. Her breakout role in The Laid-off Girl, which debuted on Douyin on June 12, brought her to a wider audience, and her Douyin account had more than 510,000 followers by August 25. On August 27, fashion magazine Cosmo Crush previewed her on its official Weibo account. Rates listed for her on Douyin's Xingtu influencer marketing platform have reportedly ranged from 168,000 yuan for videos up to 20 seconds to 258,000 yuan for videos longer than 60 seconds, though the articles caution that listed rates may not reflect actual transaction values.

Industry figures cited in the reporting suggest the economics are attractive, with some reports putting AI short drama costs at around 80,000 yuan per minute, depending on complexity and methods. The DataEye Research Institute estimated that China's AI short drama market, including animated dramas, could exceed 40 billion yuan in 2026, up about 138 percent year on year, after passing 22 billion yuan in the first five months. Hou Wenjie, secretary-general of the Shanghai-based Yu Ce Think Tank, argued that AI actors have moved past proof of concept into real monetization. He pointed to Fang's independent account, which posts everyday lifestyle content and recreates the companionship audiences associate with human influencers. The articles stress that these market figures cover AI short dramas broadly and are industry estimates, not official statistics.

Hou said AI actors offer brands greater control, predictable scheduling and fewer risks tied to personal scandals, and he expects AI characters to expand into lifestyle content and longer-term brand partnerships. He also called for more attention to labeling of virtual-person advertising, likeness rights and content authenticity. The articles note that popularity does not guarantee lasting value, and the reported removal of an advertisement featuring Fang over concerns that its claims could mislead consumers shows the risks. Questions about whether AI characters resemble existing performers too closely are also likely to grow as the technology improves. Li expects stage work to be less affected than screen work, and he anticipates closer integration of AI and human actors as the technology develops.

stories.Headline: Billionaire Bill Gates Just Issued a Blunt Warning About Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Bill Gates, the Microsoft co-founder, has issued a blunt warning about artificial intelligence in recent interviews. In a TV interview in late September, he said that if AI remains unregulated it could lead to "a billion deaths," and that self-regulation is unlikely to be enough. He urged politicians and law enforcement to start planning what safeguards and monitoring should look like, arguing that even a "kill switch" might not be sufficient. Gates later appeared on the "Decoder" podcast, where his tone was more optimistic about AI's potential to create "true abundance," though he still spoke bluntly about the risks.

The main worry Gates raised on the podcast is a difficult 20-year transition period marked by winners, losers and significant disruption. He expects AI to eliminate many jobs in areas such as telesupport and accounting because it can perform them faster, cheaper and more efficiently, and he said blue-collar work could face pressure from humanoid robots. He warned that without a choice to slow down or stop, robots could build houses, grow food and perform surgery, leaving little economic role for human labor in most goods and services. The articles note that many others share the view that AI will be deflationary and solve inefficiencies, but they also raise the question of what work will remain for people and how they will earn money.

Gates is not the only prominent voice raising alarms. The articles mention Jacob Coxon, a former AI researcher at OpenAI and Anthropic, who resigned from Anthropic earlier this year and wrote on social media that he believes there is a greater-than-10% chance AI will eliminate all humans. Critics dismissed Coxon's post as cultlike, but the articles say Gates is harder to dismiss given his long experience with technological change. Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has also issued similar warnings while his company continues to develop large language models. The article's author, Bram Berkowitz, writes that because there have been enough incidents involving AI agents and warnings from prominent figures, these concerns should be taken seriously, though no one can say for certain what will happen over the next two decades.

stories.Headline: Hochul signing bills regulating AI chats with kids and hackable baby monitors
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed two bills on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, that regulate artificial intelligence chatbots aimed at children and internet-connected baby monitors. The first bill requires monitors sold in New York to include security features that stop strangers from watching or listening in, and to carry a clear warning label. The second bans what the state calls unsafe chatbot features for minors, including bots that pretend to be human, encourage self-harm or have inappropriate conversations with children. Hochul announced the signing at a news conference in New York City. The governor's office said the measures build on earlier state actions, including the RAISE Act, a ban on AI-generated sexual abuse material, and the Safe by Design and Safe for Kids acts.

The baby monitor law, listed as S.9508/A.5175A, also requires labeling that explains the devices connect to the internet and urges users to turn on their safety features. It takes effect in 90 days, and the article notes that studies have found many such monitors have weak security and can be easily hacked. The chatbot law, S.9051B/A.10379C, bars companies from offering users under 18 features that claim to be a real person, claim a romantic, professional or authority-figure bond with a child, or use flattery to keep kids engaged. It also prohibits features that promote suicide, self-harm, eating disorders or drug and alcohol use, push children to keep secrets or avoid seeking help from adults, or offer sexually explicit content. The law includes age verification, with at least one option that does not require a government ID, and the state attorney general will enforce it, with civil penalties of up to $25,000.

Hochul said New York leads the nation on protecting children online, and described herself as the state's mom Governor. She said no company should be selling chatbots that encourage self-harm or pose as a child's friend, and that no new parent should fear hackers spying through a monitor. Attorney General Letitia James said the chatbot law sets clear legal limits to prevent harm, and that her office will keep working with government partners while allowing for safe, responsible innovation. State Senator Andrew Gounardes, who backed the monitor bill, said the devices should help parents rather than let outsiders into their homes. Common Sense Media CEO James P. Steyer called it the strongest kids' AI safety bill in the country and described dangerous chatbot features as reckless endangerment of children.

The governor's office cited Common Sense Media research showing that more than 70% of teenagers have used an AI companion at least once, and 52% use them several times a month. It also said chatbots have been linked to dependency, isolation and sexually explicit conversations, and have allegedly encouraged teens to take their own lives. New York enacted the Safe by Design Act earlier this year, which restricts unknown adults from contacting children on digital platforms and gives the attorney general enforcement power. Two years ago the state passed laws barring social media companies from collecting children's personal data and from using addictive feeds on young users, putting it in line with California's 2022 legislation. The chatbot law is set to be implemented this year, and the baby monitor requirements will begin once the 90-day period ends.

stories.Headline: Pate McMichael discusses AI’s impact on election advertisements on WFAE’s Charlotte Talks
stories.Summary:
The most recent article here reports that Pate McMichael, director of the North Carolina Open Government Coalition and an instructor of journalism at Elon University, joined WFAE's Charlotte Talks for an Oct. 27 episode titled "Artificial Intelligence in Elections." The program looked at concerns about AI-generated campaign advertisements, deepfakes and misleading content that could sway voters before the 2026 midterm elections. Host Mike Collins led the discussion, which focused on how artificial intelligence is growing in influence across political campaigns. The article was published Oct. 28, 2026, and it is the only source provided for this account.

McMichael argued that political ads are supposed to inform voters, and that the Supreme Court's rulings on campaign spending were premised on the idea that voters need more information. He said many of these ads leave viewers doubting whether claims are accurate, and that people increasingly want more transparency around them. The discussion also covered regulation: the article says 31 states have enacted some form of rules governing AI in political campaigns, while North Carolina has not adopted similar legislation despite several attempts by state lawmakers. One common requirement, according to the article, is disclosure when an ad uses AI. McMichael pointed to Alabama, Florida, Tennessee and Texas as states that require such disclosures, though he noted they are written differently from one another.

McMichael also said voters need to know who is paying for ads, since the article describes weak transparency around funding for online and social media advertising. He asked why lawmakers would not require disclosure if transparency is the goal, and he suggested that voters deserve more insight into how an ad was made and who funded it. The article does not attribute any specific legislative proposal to him beyond those comments. Other participants in the conversation were Michael Bitzer, professor of politics and history at Catawba College, and Scott Brennan, director of New York University's Center on Technology Policy, who joined to discuss emerging technology, political communication and election integrity. The article notes that the full conversation is available online.

stories.Headline: Fact Sheet: President Donald J. Trump Ended the Illegal and Discriminatory Practices of Diversity, Equity, and Inclusion
stories.Summary:
The White House published a fact sheet on October 28, 2026, saying that President Donald J. Trump has removed what it calls wasteful and unmeritocratic diversity, equity, and inclusion programs from government, education, and the private sector. The document claims that on his first day back in office, Trump rescinded orders from the previous administration and signed an executive order ending DEI programs and preferences in the federal government. It describes a long series of follow-on actions across 2025 and 2026, including orders targeting federal contracting, the armed forces, the Foreign Service, the Department of Education, the Smithsonian, higher education accreditation, school discipline, and disparate-impact liability. The fact sheet lists these as the administration's work, and the articles provided do not independently confirm the claimed results.

The fact sheet describes several specific measures and settlements. It cites a $221 million settlement with Columbia University in July 2025, a $50 million settlement with Brown University that same month, and a $60 million settlement with Cornell University and a $75 million settlement with Northwestern University in November 2025. It also says the administration paused $210 million in federal funding to Princeton and launched a review of $9 billion in federal funding for Harvard University. The document further reports that the Department of Health and Human Services froze over $100 million in funding to Duke University's medical school, and that the Small Business Administration ended race-based criteria in its 8(a) Business Development Program. Each of these is presented as an action taken by the administration, with the stated reasons attached.

The fact sheet is attributed to the White House, and its content is written from the administration's point of view. It states that the actions were taken to restore merit, fairness, and equal treatment under the law, and it characterizes DEI programs as illegal, discriminatory, or ideologically driven. Several universities, companies, and agencies are described as having changed their policies in response, including the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, which closed its DEI office, and about 90 percent of the top 400 S&P 500 companies, which cut at least some references to DEI through March 2025. The provided articles do not describe responses from the institutions named, nor do they include independent assessments of the claims or outcomes.

stories.Headline: CWRU law student’s AI innovation leads to summit invitation
stories.Summary:
Case Western Reserve University School of Law, the first in the country to require artificial intelligence in its first-year curriculum, has also asked every 1L student to design and build a legal technology solution. Second-year student Jamie Werner, who was among the first to complete the required AI training last year, was invited to the Thomson Reuters-Wickard Judicial AI Summit on Courts, Technology and the Future of Justice. The invitation followed the creation of his platform for tracking local court rules and judges' standing orders, which also offers background on judges, including their recent opinions and professional biographies. Oliver Roberts, founder and CEO of Wickard.ai, a legal AI education and consulting company that helped develop the school's curriculum, extended the invitation. The article reports that the invitation-only summit was held in New York City in October.

The summit gathered judges, academics, government officials and legal technology leaders for a national discussion about AI and the court system. Roberts said the event was organized to have a practical conversation about how AI is affecting courts and how the judiciary can respond responsibly. For Werner, the gathering showed why the legal profession needs preparation for a technology that is rapidly changing how lawyers work. He said that AI use will keep growing as the technology improves and that judges should learn about it even if they do not use it in their own work. The summit also drew attention to the role law schools play in readying students for an AI-enabled field.

Jennifer Cupar, the law school's associate dean for academic affairs, attended the summit and said law schools prepare future lawyers to use AI thoughtfully, ethically and effectively. She added that schools help students build the judgment needed to ensure these technologies strengthen the administration of justice. Matt Salerno, associate professor of lawyering skills and co-director of the Legal Writing, Leadership, Experiential Learning, Advocacy and Professionalism program, has said the required exercises give first-year students early practice with essential skills. According to the article, these exercises also help students form informed judgment about the technology that is changing legal practice. The article does not report any further events or plans following the summit.

stories.Headline: Dartmouth provost resigns following accusations he used artificial intelligence for writing
stories.Summary:
Dartmouth College's provost, Santiago Schnell, has resigned after a faculty committee concluded that he used artificial intelligence to shape his writing. The announcement came on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and the investigation followed reports from the news outlet Semafor, which ran guest columns from major newspapers through an AI filter. One of the flagged pieces was Schnell's August column in The Washington Post about AI cheating, which the filter found was entirely AI-written. The episode arrives as colleges across the country struggle to adapt teaching to assignments that AI tools can complete.

Schnell had told The Dartmouth, the student newspaper, that he uses AI for language refinement, copyediting, and improving clarity. In a follow-up statement, he said he developed the substance and wrote a draft of an email before using an AI tool to help with language and clarity. The faculty committee nonetheless found that he used AI to meaningfully alter his writing and was not forthcoming about it. Writing that predated ChatGPT's public release in 2022 was judged human-written, while his recent writing showed high rates of AI use. Schnell has referred questions to his attorneys, who had not responded to requests for comment.

University President Sian Leah Beilock said in a written statement that Dartmouth must lead through a fast-changing environment, and she stressed the need for leaders to model the transparency and human judgment expected of students and scholars. She described Schnell's departure as his own decision and said the school wishes him well. Schnell, a Venezuelan-born mathematical biologist, previously held teaching and leadership roles at the University of Notre Dame, the University of Michigan, and Indiana University, according to his LinkedIn profile. The timing also matters because Dartmouth promotes itself as the birthplace of AI, a claim tied to a 1956 summer research project on the subject in Hanover, New Hampshire. A conference marking the field's 70th anniversary, titled "What Must Remain Human?", began the Thursday after the announcement.

stories.Headline: One Tech Tip: How to get started with AI agents, and which are best for specific tasks
stories.Summary:
Agentic artificial intelligence is gaining popularity well beyond the tech industry, as companies such as Meta, OpenAI, and Anthropic compete to sell consumer-friendly AI agents. These agents are built to act proactively on a user's behalf, handling tasks like buying groceries or managing to-do lists, and they surged this year after the leading AI labs had offered agentic tools for years. Many people find it hard to tell how the companies' offerings differ or which agent suits a given job. The agents also raise a question about privacy, since they tend to perform better the more they know about a person.

Experts advise people who are starting out to use several agents rather than relying on one. Jose Artigas, a business consultant who works on AI strategy, said there is no single agent that can do everything, so he and others use a "stack" of tools from different labs. Access varies, with some agents free, some requiring a monthly subscription, and some still in testing or unavailable outside the United States. Clara Gigling, founder of Oudae Labs, described pairing agents so that one does the work while another critiques it, which she said helps catch mistakes. The article stresses that users should experiment to find what works for them.

Each company markets its agent with a different focus. Anthropic said its Claude Duet was built for professionals and small business owners, while Meta said its Muse can help with saving money, improving health, and shopping. Claude Duet, OpenAI's Dots, and xAI's Grok Bot have been described as colleague-like, and Muse and Instinct from the startup Spear Street Technology as more like personal assistants. Artigas suggested Claude Duet for a side hustle or new business, Dots for specialized technical work, and Instinct for tedious emails or booking travel. He recommended Muse as a starting point for beginners because it is user-friendly and offers prompts.

Experts say that deciding which agents to use and which tasks to hand them requires trial and error. Gigling suggested thinking about recurring tasks and delegating some of them, while being specific about goals, context, and tools. Artigas advised starting with one annoying, repeated online task, such as a long email or a flight booking, since an agent cannot fold laundry or organize a drawer. Effective agents need access to a lot of personal data, including inboxes, calendars, identification, and financial details, which has raised privacy concerns. Gigling urged users to stay curious but mindful about sharing private information, and the article notes that companies have published privacy policies describing how agents run on dedicated cloud computers and how users can control memory retention.

stories.Headline: DJI Strengthens Multi-Layer Privacy Protection System with the Launch of Local Data Mode for ROMO, Setting a New Standard for Privacy in Home Robotics
stories.Summary:
DJI announced on October 29, 2026, a feature called Local Data Mode for its ROMO 2 robot vacuum, which it says is an industry first for smart home products. When the mode is turned on, the DJI Home app is disconnected from the internet, and the robot's maps, images and other navigation data are stored and processed on the device rather than in the cloud. The feature is available starting that day for ROMO 2 through a firmware update, and users enable it under Security Settings in the Device Settings section of the app. DJI says the feature will also come to future ROMO models, and that it first pioneered the approach for its drones in 2017.

With Local Data Mode active, ROMO continues to navigate, avoid obstacles, start and customize cleaning cycles and return to its dock while offline, even during network outages. The company describes this as part of a broader multi-layer privacy system that includes passcode or one-time-code access, opt-in consent for data collection from the camera, voice, obstacle recognition and Wi-Fi functions, and an On-Site Photo setting that users can turn off without affecting obstacle avoidance. Other safeguards include end-to-end encryption during transmission, no uploads of data while offline, automatic deletion of photos older than 14 days when auto-delete is enabled, and a factory reset that permanently erases device data. ROMO also now supports Matter, allowing integration with platforms such as Apple Home, Google Home, Amazon Alexa, SmartThings and Home Assistant, though available features depend on each platform.

DJI states that ROMO devices and the DJI Home app are certified to the ETSI EN 303 645 standard, meet EU RED (EN 18031) requirements, and hold UL Solutions Diamond IoT Security certification. The company also says TV SD performed a penetration test of the ROMO P2 and the app in 2026 and found no critical, high or medium-risk issues, and that DJI holds BSI certifications to ISO 27701:2025 and ISO 27001:2026. These claims come from DJI's own press release, which was distributed through PR Newswire and republished on australiannews.net, and the articles do not include independent verification beyond the cited certifications. The release also notes that the feature will extend to future models, though no dates for those are given.

stories.Headline: Artificial intelligence use doubles in rural Nebraska, poll shows
stories.Summary:
Fifty-five percent of rural Nebraskans surveyed have now used some form of artificial intelligence tool, up from 27 percent when the 2026 Nebraska Rural Poll first asked about AI in 2024. The results, released on October 28, 2026, show a sharp rise in use, though many respondents remain doubtful about how reliable these tools are. Use varies by group, with at least three-quarters of residents ages 19 to 39 reporting they have used AI, compared with just 23 percent of those 65 and older. People with higher education levels or household incomes, along with women, were also more likely to have used the tools. The poll was conducted annually by Rural Prosperity Nebraska with funding from Nebraska Extension.

Heather Akin, an associate professor of agricultural and environmental sciences communication at the University of Nebraska–Lincoln, said the growth shows AI is becoming part of everyday life for many rural residents. She said rural people should have chances to explore what AI can do, understand its limits and decide when to use it. Akin added that building access to AI and related literacy would help Nebraskans prepare for a technology that continues to change. Her comments were part of the poll report released by the university.

Although most respondents have used AI tools, few use them to learn about specific topics. Just over one in 10 said they often or frequently use generative AI to learn about education and skill development (16 percent), topics affecting them or their family (14 percent), and science and technology (12 percent). Respondents also expressed interest in learning more about AI, with 45 percent somewhat or extremely interested in how to protect their privacy, 36 percent in how to evaluate response accuracy, 33 percent in how bias can occur, and 28 percent in using it ethically. Mary Emery, director of Rural Prosperity Nebraska, said the interest in privacy, accuracy and bias shows residents want to use AI responsibly, not just understand what it can do.

Emery said accessible learning opportunities could help Nebraskans build confidence in these tools and make informed choices about when and how to use them. The full "Artificial Intelligence" report will be highlighted in a Rural Poll webinar at noon Central Time on November 18, and the full report is available on the Nebraska Rural Poll website. The 2026 poll marks the 31st year of tracking rural Nebraskans' views on policy and quality of life, and it is described as the largest and longest-running poll of its kind. Questionnaires were mailed in April and May to nearly 6,900 households, and 881 households from 86 of the state's 93 counties responded, with a margin of error of plus or minus 3 percent.

stories.Headline: Malaysia seizes servers with advanced AI chips suspected of violating export controls
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's customs department said it had seized 30 servers fitted with advanced artificial intelligence chips in a suspected breach of export controls. The servers were intercepted on October 15 in the free trade zone at the country's main airport during an inspection. Officials believe a syndicate is using Malaysia as a transit point to send the chips on to another Asian country. The shipment is valued at about 50 million ringgit, or $12.2 million.

Malaysia introduced permit requirements last year for the export, transit and transshipment of high-performance AI chips of U.S. origin. The rules followed pressure from Washington, which wants to keep sensitive technology from reaching China through third countries. Officials say the servers came from an Asian country and were falsely declared as electric components to avoid detection. They were then to be re-exported to another Asian country without the permit that was required. Customs said the case reflects an effort to avoid restrictions while the equipment moves onward.

The customs director at the airport, Aspalila Ag Tuah, said the shipment appears linked to a syndicate behind five attempted smuggling operations. One of those earlier operations took place in June, when customs seized 72 servers containing advanced AI chips at the same free trade zone. A Malaysian company that helped arrange the shipment has been asked to assist the investigation. Aspalila declined to say where the chips originated or where they were ultimately headed, saying the case was still under investigation.

Washington has sought to limit China's access to advanced semiconductors in order to curb Beijing's artificial intelligence and military capabilities. The articles do not say whether any charges have been filed or whether the investigation has reached a conclusion. They also do not identify the syndicate or the companies involved beyond the Malaysian firm that facilitated the shipment. Further details about the origin and destination of the chips remain unreleased while the probe continues.

stories.Headline: How to set guidelines for using AI in the classroom | Annie Chestnut Tutor and Jonathan Butcher
stories.Summary:
Teachers across the country are trying to guide how students use artificial intelligence, but the authors argue that clearer boundaries are badly needed. The column, written by Annie Chestnut Tutor and Jonathan Butcher, was published in Elko Daily Free Press and the Quad-City Times in late October 2026. It notes that the Heritage Foundation, where both authors work, has found that many school districts still lack a clear policy on AI use. Schools are only beginning to set rules for student use, and some teachers say they have no guidance at all.

The authors point to a survey in which many teachers reported that their districts had not yet written policies on AI, and they cite a case where a school district's AI rules left students and families unsure what was allowed. They describe the need for guidelines that cover when students may use AI for assignments, how to cite AI-generated work, and how to protect student data. They also say that some schools have adopted AI tools for lesson planning and that those tools raise questions about accuracy and privacy. The column suggests that policies should separate acceptable uses from prohibited ones so that teachers and students know where the lines are.

The authors place responsibility on school boards, district administrators, and state education departments, which they say should set clear rules and publish them. They argue that teachers should not be left to decide these questions alone, and that the people who set policy should be accountable for the rules they adopt. The authors do not claim that schools are acting in bad faith, but they say that good intentions are not enough without written standards. Their central recommendation is that policymakers act soon rather than waiting for problems to appear.

The column places the debate within a larger discussion about how AI is changing education, and it notes that several states and districts have begun drafting guidance. The authors suggest that such guidance should be reviewed regularly because the technology is changing quickly. The article does not describe specific deadlines or enforcement steps. It ends by urging parents, educators, and local leaders to press their districts to write and publish AI guidelines for classrooms.

stories.Headline: Ahead of US midterms, ChatGPT draws images "depicting election interference or that may discourage voting" in a cartoon style, ignoring photorealism requests (Katelyn Chedraoui/CNET)
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has set up an election "war room" ahead of the US midterms, which it said it would run starting the week of the vote and continuing until all ballots are counted. The company calls it the Election Operations Center, and it is meant to spot the spread of misinformation and other attempts to disrupt the elections. The center will monitor real-time events and take in reports of unexpected model behavior or suspected violations of OpenAI's terms. Its focus is largely on abuse of the company's own tools, such as ChatGPT. The announcement came via an exclusive to Politico's Decoded newsletter.

Josh Lawson, OpenAI's head of civic and strategic risk, is leading the center. He told Politico the company has put considerable effort into helping users get reliable voting information and combating misuse of its tools. He described the center as building on years of similar work, bringing teams together to respond quickly to emerging issues as people head to the polls. Politico reported that the company is bringing hundreds of employees together for the effort. OpenAI, in other words, is presenting itself as a defender of the democratic process.

The move comes amid broader worries that AI could distort the midterms through misleading images, audio and video, along with misinformation generally. Politico noted that bad actors may try to use OpenAI's tools and those of other companies to disrupt free and fair elections. A separate report by CNET, whose headline appeared alongside these articles, said ChatGPT draws images depicting election interference or that may discourage voting, typically in a cartoon style, even when users ask for photorealism. The articles do not say how often such images are produced. They also do not describe what enforcement steps the center will take in specific cases.

Taken together, the reporting shows a company preparing for a period of heightened scrutiny rather than announcing a new rule for users. The articles do not say how the center will coordinate with election officials or outside groups. The timing of the announcement, shortly before the vote, suggests the company expects the most activity in the days around election day. Further details about the center's operations, and any findings it produces after the midterms, would be needed to judge how it performs.

stories.Headline: Using artificial intelligence to step up the fight against doping
stories.Summary:
Officials from the World Anti-Doping Agency and representatives from 26 countries gathered in Santorini, Greece, for the 3rd Anti-Doping Summit of Central and Eastern European Countries, where the use of artificial intelligence in the fight against doping was a central topic. The event examined new technologies that could support data analysis, improve test planning and assist investigations. Some of these tools can process large volumes of information, which could benefit many competent organisations. However, participants also recognised that the same tools could be exploited by people trying to cheat. The discussions aimed to set out how these technologies might be used responsibly and effectively.

Sébastien Gillot, director of WADA's European Office, said that artificial intelligence gives anti-doping bodies a powerful means of spotting trends and patterns that offenders may be using. He noted that the technology could help improve testing in particular. He also warned that tools helpful to investigators could equally be used by those who cheat, so the sector needs to understand how to deploy them to its advantage. Dora Hegyi, a former Hungarian gymnastics champion and vice-chair of WADA's Athletes' Council, said the talks covered how athletes could become better informed and how national bodies could work more efficiently. She added that participants also discussed the legal questions and what athletes themselves think about the use of AI.

Penny Konitsioti, a lawyer and vice-chair of the Disciplinary Committee of Greece's National Anti-Doping Organisation, said that athletes must be told at the outset when a platform's search could later be used in legal proceedings. She argued that this warning should be clearly stated in the terms of use rather than buried in small print. She also stressed that artificial intelligence should support competent authorities, such as by helping gather evidence or assisting a sports judge, but should never replace established procedures or human judgement. Participants agreed that safeguards must accompany any technological progress, including human oversight of disciplinary cases.

Transparency and the protection of personal data were strongly emphasised, since modern digital systems create new opportunities but also demand careful handling of sensitive information. Hegyi argued that trust is needed, meaning AI systems should be developed with athletes rather than only for them, if future programmes are to succeed. Transparency, data security and human oversight were identified as essential to maintaining confidence in the testing system. Participants also discussed changes to therapeutic use exemptions and results management procedures. The summit reaffirmed that the global anti-doping community aims to apply reliable, consistent procedures while fully respecting international rules and athletes' rights.

stories.Headline: Tata Communications to Build India's AI Super Highway
stories.Summary:
Tata Communications announced on October 28 and 29, 2026 that it plans to invest close to USD 450 million to build an AI super highway in India. The network is described as a high-speed, low-latency fabric linking the country's key AI data-centre corridors. The company says it will lay around 10,000 kilometers of new long-haul fiber across India. The announcement came through a PR Newswire release, with a version dated October 28 and another carried by The Manila Times on October 29.

The project is meant to create one of the country's largest AI-ready connectivity networks, integrated with Tata Communications' global backbone. The company says this will give customers an end-to-end system able to handle the performance, resilience and scale needed for next-generation AI workloads. The articles tie the plan to India's expanding data centre industry, which they expect to grow quickly as cloud adoption, AI deployment and data localisation requirements increase. They also note that connectivity is becoming as important as computing power and energy supply. A Tata executive has described the network as a way to help India attract global AI and cloud business.

Rupesh Chokshi, Chief Product and Technology Officer and Executive Vice President at Tata Communications, is quoted in the release. He said the AI economy needs a network built for speed, scale and resilience, and that his company's AI Network Fabric builds on its long role in India's digital economy. Separately, Ganesh Lakshminarayanan, Managing Director and CEO of Tata Communications, is quoted in Data Center Dynamics saying the company is building one of the most comprehensive data centre connectivity platforms in the market. He added that a growing share of the expansion is driven by anchor customer commitments and contracted demand.

The first phase will focus on the Mumbai, Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai corridor, which the company calls one of India's most important AI and hyperscale growth routes. Later phases will extend into East Coast and Western India data centre areas, including Vizag, Bhubaneswar, Jamnagar and GIFT City. By linking these corridors with international cable landing stations, the company says it will connect India with major global AI hubs. Tata Communications also plans to keep supporting existing enterprise and data centre customers by expanding its current National Long Distance and metro network.

stories.Headline: Digital Countermeasures Inc. Founder Dr. Terrance E. Dillard Discusses AI, Privacy and Human Autonomy on Power Ace Radio's PAR Real Talk
stories.Summary:
Dr. Terrance E. Dillard, a cybersecurity and privacy professional, AI practitioner and educator and founder of Digital Countermeasures Inc., appeared on Power Ace Radio's PAR Real Talk, hosted by Pally, to discuss how artificial intelligence, predictive analytics and the collection of personal data may affect privacy and individual autonomy. The interview was published on Spotify and shared through Power Ace Radio's Facebook page, and the press release announcing it was issued on October 29, 2026. A further broadcast is scheduled for Sunday, November 1, 2026, at 6 p.m. UK time. The episode is titled "PAR Real Talk with Dr. Terrance E. Dillard – Erosion of Privacy: The System Knows You Better Than You Know Yourself."

The conversation covers the digital infrastructure behind artificial intelligence and the personal data created through everyday activities such as online searches, shopping, location services, social media and digital transactions. Dillard also discusses how predictive analytics and algorithms can spot behavioural patterns, anticipate preferences and shape the content and recommendations people see online. The discussion centres on what it means if AI systems can anticipate people's actions and potentially influence their decisions. Drawing on his book, Erosion of Privacy, he argues that privacy concerns can build gradually as people trade personal information for digital convenience. The articles do not describe any new rule, law or regulatory change.

Responsibility for the interview and its content rests with Dillard and Digital Countermeasures Inc., which the articles describe as focused on cybersecurity, AI, privacy, digital resilience and technology education. The articles present these as the views expressed in the interview and do not describe any independent review or response from other parties. Postmedia notes that it has not reviewed the content, which was supplied by Newsfile as partnership content. Dillard is described as a Ph.D., MSIA and CISSP holder and a U.S. Air Force Gulf War veteran, and his book is available in hardcover, paperback, Kindle and audiobook formats. Further details are available on the company's website, dcmeasures.com.

stories.Headline: What is it like to work when your co-workers are AI agents?
stories.Summary:
Dhruv Amin, founder of the AI startup Anything, works alongside roughly 150 AI agents and only 15 human employees, and he predicts that within a year every company will have more AI co-workers than human ones. The reporting describes these agents as software that handles tasks without human intervention, such as scheduling, coding, search engine optimization and stocking the office kitchen. Across San Francisco's tech scene, agents have become a status symbol, a way for companies to show they can do more with less. Workers boast about how well their agents answer emails and give sales pitches.

The tools are being pushed hard by a wave of startups and big tech firms, including Viktor, Lindy, OpenAI's Dots, Anthropic's Claude Cowork and Microsoft's Scout. Lindy, for example, cut about one-third of its staff, from almost 50 employees to about 20, and filled many open roles with agents, though it is still hiring for some positions. Startups treat a high ratio of agents to humans as a point of pride, since delegating to an agent costs less than hiring. Corporate America appears to be following, with about 40% of large organizations using AI agents in some capacity between May 2025 and June 2026, according to McKinsey, up from 27% the year before. Boston Consulting Group found that companies expect to cut their workforces by 10% to 15% over the next few years as they hand more work to AI.

The agents have also created friction. Jay Blumenfield, who runs a Los Angeles production company, used an agent to produce a schedule and call sheet after he fired an assistant director on a shoot, and he now runs his company with a suite of agents and no assistant. Lindy's Haneen Azhar said she worries about the jobs being eliminated and about how the shift will affect people trying to enter the workforce. Workers who oversee agents say they spend much of their time fixing errors, such as a recruiting agent mixing up candidates with similar names or inventing parts of a résumé. Founder Brooke Hopkins of Coval said she has banned her company from using agents to contact customers, arguing that the practice seems lazy and sends the wrong message, and contractor Duncan McClure said recruiter emails from agents made him less willing to work with those employers.

Many of the people quoted say the technology cannot fully replace human workers, but it is changing which skills matter. Tarek Abillama of River said workers now must check agents' output and give feedback, and that "we all became managers," while Azhar said she now values the ability to coordinate and delegate over years of experience. Blumenfield said the industry is reluctant to talk openly about using AI, and he argued that the company should be honest about how it helps. Amin, for his part, says agents have made him more productive, yet he has not stopped working on weekends.

stories.Headline: Canada announces landmark investment in Cohere to scale secure, sovereign AI
stories.Summary:
Canada has announced a landmark investment of up to $1.6 billion in Cohere, a Toronto-founded company that builds secure AI systems for businesses and governments. Prime Minister Mark Carney made the announcement on October 29, 2026, in Montreal. The investment is an equity stake, made alongside private investors including NVIDIA, Bell and Schwarz Group. It will be made in stages, and Cohere's own funding round is targeting up to C$7 billion at a C$35.7 billion valuation, according to the Politico report. The government says the money will help Cohere build more advanced models, scale its computing infrastructure and grow its workforce.

In return, the company has committed to create at least 1,000 new high-paying Canadian technical jobs by 2030 and to commit at least $1.7 billion to additional computing infrastructure in Canada by 2030. Cohere will also keep its Canadian incorporation and headquarters, invest in research partnerships with Canadian institutions and work with the Canadian AI Safety Institute. Regular reporting on progress against these commitments is required as the funding is released. The government argues that this gives Canada a share in the company's success and holds it accountable for delivering benefits to Canadians. Carney described the move as a step toward securing the country's access to key technologies.

Carney framed the investment as a matter of national security and sovereignty, saying Canada is not waiting for others to decide the future of AI. He argued that sovereignty now depends on secure access to semiconductors, critical minerals, payment systems and artificial intelligence, among other things. Evan Solomon, the minister responsible for artificial intelligence and digital innovation, said Canadian companies should not have to leave the country to succeed globally. Aidan Gomez, Cohere's co-founder and chief executive, said the company wants to grow in Canada and expand its ability to serve customers with secure, sovereign technology. He thanked the government for its support.

The announcement comes just before a Canada-EU summit in Montreal, where European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President António Costa are scheduled to meet with Carney on Friday. Von der Leyen cited Cohere's merger with the German company Aleph Alpha as an example of deeper cooperation, and the two sides plan to discuss AI safety and governance. The summit also takes place amid economic threats from U.S. President Donald Trump against both Canada and the EU. Politico reported that Carney dismissed suggestions that the summit could draw reprisals from Trump. The articles do not describe further details of how the stage-by-stage funding will proceed beyond the reporting requirements.

stories.Headline: Goodwin Launches AI Governance Benchmark in Anthropic’s Claude for Legal
stories.Summary:
Goodwin, the global law firm, has made its AI Governance Benchmark available inside Anthropic's Claude for Legal, giving legal teams a way to check how well their organizations oversee artificial intelligence. The firm built the tool in Claude, and it is part of Anthropic's new gallery of ready-to-use artifacts. The announcement was reported on October 28, 2026. Users can look for gaps in their governance and decide which areas deserve attention first.

The Benchmark works through a short set of questions about an organization's AI use and governance. Once those are answered, the tool produces an assessment that points out potential shortcomings and suggests priorities. Users may also choose to connect with Goodwin for further help. Kaitlin Betancourt, co-chair of Goodwin's AI Practice, said the assessment takes about five minutes to complete.

The Benchmark draws on the Health Check component of Goodwin's recently launched AI Governance program, which serves companies, boards and private equity sponsors. That program also offers tailored readiness materials and the AI Decision Desk, an annual subscription that provides legal answers and real-time monitoring of AI regulation, enforcement and market practice. Gary Sangha, Goodwin's director of AI product and platforms, said the tool puts the firm's Health Check directly into companies' hands so legal teams can judge their governance needs. Betancourt added that legal teams are being asked to move fast on AI, and that governance should not be what holds them back.

Robert Mahari, head of Claude for Legal at Anthropic, said law firms know what good practice looks like, and that the product is most powerful when that first-hand experience is built into it. He described Goodwin's Benchmark as a practical way for legal teams to evaluate their AI governance and learn what to tackle next. Goodwin's AI practice advises companies, startups and investors on AI governance, intellectual property, data and cybersecurity risk. The firm is also changing its internal legal workflows through its proprietary Regina OS platform, and its wider practice focuses on healthcare, investment funds and capital, life sciences, private equity, real estate and technology.

stories.Headline: The Fed Holds Interest Rates in a 10–2 Vote. Here's What This Means for Artificial Intelligence (AI) Stocks.
stories.Summary:
The Federal Reserve held its benchmark interest rate steady at 3.75% to 4% on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, but the decision was not unanimous. Ten members voted to hold, while Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack voted to raise rates by a quarter of a percentage point. The S&P 500 briefly rose about 30 points when Fed Chair Kevin Warsh began his press conference, but it gave those gains back by the end of the session. The Fed also skipped its summary of economic projections, the so-called dot plot, so investors had little insight into the dissenting members' thinking.

Chip stocks responded well to the pause, with the VanEck Semiconductor ETF finishing up 1.7% against a 0.3% gain for the S&P 500. Growth and technology companies are especially sensitive to interest rates because more of their earnings arrive far in the future, and higher rates lower the present value of those earnings. AI infrastructure companies are particularly exposed right now because many are borrowing tens of billions of dollars to fund new data center construction. CoreWeave, a leading provider of cloud computing for AI, rose 5.6% in the regular session. A month earlier, Fed futures had indicated a chance of more than 50% of a rate hike.

Warsh called the decision a "hawkish skip," which signals that the Fed is likely to raise rates later, and he described the economy as strong. According to the CME FedWatch tool cited by The Motley Fool, investors now see a 78% chance of a rate hike at the December meeting and expect the federal funds rate to reach 4.5% to 4.75% or higher a year from now. A Bloomberg columnist, Jonathan Levin, wrote that Warsh is an optimist about AI, having argued in a Wall Street Journal column that the technology would act as a significant disinflationary force. Levin warned that if the AI boom stalls, Warsh might be pushed to abandon further rate increases, and he argued that a quarter-point hike in December would still be prudent.

Levin also noted that the Bloomberg Artificial Intelligence Index of 50 companies fell as much as 10% this month, amid worries about slowing revenue growth and financing strains for data center companies. Bond yields rose for CoreWeave and its peers, and Levin said the Fed was right to pause but should not give in to inflation that has run above its 2% target for almost six years. Swaps implied roughly 83% odds of a December hike after the decision, down from about 95% beforehand. Whether the Fed moves again will depend on how credit conditions and the AI trade develop in the coming months.

stories.Headline: DIDWW Partners with IdentityCall to Enhance AI Call Analytics
stories.Summary:
On October 28, 2026, DIDWW, a licensed global telecom operator connecting human and AI communications across more than 90 countries, announced a partnership with TechAI Solutions, a software provider building AI-powered business tools. The deal combines DIDWW's voice services with IdentityCall, TechAI Solutions' AI call analytics and quality management product. The announcement was published by GlobeNewswire from Dublin and carried by several outlets that day. Both companies framed the partnership as a way to make sure AI-analyzed phone calls connect reliably.

IdentityCall lets managers review every submitted call rather than the small sample most companies check. The tool transcribes, summarizes and categorizes calls, pulls out agreed actions, and scores each one against a company's own criteria. Its analysis looks at the content of a conversation instead of only keywords, and it can deliver results in a different language from the call itself. The product serves sales, support, dispatch and HR teams and is expanding into the Netherlands and the UK.

DIDWW's role is to carry the calls over its own geo-redundant network, with local numbers and SIP trunks that teams can connect to AI tools such as ElevenLabs, Retell, Vapi, LiveKit and IdentityCall. TechAI Solutions' CEO, Rima Vaskiene, said the company built IdentityCall so that no valuable insight from a customer call is lost, and she said DIDWW's local numbers suit clients who are growing into new markets because the call quality underpins the analysis. DIDWW's CEO, Karolis Jurys, said businesses are adding AI to every stage of the phone call and that DIDWW built its voice infrastructure for both people and AI so calls connect reliably in any market customers want to reach. He said the company was glad to support TechAI Solutions as it expands into the Netherlands, the UK and beyond.

The releases did not give financial terms or a timeline beyond those expansion plans. The announcement fits a broader push in which businesses use AI to answer, route and review customer conversations, and both firms describe their products as tools for that work. TechAI Solutions said it begins with a specific business problem and aims to make AI part of everyday work, and it pointed to earlier work with Laista and Wise Monks. The articles do not report customer results, pricing or any independent assessment of how the two products perform together.

stories.Headline: Instead of peeking at the future ‘outside’, Korea must find its own ‘new AI coordinates’
stories.Summary:
Korea's Kyunghyang Shinmun published an opinion piece on October 28, 2026, arguing that the country should stop looking abroad for models of artificial intelligence policy and build its own framework. The author begins with the sharp split in public debate, where one camp expects AI to boost growth and offset the demographic decline, while the other warns that falling behind will doom the nation. Both camps, the piece argues, treat AI as an unstoppable force and society as something that must simply adapt. The author claims this framing hides the real question of where society should be heading.

The piece makes the case that technology takes its shape from the institutions it meets, using Korea's COVID-19 epidemiological tracking system as an example. The capability to map large datasets existed by 2014, but the system only emerged after the MERS outbreak prompted legal revisions, the removal of barriers between ministries, standardized data formats, and privacy safeguards. The author describes AI as a mirror that reflects existing prejudices and structural problems and a megaphone that amplifies them. The piece then sketches three phases of modern Korean society, a closed hierarchical era, an open liberal era after 1987, and a fractured winner-takes-all society after the 1998 currency crisis. It says this fracture has produced what the author calls a three-no society marked by distrust, discontent, and anxiety, which AI could accelerate.

The author places much of the responsibility on institutions and on the people who design and run them, arguing that opacity has moved from personal networks into algorithms that set platform fees, welfare screening, and credit scores. The piece also cites the Seongsu Bridge collapse, the Sampoong Department Store collapse, and the Sewol ferry disaster as examples of slow-building disasters rooted in past growth-at-all-costs policies. The author warns of three waves of change, one affecting personal cognition as people outsource thinking, one hitting organizations as automated agents replace the routine tasks through which newcomers learn, and one from physical AI reaching care, logistics, construction, and manufacturing. The piece says Korea cannot simply copy the American market model, the Chinese state model, or the European regulatory model, and proposes "dignity" as the goal, built on safety, cohesion, inclusion, and capability. The excerpt ends before the author details the specific measures, so the articles provided do not include the full set of proposed changes or numbers beyond the dates above.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] Ozelle to Spotlight Scalable AI-Assisted Hematology
stories.Summary:
Ozelle, a company founded in Silicon Valley in 2014, announced on October 28, 2026 that it will showcase its O-Cyte 1 automated hematology analyzer at MEDICA 2026. The company says that as AI-assisted morphology becomes part of routine hematology, laboratories need more than automatic cell classification, since cell images must remain available for professional review while analyzers also meet daily testing and maintenance needs. The O-Cyte 1 combines complete blood count testing and 7-part white blood cell differentiation with high-resolution cell imaging and AI-assisted classification in one instrument. Its cell images are linked to numerical results so that laboratory staff can examine visual evidence when needed. The announcement was prompted in part by the International Council for Standardization in Haematology, which approved a new digital morphology standardization project at its October 14 to 15 General Assembly.

The analyzer is built for changing workloads and routine service. A standalone unit delivers up to 60 tests per hour, while a six-unit cascade reaches up to 360 tests per hour. Its integrated reagent kit and key fluid-contact components are housed in consumables, which the company says simplifies reagent handling and reduces routine maintenance. Built-in self-checks and replaceable modules are intended to make faults easier to identify and service. Ozelle also says scalable configurations can serve laboratories with different testing volumes and give distributors a path for future capacity expansion.

Ozelle is the company responsible for the product and the announcement, and it describes the O-Cyte 1 as part of its vision for the fourth generation of hematology analysis. The company says this approach aims to make morphology intelligence more consistent, reviewable and scalable across routine workflows. Ozelle will also feature the EHBT-75, which combines 7-diff hematology with cell imaging and morphology analysis, and the EHBT-50, which integrates hematology, immunoassay and dry biochemistry in a compact platform. Visitors can also see Open Dx, its AI Workbench for AI-assisted report review and result sharing. The company will exhibit at MEDICA 2026 from November 16 to 19 in Hall 1, Booth D63, at Messe Düsseldorf in Germany, where it plans to discuss distribution opportunities.

stories.Headline: AI token use may jump 78% as falling prices fail to guarantee lower costs - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
Accenture Research has released a report predicting that consumption of artificial intelligence tokens will rise sharply over the next two years, even as the price per token falls. According to the report, average token prices could drop by about 19 percent over 24 months, while token use could climb by roughly 78 percent. The findings were published in late October 2026 and reported by ANI, and they suggest that rising usage may cancel out the savings businesses expect from cheaper tokens. The report's central message is that lower unit prices do not automatically mean lower total spending.

The research also points to a gap in how companies track their returns on AI. Only 35 percent of organisations said they could precisely calculate the cost per business outcome for their highest-volume AI use case. The report examined what companies would do with savings if prices fell by 25 percent or more, finding that only 5 percent would keep the savings. By contrast, 42 percent would expand AI use to more employees, and 35 percent would adopt applications they had previously judged too expensive. Accenture said organisations must therefore decide how to direct the additional capacity AI creates.

Accenture's survey indicated that 60 percent of executives plan to move freed-up capacity toward higher-value or more strategic work, and 51 percent intend to put it into growth initiatives. The report also stressed the continuing role of people, noting that 70 percent of surveyed organisations use AI mainly to augment human effort while only 4 percent use it mainly to replace workers. Accenture advised businesses to keep reassessing how work is divided between people and AI, to track the cost of delivering business outcomes, and to reinvest released capacity where it can create the most value. The article does not describe specific regulatory steps or further publications following the report.

stories.Headline: Microsoft, Google report booming AI revenue as the tech reshapes business
stories.Summary:
Alphabet's Google, Microsoft, and Amazon face a collective test this week as they report quarterly earnings and must explain their spending on artificial intelligence. Their results, which account for more than a third of the S&P 500's earnings, follow Meta's report and come as investors weigh how much the companies are spending against the returns they expect. The central question is what the AI spending figure is and how it compares with those expected returns. Bank of America strategist Savita Subramanian wrote on Tuesday that all eyes would be on AI monetization versus spending.

Justifying the spending has been a feature of earnings reports for the past two years, but the stakes are higher now because economic conditions and the investing environment have shifted. A recent tech sell-off has put AI financing in the spotlight, and investors have voiced mixed feelings about Meta selling shares and borrowing to fund its AI ambitions. Demand for financing has intensified competition for capital, pressuring tech companies to raise large sums in advance. The article also notes that Wall Street is preparing IPOs for two frontier AI labs, Anthropic, possibly next month, and OpenAI, likely next year.

Business behavior toward AI is also changing, according to the reporting. Companies are becoming pickier, scaling back, using less expensive models, and trying different services, a slowdown the article says suggests heavy demand for computing existed mainly when it seemed free. Because that demand is price-sensitive, justifying AI costs will matter more. Meta has reoriented itself around the division behind its Muse product, which it envisions as a large service network and revenue engine, and the early success of personal assistant AI agents has also reshaped product priorities. The bull case holds that the cash may not arrive soon but will eventually flow, and the article says Microsoft, Google, and Amazon will also have to supply answers this week.
