stories.Headline: Canada to Take Equity Stake in AI Firm Cohere
stories.Summary:
Canada will invest up to CAN$1.6 billion, about US$1 billion, in the Toronto-founded AI firm Cohere, Prime Minister Mark Carney announced on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The federal money is meant to build sovereign AI alternatives that can rival those of the United States and China. Carney made the announcement ahead of a major Canada-EU summit in Montreal. Cohere, founded in 2019, focuses on models for businesses and governments rather than consumer applications, which sets it apart from firms such as OpenAI and Anthropic.

Carney said the investment would help decide where AI is built, how it is governed and whom it serves, and he argued that Canada should not wait for others to make those decisions. He warned that concentrating AI systems in a few companies carries systemic risks, saying that such firms may call themselves global but often act nationally when it counts. Cohere is led by Aidan Gomez, an AI researcher who co-authored a seminal paper that helped lay the foundations for modern AI systems. The company's funding round targets CAN$7 billion and would value it at CAN$35.7 billion.

Gomez said the company is now the largest AI company outside the United States and China. The company has also moved to expand across the Atlantic. In May, Cohere announced a deal to acquire German AI firm Aleph Alpha, creating a combined entity with headquarters in both Toronto and Berlin, a deal backed by Ottawa and Berlin. Gomez told AFP in June that Europe risks total technological irrelevance without sovereign capabilities of its own.

At the announcement, he said organizations want technology they can trust and control, and he pledged that Cohere would stay rooted in Canada. EU chief Ursula von der Leyen cited the Cohere-Aleph Alpha merger in remarks before the summit, pointing to strong appetite for teaming up. Brussels and Ottawa are working toward unprecedented levels of cooperation, including alignment on AI policy. The articles do not say when the funding round will close or what conditions the government attached to its stake.

stories.Headline: [PRNewswire] SGH's AI tool wins international award
stories.Summary:
Singapore General Hospital, or SGH, has won the Silver Award in the Dr Prathap C Reddy Excellence Award for Clinical Quality and Patient Safety at the International Hospital Federation Awards 2026 for its Augmented Intelligence in Infectious Diseases tool, known as AI2D. The award was presented on 21 October 2026 at the 49th IHF World Hospital Congress in Seoul, South Korea. The tool also scored at the top of the IHF i-to-i Innovation Hub 2026. The awards drew more than 750 entries from 38 countries and territories, and AI2D was one of eight finalists in its category. The other finalists came from hospitals in Indonesia, Italy, Oman, the Philippines, South Korea and Saudi Arabia.

AI2D is an artificial intelligence tool that helps doctors decide whether patients with pneumonia or other lower respiratory tract infections need antibiotics. It was developed by a team led by Associate Professor Andrea Kwa and Ms Sarah Tang, with collaborators from SGH's Infectious Diseases department, DXC Technology and Synapxe. The tool was trained on clinician-reviewed data from 18,000 patients and is 90 per cent accurate in identifying who needs antibiotics. It runs in the background of existing clinical systems, so doctors do not have to enter extra information, and it supports rather than replaces their clinical judgement. It has been in use at SGH for more than a year.

Associate Professor Kwa said that being recognised among entries from around the world endorses years of work by a multidisciplinary team. She said the tool turns routinely collected clinical data into insights that help doctors make better-informed decisions and reduce unnecessary antibiotic use. Associate Professor Loo Chian Min, Chairman of SGH's Medical Board, described antimicrobial resistance as a silent pandemic. He said AI2D shows that AI can act as a force multiplier for clinicians rather than a replacement, and that he was proud the work was being recognised globally.

The articles explain why the tool matters. About half of SGH's inpatients are on antibiotics at any one time, and doctors often start treatment before test results confirm whether an infection is bacterial. Unnecessary use can cause side effects and add to antibiotic resistance. SGH's antimicrobial stewardship team now uses AI2D to prioritise cases, so all lower respiratory tract infection cases are reviewed, compared with around 30 per cent previously. Doctors stepped in to stop antibiotics in about 15 per cent of cases before the tool, a rate that has risen to nearly 43 per cent with it.

stories.Headline: California Enacts AI Spokespeople, Chatbots and Content Disclosures Laws - The National Law Review
stories.Summary:
California's governor recently signed three artificial intelligence bills into law, and the articles say two take effect January 1, 2027 while one took effect immediately. The first, SB 1000, amended the California AI Transparency Act and took effect on signature, September 30, 2026. It covers providers of publicly accessible generative AI systems in California and removes the former threshold of more than a million monthly visitors or users. Systems designed primarily as assistive technology are exempt until January 1, 2029. The bill also requires covered providers, where technically feasible, to embed a latent disclosure in images, video, and audio their systems create or alter.

That disclosure must name the provider, the system and version, the creation or alteration date and time, a unique identifier, and whether the system made or changed the content. It may be given directly or through a link to a website with the information. Covered providers must also offer a free, publicly accessible disclosure verification tool, directly or through a qualifying third party. The tool must let users assess whether content is AI-generated or AI-altered, show the system provenance of the content's data, and avoid outputting personal data unless the person concerned gave informed consent. The second law, SB 1050, was signed by Governor Gavin Newsom on September 16, 2026, and takes effect January 1, 2027.

SB 1050 covers synthetic performers, which may be visual replicas or synthetic voice-over narrators, in advertisements for products or services. Under it, anyone who creates and publishes an advertisement in California that prominently features a synthetic performer must include a clear and conspicuous disclosure near the performer, visible and held long enough for a reasonable consumer to understand it. The articles define a synthetic performer as a digital figure, voice, or representation made wholly or partly with artificial intelligence, machine learning, or similar techniques, which appears human and cannot be based on or intended to depict a specific identifiable person. The articles note this differs from laws in New York, Tennessee, and Washington, which focused on deepfakes and digital replicas of identifiable people. The third law, AB 1609, was signed September 28, 2026, and also starts January 1, 2027.

AB 1609 applies to large private businesses with more than $500 million in national gross annual revenue that serve California customers. Those businesses may not represent that an AI customer service chatbot is human, and must disclose the chatbot's nature in the interaction's medium whenever a reasonable person could believe they are talking to a human. They must also offer a simple way to request a human agent during at least regular business hours, make a good-faith effort to connect the customer with a human within 15 minutes of the request, and, if that is not possible, let the person schedule an appointment within one business day. The authors, attorneys Liisa M. Thomas and Kathryn Smith of Sheppard, Mullin, Richter & Hampton LLP, say these laws signal a trend in AI and privacy regulation and expect more to follow quickly. They advise companies to review how adaptable their privacy and AI governance programs are to coming changes in this and other state laws.

stories.Headline: Could next-gen artificial intelligence help map out future space outposts?
stories.Summary:
Researchers at The Ohio State University have built an artificial intelligence framework that could help plan future trips to the moon. Developed by Gokce Inal, a PhD candidate in civil, environmental and geodetic engineering, the system is meant to help scientists judge possible lunar landing sites, flag hazards that future crews could face, and search new areas for valuable geologic features. The work was presented this month at the 58th Annual Meeting of the Division for Planetary Sciences of the American Astronomical Society. Inal said the findings were shared as part of a broader effort to bring together artificial intelligence and planetary science.

The system, called LUMINA, is an extension of an earlier lunar model known as LLaVA-LE, which could describe lunar terrain and answer science questions. LUMINA adds the ability to plan and carry out multistep analyses, evaluate candidate landing sites, and explain the evidence behind its recommendations. Early results show it can make complex lunar observations and produce meaningful commentary on landing sites, which could help planners find areas rich in water ice and other resources. Inal designed the tool as a decision-support system rather than a semi-autonomous machine, so that it works alongside mission planners who make the final calls.

She described the goal as an active scientific assistant rather than a passive tool that only answers questions. Alper Yilmaz, a co-author and professor in the same department at Ohio State, said the approach could also apply to other planetary bodies, including Earth, Mars and some asteroids. He noted that few GPT-like map models currently exist for space exploration, and that the team aims to make its model generalizable to other surfaces. Yilmaz added that as datasets grow more advanced, efficient tools will be needed to sort through them, since finding the best landing spots would otherwise be like searching for a needle in a haystack.

He also said such a system could act as another set of eyes to verify and question findings in a harsh environment. The team plans to test LUMINA on new high-quality lunar data and to further evaluate how well it supports mission planning as the system develops. Inal noted that NASA's Artemis program creates important opportunities for this research, and that new lunar data could improve systems like hers. Reporting on the work came from Ohio State News and Newswise, which both credited the research to the university.

stories.Headline: The 5 forces creating urgency around ethical AI adoption
stories.Summary:
Jeffrey Saviano, a senior lecturer at the MIT Sloan School of Management and a former EY executive, has argued that organizations face five pressures that make adopting ethical AI urgent. His view appears in an excerpt from his new book, "Boundaries of Tolerance: A Foundational Model for Ethical AI Strategy and Governance," published by Wiley, with the excerpt released on October 28, 2026. According to the piece, artificial intelligence is driving innovation across industries while also creating risks and ethical consequences that traditional enterprise risk frameworks no longer handle well. Saviano frames AI governance as a leadership question that reaches the boardroom and senior executive teams, not only technologists or regulators. The article describes the human cost of governance gaps.

A patient's diagnosis can be compromised by a model trained on incomplete or biased clinical data, and a job candidate can be rejected by an automated hiring system shaped by outdated employment patterns. Small input errors can cascade into outcomes that reinforce inequality and erode stakeholder trust. Saviano prefers the term "ethical AI" over "responsible AI" because it stresses the role of leadership judgment in designing and deploying these systems. He also argues that ethical AI strategy has become a leadership necessity as AI moves into core operations across nearly every industry. Saviano identifies five forces behind this urgency.

Competitive pressure pushes companies to deploy AI quickly, often before leaders have clarified how it should be governed. AI also changes how risk behaves, since minor problems can escalate rapidly once systems spread through an organization. Investors and markets are beginning to ask who oversees AI risk, in ways that resemble earlier scrutiny of cybersecurity. Employees across functions are raising ethical questions about data, deployment, and responsibility, and when decision authority is unclear, those concerns either go unvoiced or are settled informally. Finally, public expectations about fairness and human dignity are rising, shaped by civil society groups and scholars, and compliance alone no longer answers them.

Saviano concludes that these forces have changed what leadership must do. Ethical AI strategy is no longer a discretionary add-on, and leaders must decide what their organizations will tolerate from intelligent systems when regulatory guidance is incomplete. He argues that this responsibility cannot be delegated to regulators, which explains why ethical AI governance now belongs in the boardroom and C-suite. The excerpt does not describe specific regulatory deadlines or enforcement steps beyond these points.

Articles.Title: The 5 forces creating urgency around ethical AI adoption

stories.Headline: Using AI to improve lives: UTulsa students advance prosthetic research - The University of Tulsa
stories.Summary:
Students at The University of Tulsa are using artificial intelligence to study how prosthetic limbs affect the comfort and confidence of people who wear them. The work takes place in the biomechanics laboratory of John M. Henshaw, department head of mechanical engineering and Harry H. Rogers Endowed Chair in Mechanical Engineering. Students combine engineering, healthcare and machine learning to find out why one prosthetic device may feel more comfortable than another. The article reports that the project brings students from several disciplines together.

Maddie Fulk, a master's student in mechanical engineering, and fellow student researcher Maura Wahl analyzed data collected from people with below-the-knee amputations as they walked with different prosthetic devices. Motion sensors placed across the body recorded hundreds of measurements tied to gait, balance and movement. Using machine-learning techniques, the students looked for the measurements that best separated one device from another. The article says the model consistently flagged movement near the pelvis as one of the strongest indicators, which suggests changes near the body's center of mass may reveal how users experience different prosthetics.

Henshaw described the model as very successful and said it revealed patterns that would have been hard to find with traditional methods alone. Wahl said many people may not know that a better option exists, and that some wear prosthetics that do not work well with their bodies. The team is now investigating whether sensors in smartphones could eventually gather similar movement data during everyday activities. The article notes that such an approach could make prosthetic evaluation more accessible and scalable.

Andreas Polycarpou, dean of the College of Engineering & Computer Science, said the project reflects the kind of hands-on experience that sets a UTulsa education apart. He said students are working with faculty mentors on real-world problems using technologies such as AI. The article adds that the experience is shaping career plans, with Fulk aiming for medicine and Wahl considering graduate study in prosthetics and biomedical engineering. The article is a university feature, so it describes the research as ongoing rather than reporting final outcomes.

Articles.Title: Using AI to improve lives: UTulsa students advance prosthetic research - The University of Tulsa

stories.Headline: $20M grant renews UH role in AI research to improve engineering design
stories.Summary:
The University of Hawaiʻi at Mānoa will keep helping develop artificial intelligence tools that could make it faster and less expensive to design and test products such as airplanes and wind turbines, following a new $20 million federal grant. Three Mānoa faculty members, Assistant Professors Chrisy Xiyu Du and Andrei A. Klishin of the Department of Mechanical Engineering and Associate Professor June Zhang of the Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, will serve as senior personnel in the National Science Foundation AI Institute in Dynamic Systems. The five-year award renews the institute's work, which the NSF first funded for 2021 through 2026, and it will cover its next phase of research from 2026 through 2031. The award supports a collaboration among several universities that uses AI to understand and predict how complex physical systems behave.

The institute focuses on AI that learns from physical data and the laws of science, rather than general-purpose tools that mainly handle text and images. Engineers could use these methods to test ideas more efficiently, reduce the need for costly computer simulations and improve designs before building expensive prototypes. The funding also gives participating faculty flexibility to pursue research questions over several years, support graduate students and postdoctoral researchers, and work with experts at other universities. The article describes Klishin's 2025 study, which developed a method to help AI identify the underlying rules behind noisy, real-world data, and Zhang's work on teaching AI systems to train themselves when data is limited.

Klishin said that AI can help engineers go beyond predicting how a system will behave and explore how to make it work better, adding that combining AI with an understanding of physics can help researchers test more ideas and improve designs. The article also points to HydroGym, an open-source platform developed through the institute that lets researchers test AI methods for predicting and controlling fluid flows. Such tools matter for designing aircraft, ships and wind turbines, and the platform aims to make simulation tools more accessible so researchers can build on one another's work. The institute is led by the University of Washington, with Mānoa as a participating campus alongside Harvard, Columbia, the University of Michigan and Caltech.

Articles.Title: $20M grant renews UH role in AI research to improve engineering design

stories.Headline: AI Is Thriving at Capital One | Thomas H. Davenport and Randy Bean - MIT Sloan Management Review
stories.Summary:
Capital One, the U.S. bank, has been using data and analytics for decades, and according to a column by Thomas H. Davenport and Randy Bean published in MIT Sloan Management Review on October 28, 2026, it is now expanding its use of artificial intelligence across several areas of the business. The authors say the bank, founded in 1994 as a spinout from the credit card business of Signet Bank, is the eighth-largest U.S. bank by assets as of September 2026 and ranks second among global banks in AI capabilities in the 2025 Evident AI Index, behind only JPMorgan Chase. The column is based on interviews with Prem Natarajan, the bank's chief enterprise AI officer and chief scientist, and Amy Lenander, its chief data officer. Neither the authors nor the executives describe a single new rule or law, so the piece is better understood as a profile of current practice than as an announcement of a discrete change.

The articles report several concrete uses of AI at the bank. In customer service, generative AI helps human agents find accurate answers faster, and agentic AI produces call summaries, which several hundred agents now use, with the summaries added to customer records. In risk and compliance, the bank built an intelligent assistant for auditors that Natarajan said reduced quality errors by 85 percent and saved an estimated 5,000 hours across 30 auditors in a few months, with one audit task falling from five hours to three minutes. Lenander said the bank analyzes call transcripts and clickstream data with generative AI to spot near-real-time trends, and it manages data as "data products" owned by the teams closest to them. The bank has also begun marketing Databolt, a data tokenization tool built internally to protect sensitive information in AI workflows, through Capital One Software, its second product after Slingshot, a cloud spending tool.

Natarajan argued that measuring AI purely by quarterly return on investment is premature and shortsighted, saying, "You can't achieve transformation if you're focused on quarterly ROI," and that "the ultimate ROI is a happy customer." Lenander framed the bank's current work as an extension of its long history of automated decisioning, moving from regression to machine learning to generative AI, and she said that proprietary, unified data gives the bank a competitive advantage. The authors conclude that the company remains a leader in data-driven and AI-driven enterprise practice, and they describe this as a trait deeply embedded in its culture. The column does not indicate any further deadlines or planned milestones beyond the initiatives it describes.

Articles.Title: AI Is Thriving at Capital One | Thomas H. Davenport and Randy Bean - MIT Sloan Management Review

stories.Headline: AI Doesn’t Have To Be an Empire. It Can Be a Bicycle.
stories.Summary:
Karen Hao, an award-winning journalist and author of Empire of AI, gave a talk at Lorimer Chapel at Colby College as part of the Davis Institute for Artificial Intelligence's Distinguished Lecture Series. In the talk she compared today's largest AI companies to historic empires and argued that ordinary people can push back against them. The audience, which included students from Bowdoin College, gave her a standing ovation when she finished. Stacy Doore, Clare Booth Luce Associate Professor of Computer Science, introduced her. Doore called Hao a powerful ally for advocates of ethical AI.

Hao said that companies such as OpenAI are pursuing a scale-at-all-costs approach that consolidates economic and political power. She drew parallels with past empires, saying these companies claim resources that are not theirs, exploit large amounts of labor, monopolize knowledge production, and justify their actions with a moral and existential imperative. She warned that training ever-larger models risks eroding intellectual property and requires data centers that use large amounts of energy, freshwater, and minerals for computer chips. Her alternative was to build smaller, task-specific systems, which she likened to bicycles rather than rockets. She cited AlphaFold by DeepMind, which predicts protein structures, as an example of a tool trained on a curated dataset that does not need supercomputers to run.

Hao pointed to grassroots resistance as proof that the trend is not inevitable. She described Tucson, Arizona, where Amazon proposed a $3.6-billion data center called Project Blue, and where residents formed the No Desert Data Center Coalition to fight it. She said the coalition packed city hall on a day when temperatures reached 114 degrees Fahrenheit, and the council voted 7-0 to stop the project in its current form. Her message to the audience was that individuals can resist the idea that giant AI companies are all-powerful. She summed up her view by saying that when people rise, empires fall.

Articles.Title: AI Doesn’t Have To Be an Empire. It Can Be a Bicycle.

stories.Headline: Solving an urgent math problem: How to educate grad students amid AI disruptions
stories.Summary:
Harvard faculty held a two-day summit this fall on revising doctoral mathematics education for the age of artificial intelligence. Two dozen prominent mathematicians attended, and they produced a report with urgent recommendations after the field was jolted this year by rapid advances in AI. The report's authors argue that a written dissertation alone no longer proves mastery. Its recommendations also include more rigorous oral questioning and stronger training in human-to-human communication.

The summit brought together seven Harvard faculty and 17 colleagues from institutions including the University of California, Berkeley, Stanford, Brown, MIT, Princeton, the University of Texas at Austin, and Johns Hopkins University. The report calls for "rigorous in-person assessment" every year by multiple faculty, who would give detailed feedback to students. It also says the dissertation defense should move from a largely ceremonial event shortly before graduation to a more exacting verbal examination. Take-home exams are described as largely obsolete, and homework should play a minimal role in assessment because AI can complete it. Students are advised to use AI tools to supplement their thinking rather than replace it.

Melanie Matchett Wood, William Caspar Graustein Professor of Mathematics and director of graduate studies, said the pace of AI progress could transform the field over the next few years more than it has changed in a century. Wood, who co-organized the summit, observed that AI can now produce work that could have passed as an acceptable doctoral thesis a couple of years ago. Dan Freed, Shiing-Shen Chern Professor of Mathematics, co-organized the summit and said its aim was to produce proactive recommendations to guide Ph.D. students. Lauren K. Williams, Dwight Parker Robinson Professor of Mathematics, who took part, said that many people wrongly believe fewer interesting problems remain, when in fact the field is infinite and needs more mathematicians.

The report, which draws on several leading math programs but targets universities everywhere, strikes an optimistic note while warning against uses of AI that stunt intellectual growth. Its authors say AI can help with figures, literature searches, proofreading, and quick overviews of unfamiliar topics, but students should be careful before offloading anything that helps them learn to think. Harvard's math program enrolls about 60 Ph.D. candidates, and current students face a different landscape than graduates of a few years ago. Wood summed up the goal this way: "We want as much human understanding of mathematical truth as we can get," and the mechanics of demonstrating understanding may simply look very different.

Articles.Title: Solving an urgent math problem: How to educate grad students amid AI disruptions

stories.Headline: Spending it faster: What a 10,000-agent proof means for AI’s borrowed expertise
stories.Summary:
OpenAI said in September that an unreleased internal model had produced a proposed solution to the Navier-Stokes existence and smoothness problem, one of the seven Millennium Prize Problems. Roughly 10,000 agents ran in parallel for 88 hours, at a compute cost of millions of dollars, which the company's Sébastien Bubeck said was about a thousand times what it had previously spent on a single problem. The proof has not been verified, and under the Clay Mathematics Institute's rules a proposed solution would need to appear in a qualifying publication, wait two years, and gain general acceptance before any prize could be considered. OpenAI has said it does not intend to claim the prize.

A few weeks later, on Oct. 6, OpenAI released 722 manuscripts claiming progress on 372 open problems across several areas of mathematics, all produced by the same internal model. Only 162 of those manuscripts included machine-checkable formal proofs, and a group calling itself the Association for Human Mathematics criticized the release as a demonstration of power rather than scholarship. OpenAI withdrew three of the manuscripts after an internal audit found a sign error that invalidated one argument and the constructions in two dependent papers. The author argues that the episode shows AI is strongest at work inside frames people already built, and that the scale of machine output now means human understanding, not production, is the real limit on science.

The article's central concern is a mismatch: far more machine-generated results than people qualified to evaluate them, and no institution outside pure mathematics for verifying such claims. The author argues that absorbing a result requires changes in people, which happen one person at a time, while producing results has become a scalable industrial process. The article recommends that Congress reverse a proposed 40 percent cut to National Science Foundation graduate fellowships and fund paid verification teams. It also points to a May case, in which an internal OpenAI model disproved Paul Erdős's unit distance conjecture, where nine mathematicians checked the proof and published a companion paper. The author notes that this verification worked partly because the argument was short and the volunteers were available, and cites Melanie Matchett Wood's view that it may be easier for AI to convince mathematicians it has a proof than to produce a correct one.

The author draws on William Thurston's 1994 essay, which holds that mathematics is valuable for the understanding it produces rather than the statements it stores, and on the history of research that sat unread for years. The article describes how Lawrence Craven's early observations about aspirin went ignored for about 20 years until later work confirmed them. Taken together, the author's position is that unread results do little good, and that verification capacity must grow alongside AI output. The article does not describe a specific next step beyond the policy recommendations above.

Articles.Title: Spending it faster: What a 10,000-agent proof means for AI’s borrowed expertise

stories.Headline: Five Caltech Faculty Selected by Meta to Help Solve Open Problems in AI
stories.Summary:
Caltech has been selected by Meta as one of five academic partners in the United States to receive access to the company's latest artificial intelligence models, along with research funding and collaboration opportunities. The announcement, dated October 28, 2026, names five Caltech faculty members, and the new agreements expand a strategic partnership between the Institute and Meta. The work spans physics, chemistry, biology, computer science, and mathematics. Each selected faculty member will receive a research grant for up to three years, along with access to Meta's frontier Muse AI models through its first-party application programming interface.

The projects are designed to test whether AI can go beyond summarizing existing knowledge, according to Meta's announcement. The researchers will explore whether these systems can help formulate and prove conjectures, predict unseen outcomes, build verifiable artifacts, and generate hypotheses that scientists can test and refine. Anima Anandkumar, the Bren Professor of Computing and Mathematical Sciences, is developing TorchLean to verify AI-generated code, proofs, and specifications without manual inspection. Sarah E. Reisman, the Bren Professor of Chemistry, will build a reaction benchmark from unpublished lab notebook records to test whether models can predict outcomes on truly new data. Matt Thomson, professor of computational biology, is working toward an "AI theorist" that can model collective behavior in biological systems.

Nai-Chang Yeh, the Thomas W. Hogan Professor of Physics, is addressing the tendency of language models to produce descriptions of physical systems that sound plausible but break fundamental principles. Her framework forces models to build candidate physical representations under explicit constraints. Tony Yue Yu, professor of mathematics, is building MathDB Frontier, a community-curated database and benchmark that will assess whether large language models can perform genuine mathematical reasoning. The database builds on MathDB, which contains more than 86,900 research-level open problems. Caltech officials and Meta both framed the work as an effort to use the models to accelerate scientific discovery.

The partnership began in 2016 with research collaborations and corporate gifts supporting six faculty members. A more formal agreement followed in 2024, focused on giving robots a sense of touch, such as heat or texture, and on materials discovery across organic and inorganic substances. That partnership is led by Chiara Daraio, the G. Bradford Jones Professor of Mechanical Engineering and Applied Physics, and it provides unrestricted funding, collaborative research, and a small Meta facility on campus within the Beckman Institute. For the new grants, faculty brought their research questions to Meta, which matched them with suitable AI tools. Meta's announcement said the company believes the future is for everyone, and it expressed excitement about supporting university-led research that uses its models to accelerate scientific breakthroughs.

Articles.Title: Five Caltech Faculty Selected by Meta to Help Solve Open Problems in AI

stories.Headline: Humanlike design of AI voice assistants helps users disregard security risks, study finds
stories.Summary:
A study by Andrew Chen, Ronald G. Harper Professor at the University of Kansas School of Business, finds that humanlike design in artificial intelligence voice assistants leads users to overlook security risks. The article, titled "Sounds Good and Feels Better," appears in the journal Information & Management and was published on October 29, 2026. Chen's team surveyed 277 users of these assistants and analyzed the responses with structural equation modeling. The findings show that when a voice assistant seems more human, people feel more enjoyment, and that enjoyment reduces both their perception of security risk and their desire to stop using the product.

Chen explained that people tend to judge a machine the way they judge other people, so a friendlier voice or a more attractive appearance builds trust. He said that anthropomorphism, the assignment of human traits to nonhuman things, now shapes features in products such as Apple's Siri and Amazon's Alexa. Many customers adopt these assistants mainly for convenience, since they are always ready to answer questions or offer suggestions without a computer. Privacy remains a concern for some people, but the study found that humanlike design does not lower perceived risk directly. Instead, the effect works mainly through the enjoyment users feel.

The researchers found that affective appraisal, the emotional reaction a user has, interacts with cognitive appraisal, the careful thinking about what sits behind the technology. Chen said that the relationship is not linear but quadratic, so as users grow more comfortable, they reduce their risk perceptions even further. He said he hopes designers will invest in the enjoyment side of these systems, not only in function, while cautioning against training AI to become too strong in emotional or spiritual qualities. Chen also described a friend who asked him to unplug an Echo because he worried about recording, which shows that some users remain wary.

The study was co-written with Yixiu Yu and Sisheng Liang of Central Michigan University, Haoqiang Jiang of California State University Channel Islands, and Rui Sundrup of the University of Louisville. Chen has been a KU faculty member since 2006 and researches human-computer interaction. He is now working on multimodal ways to improve interactions with AI systems. The articles do not describe any further publication or product changes that would follow from the research.

Articles.Title: Humanlike design of AI voice assistants helps users disregard security risks, study finds

stories.Headline: How Do We Teach And Learn In The Age of AI?
stories.Summary:
The University of Maryland, Baltimore published a feature on October 29, 2026, asking how teaching and learning should change in an age of artificial intelligence. The piece opens with a century-old worry, attributed to Socrates, that writing would weaken memory, and uses it to frame today's concern that AI could let students skip the thinking that learning requires. It notes that earlier technologies, such as map apps and smartphone contact lists, already shifted what people remember and do themselves. The article then describes a turning point at Brown University, where Professor Roberto Serrano gave a take-home exam whose average score of 96 out of 100 suggested students were relying on AI. When he moved the final to an in-person, closed-book format, many students withdrew and the average fell to 48.

The article reports that universities are responding in different ways, with some taking firm stances and others weighing whether to adapt. The University of Chicago banned AI in its core social science courses, and its law school banned laptops, tablets, and wearable electronics in first-year classes to encourage handwritten critical thinking. Duke University has barred applicants from using AI to write admissions essays. The article also cites more than $4 trillion in AI investment over the past two years as a sign the technology is not going away, which leads some educators to argue for teaching students to use it well. Opinions differ on who should set rules, whether broad university policies or individual professors, and the article notes that inconsistent rules across classes could confuse students.

The views of the people quoted are summarized here. Donald J. Tobin, a University of Maryland Francis King Carey School of Law professor, argues in Juristnews that restrictive AI policies misjudge where the intellectual work lies, since lawyers increasingly need to direct and evaluate machine-generated drafts rather than start from a blank page. A University of British Columbia survey found that about three quarters of students felt unrestricted AI use harms their learning, and an AAC&U study raised concerns about shorter attention spans and cheating. The article frames the central questions as how to preserve deep disciplinary understanding and how to ensure students and faculty gain basic competence with AI tools for their studies and professions.

The discussion was the subject of an October 28, 2026 episode of the program Virtual Face to Face, hosted by Roger J. Ward, with UMB faculty panelists. Isabell May, who heads the UMB Writing Center, and Scott Riley of the School of Pharmacy, who co-hosts a teaching podcast, were among those named. Riley is also scheduled to lead a January online session on transparent teaching with AI. The article points readers to a full one-hour video of the discussion.

Articles.Title: How Do We Teach And Learn In The Age of AI?

stories.Headline: NIH Awards Morgan State $520,000 Grant to Advance Biomedical Artificial Intelligence Research
stories.Summary:
Morgan State University has received a four-year research award of approximately $520,000 from the National Institutes of Health, through the National Library of Medicine, to study how artificial intelligence can better process and interpret complex biomedical information. The project began on September 10, 2026, and runs through July 31, 2030. It is titled ORBIL-AI, short for Orthogonality-Regularized Biomedical Information-theoretic Learning. The award was announced in a university release dated October 29, 2026.

The project is designed to answer a basic question about modern AI: when several sources of biomedical data are combined, which parts add useful, complementary information and which parts merely repeat what is already there. Support comes through the NIH Support for Research Excellence program, or SuRE R16 program, which provided an initial award of $130,134 with the rest anticipated over the four years. The research aims to establish mathematical and computational principles that could make biomedical AI systems more efficient, interpretable and reliable. The release says the findings could also bear on model generalizability and calibration.

Timothy Oladunni, D.Sc., an assistant professor in the Department of Computer Science within the School of Computer, Mathematical and Natural Sciences, leads the project as principal investigator. He said that combining data from different sources can improve predictive accuracy but that understanding how those sources interact requires a stronger mathematical foundation. He described the NIH-funded work as developing and testing principles that explain when combining information helps and how those relationships affect model performance. The release also quotes him saying the research reflects the university's commitment to new computer science theory applied to important biomedical problems, and that it gives students a chance to take part in fundamental research.

The work builds on Dr. Oladunni's earlier research on redundancy and complementarity in multimodal machine learning. In April 2025 he presented that work at a Yale University computer science colloquium, arguing that adding more data sources can introduce overlap and extra computational cost without improving predictions. He also introduced a theory called Complementary Feature Domains. In 2025 he held a visiting faculty research fellowship at Yale, which the release says gives the new award a way to extend that cardiovascular and computational research at Morgan State. The release does not say when the first results will be published.

Articles.Title: NIH Awards Morgan State $520,000 Grant to Advance Biomedical Artificial Intelligence Research

stories.Headline: UC San Diego Launches Center for Principled Agentic Intelligence
stories.Summary:
UC San Diego announced on October 28, 2026 that it is launching the Center for Principled Agentic Intelligence, known as CPAi. The center is a partnership between the Halıcıoğlu School of Data Science and Computing and the School of Arts and Humanities. It is meant to study how people can understand, evaluate and trust AI agents, which are systems that plan and carry out complex tasks with limited human direction. The center's work is organized around three principles: alignment, which asks whether a system behaves as its developers and users intend; trust, which calls for verifiable evidence of reliable performance; and responsibility, which concerns the accountability of those who build and deploy these systems.

The center opens with two initiatives. The first, AI Alignment and Society, is co-led by Mikhail Belkin and Eddy Keming Chen and will examine how training and evaluation shape AI behavior, and how researchers can tell whether increasingly capable systems keep acting in line with human intentions. The second, Agentic AI System Evaluation, is co-led by Tauhidur Rahman, Lily Weng, Haojian Jin and Rose Yu and will develop methods to independently assess the reliability of these systems. That team plans an open-source testbed that can simulate real-world tasks and show how and why an agent fails, stays within set boundaries, or can be audited. The aim is to put such evaluation tools within reach of researchers and organizations outside the companies that build the systems.

The center launches with $1 million in support over three years for its two research initiatives, and the Halıcıoğlu School will also give participating researchers access to a shared computing cluster valued at $250,000. The effort will draw on UC San Diego faculty, postdoctoral researchers, visiting scholars, and collaborators from other universities and industry. UC San Diego Chancellor Pradeep K. Khosla said universities have an important role in making sure AI development serves people and society, and that the center reflects the university's commitment to shaping AI's future rather than only responding to it. Rajesh K. Gupta, dean of the Halıcıoğlu School, said the center builds on the university's earlier contributions to the foundations of modern AI. Cristina Della Coletta, dean of the School of Arts and Humanities, said humanistic expertise is needed alongside technical work to keep AI aligned with human values and the common good.

Articles.Title: UC San Diego Launches Center for Principled Agentic Intelligence

stories.Headline: New initiative will explore AI’s role in society, humanities
stories.Summary:
The Cornell College of Arts and Sciences has launched a new program called the Humanities, Social Sciences + AI initiative, which was announced in an article published on October 29, 2026. The program is designed to help students and scholars understand how artificial intelligence affects culture, governance, ethics, communication, creativity, labor and social organization. It is administered by the college and aims to prepare students to shape an AI-driven world while encouraging interdisciplinary teaching, research and public engagement. The first year is funded through the Cornell AI Initiative and a gift from John Josephson '83 and Carolina Zapf.

The initiative has three core components meant to bring together faculty, students, postdoctoral scholars and outside practitioners. Its intellectual center is a postdoctoral fellowship program that is currently recruiting five fellows for appointments of up to two years. These fellows will research the social, political, ethical, cultural and economic effects of AI while also teaching undergraduate and graduate students. Applications for the fellowships are being accepted through November 15. A separate visitor program will bring people working on AI in real-world settings to campus for public talks and conversations with students and faculty.

The first distinguished visitor, Paul Graham '86, founder of Y Combinator and co-founder of Viaweb, was on campus during the week of October 26. He gave a public talk titled "How to Turn Yourself Into a Startup Founder" and led a faculty forum on what AI means for the humanities and social sciences. The article says that five to six AI practitioners-in-residence, drawn from industry, government, civil society and the cultural sectors, will each spend one to two weeks on campus giving lectures, running workshops, advising research and collaborating across departments. The initiative is being led and promoted by Dean Peter John Loewen, the Harold Tanner Dean of Arts and Sciences, who said the goal is to ensure AI develops in ways that strengthen society, democracy and human flourishing.

The initiative also includes an interdisciplinary university-wide minor called AI & Society, which is still in development and will draw on political science, philosophy, history, literature, economics and sociology. Additional planned activities include an annual AI and Society symposium, research workshops, professional development for postdoctoral scholars, and outreach and communications efforts. The article presents the initiative as a way to position Cornell as a leader in linking AI with humanistic and social scientific scholarship, building on its existing strength in technical AI development. The article does not provide a timeline for the minor's launch or for the first symposium.

Articles.Title: New initiative will explore AI’s role in society, humanities

stories.Headline: Coping with AI in our Communities
stories.Summary:
A four-part public forum series titled "Coping with AI in our Communities" is being held at College of the Atlantic, a college in Maine, running from October 25 through November 15. The series, announced on the college's website on October 28, 2026, is organized around current research on the problems people face in coping with advanced AI systems. The organizers say these systems increasingly behave less like obedient tools and more like insubordinate employees, independent agents, threatening competitors, and manipulators. Speakers will examine local and global challenges along with strategies for responding in individual lives and communities.

The series is free and open to all, though pre-registration is required for those who want to attend online. Sessions take place on Sundays at 6 p.m. in Room 102 of the Center for Human Ecology and are streamed live over Zoom. The dates and themes are October 25, on challenges and strategies for coping with AI in peaceful, ecological and spiritual ways; November 1, on negotiating futures with AI through a peace studies approach; November 8, on reclaiming digital commons in Maine through human-ecological approaches to community empowerment; and November 15, on spiritual approaches to AI drawing on Catholic, Quaker and Buddhist perspectives. Questions can be directed to the listed email address or to the phone number 207-460-1163.

The forums are presented by College of the Atlantic, and the announcement frames them as an alternative to approaches taken by researchers and companies, which the announcement says have been trying to engineer control over AI machines while also making them more capable at engineering than humans. The forum instead draws on peace studies, human ecology, and diverse spiritual and faith traditions. The organizers pose the central questions of how people can benefit from helpful AI while safeguarding families, companies and communities, and how they can keep their futures human. A recording of highlights from the first forum in the series is already available, according to the announcement.

Articles.Title: Coping with AI in our Communities

stories.Headline: Alumnus to speak on ‘AI in mental health’ for February Paris Lecture
stories.Summary:
Campbell University announced that Dr. Samuel Faulkner, a 2013 Campbell graduate, will be the featured speaker at the annual Paris Lecture on February 8 at the Oscar N. Harris Student Union. His talk is titled "Faster Than the Evidence: What AI Is Already Doing in Mental Health." Faulkner is a licensed psychologist and nationally certified school psychologist. The announcement was published on October 29, 2026.

Faulkner serves as clinical director of the NEST Clinic, a school-integrated psychiatric clinic that offers outpatient and partial hospitalization services, which he designed and launched through the Central Susquehanna Intermediate Unit in Pennsylvania. Earlier, he held directorships at Geisinger, where he led the Pediatric Bridge Clinic and pediatric behavioral health consultation across several emergency departments and a children's hospital. He also served as an assistant professor of psychiatry at Geisinger Commonwealth School of Medicine. His current research examines how AI tools respond to people in crisis, including safety protocol design and evaluation of crisis response in AI systems.

According to Faulkner, artificial intelligence has entered mental health care faster than the evidence supporting it. Such tools are already writing clinical notes, screening for risk, triaging patients and answering people late at night. He argues that most of these tools arrived without the kind of testing expected of other clinical interventions. His lecture will look at what research supports, where the tools studied and the tools people actually use have diverged, how these systems fail, and which ethical questions remain unanswered. He said students and faculty will leave with better questions to ask of these tools and a clearer view of why frontline clinical judgment should shape how they are built.

The Paris Lecture Series is made possible by a gift from Dr. John Viehe, who taught at Campbell for many years after a career in military intelligence. The series honors his mother, Ethel Paris Viehe, and his aunts, Florence Edith Paris and Cora Paris Hagen. Faulkner earned his Bachelor of Science in Psychology from Campbell in 2013 and his Ph.D. in Health Psychology, with a concentration in pediatric school psychology, from East Carolina University. Campbell named him Distinguished Alumnus in Psychology in 2021, and he is the founder of Dr. Sam's Solutions, LLC.

Articles.Title: Alumnus to speak on ‘AI in mental health’ for February Paris Lecture

stories.Headline: Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue
stories.Summary:
A University of Florida computer science professor, Sumit Jha, has developed a system aimed at stopping artificial intelligence agents from drifting off their assigned tasks. The system, called ATLAS, monitors a large language model as it generates output and senses when the model starts to stray, then steers it back on course. The work was described in a paper titled "Drift No More: Spectral Locking for Long-Horizon Open-Weight Multi-agent AI," co-authored by Jha along with Vishal Pramanik, Maisha Maliha and Susmit Jha. The paper has been accepted to the 2026 Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing, which runs October 24 to 29 in Budapest.

The approach works inside the model itself rather than checking answers after the fact. ATLAS does not require retraining the model, does not add significant computing demands, and does not slow the model down, according to the university. Jha described the problem as "role decoherence," where an agent given a long-running role gradually loses track of that role as it accumulates many other instructions. The system continually reinforces three questions: what the mission is, what the agent is responsible for, and what is currently true. When drift is detected, it applies the smallest set of internal changes needed to return the model to its original task, and it does nothing when the agent is still on track.

Jha, a professor in the university's Department of Computer and Information Science and Engineering, is the researcher leading the work and framed it as part of a broader effort to make AI systems more controllable and understandable. The article ties the research to recent reports of AI agents gaining more autonomy and sometimes behaving in unintended ways, including agents accessing government websites and an Anthropic model submitting an anonymous tip to a police department in July about an unsolved murder. Jha said the goal is to correct drift before it reaches the next message, so that other agents do not build on the error. The article does not describe deployment plans or results beyond the paper's acceptance, so it is not clear when or how the system might be used outside research.

Articles.Title: Engineering researcher seeks to prevent AI agents from going rogue

stories.Headline: Memorandum of Understanding Between The Government of the United States of America and the Government of Finland Regarding the Technology Prosperity Deal
stories.Summary:
The United States and Finland have signed a Memorandum of Understanding on a Technology Prosperity Deal, a framework for joint work on science and technology. The document was published by the White House on October 29, 2026, at 05:00 UTC. It states that both governments want to strengthen industrial cooperation and speed up the development, deployment, and adoption of emerging technologies. It builds on a 1995 agreement on scientific and technological cooperation signed at Washington, as well as earlier joint statements on quantum information science and advanced wireless communications. The memorandum says its aim is to enable collaboration in several areas, including next-generation connectivity, quantum advantage, energy leadership, advanced semiconductors, space, secure artificial intelligence systems, biotechnology, research security, shipbuilding, and Arctic technology.

The memorandum sets out specific areas of planned cooperation rather than binding obligations in the text provided. In telecommunications, the two sides intend to coordinate on research and development, finance exports of trusted technology stacks, and align positions in international bodies such as the International Telecommunication Union, including ahead of the 2026 ITU Plenipotentiary and the 2027 World Radiocommunication Conference. In quantum technology, the plan includes aligning supply chains, supporting commercial pipelines between the two countries, and endorsing the adoption of post-quantum cryptographic standards. On energy, the participants plan work on small modular reactors, nuclear fuel lifecycle issues, geothermal technology, energy storage, critical minerals, and fusion.

The article also says the participants intend to deepen cooperation on space security, space exploration, and commercialization of space technology. The memorandum is presented as a joint commitment by the Government of the United States of America and the Government of Finland, which refer to themselves as the Participants. The text does not name individual officials as authors or signatories in the portion provided. It describes the arrangement as a way to strengthen stability, security, and competitiveness through deeper ties with strategic partners.

The document uses language about fortifying freedom and prosperity for future generations and elevating the U.S.-Finland alliance. The articles provided do not describe next steps, implementation timelines, funding amounts, or a formal review process beyond the listed intentions, so those details are not available here. The memorandum is one of several bilateral science and technology arrangements the two countries have pursued, and it extends an existing cooperation framework rather than creating a new one from scratch. More to follow.

Articles.Title: Memorandum of Understanding Between The Government of the United States of America and the Government of Finland Regarding the Technology Prosperity Deal

stories.Headline: CMU to Host Challenge to Put Scientific Data to Work With AI
stories.Summary:
Carnegie Mellon University will host the inaugural ProtoStar Challenge, a new initiative announced on October 29, 2026, with partners including Hugging Face, the Open Research Community Accelerator and the Astera Institute. The effort aims to make scientific datasets easier for researchers and AI tools to use, since data is often scattered across systems, stored in incompatible formats or missing documentation. The challenge is scheduled for November 2 to 13 and centers on energy and climate resilience, one of the grand challenge areas guiding CMU's Miami campus. Universities taking part through the Open Forum for AI include Purdue, Georgia Tech, Arizona State and George Washington University.

The first challenge, called Climate Risk Intelligence, will use AI to analyze extreme weather trends and suggest climate adaptation strategies. Participants will work with historical temperature and precipitation records from 210 U.S. cities. Teams from inside and outside CMU are eligible to join. The projects are meant to test what makes scientific knowledge reusable, and organizers say documenting what works and where participants run into obstacles should help improve the infrastructure behind open science. The program is intended as a recurring series hosted by partner universities.

Jignesh Patel, founding dean and vice president of CMU Miami, said addressing energy and climate challenges requires both environmental knowledge and computational expertise, and that the challenge brings those strengths together around specific scientific problems. Avijit Ghosh, lead technical AI policy researcher at Hugging Face, said the company wants to work directly with academic partners, learn how they use its tools and develop approaches that make AI-ready open science more effective at scale. Sayeed Choudhury, associate dean at the University Libraries and executive director of the Open Forum for AI, said universities have long created and hosted scientific datasets and called ProtoStar an infrastructure-building program. He also encouraged researchers to share suitable datasets and models through Hugging Face, which appears on the NIH list of generalist repositories.

The University Libraries have funded access to Hugging Face's Academia Hub for students, faculty and staff across CMU's campuses, and it will serve as the central workspace for the ProtoStar challenges. The collaboration extends a longstanding Libraries commitment to making research broadly accessible and usable, and it builds on the Libraries' role in founding the Open Forum for AI, which seeks human-centered, responsible and transparent AI. The articles frame the work as a step beyond simply publishing research, focusing on whether scientific data can actually be put to use. They do not describe outcomes or results from the challenge.

Articles.Title: CMU to Host Challenge to Put Scientific Data to Work With AI

stories.Headline: Incoming first-year students build AI literacy in summer engineering programs
stories.Summary:
Penn State's Center for Engineering Outreach and Inclusion has reworked two summer programs for incoming first-year students to build artificial intelligence literacy, according to a university release dated October 28, 2026. The changes were made to the six-week Engineering Summer Bridge program and the four-day Multicultural Engineering Program Orientation, known as MEPO, which runs the week before fall classes begin. This summer, Engineering Summer Bridge added weekly Critical AI Literacy Lunch and Learns, lectures on the development and deployment of AI systems. The lectures drew on research from the AI Institute for Societal Decision Making, an initiative led by Carnegie Mellon University with collaborators including Penn State. Students used the lunch sessions to plan solutions for disaster response and recovery, starting from the communities they wanted to help rather than forcing AI into their designs.

The lunchtime format was chosen to keep the setting low stakes so students could engage without becoming overwhelmed. The sessions also cover cognitive and social sciences, parts of the humanities, and human-AI interaction, which the program presents as a foundation for future coursework and careers. MEPO's design competition has used a custom chatbot since 2024, developed with Penn State's Human in Computing and Cognition Lab. The chatbot is trained to guide students through each year's challenge, improve factual accuracy, and avoid suggesting complete solutions. Students described using it to test their understanding of their scenarios, and one team worked on helping hazmat crews contain dangerous gases in a skyscraper.

Christopher Dancy, an associate professor at Penn State who directs the lab and is a principal investigator in the AI institute, led the Lunch and Learn design and said the aim was to give students a solid base before they take on AI-heavy coursework. Lauren Griggs, director of the Multicultural Engineering Program that runs both programs, said students from underrepresented groups who took part in either program were more likely to stay in the College of Engineering than similar students who did not. She framed the programs as a way to keep human connection central as AI systems become more common. The article names sponsors for both programs and notes that the AI institute work is supported by National Science Foundation grant IIS 2229881, with the MEPO work supported under award 2144887. It does not describe any further changes planned for next summer.

Articles.Title: Incoming first-year students build AI literacy in summer engineering programs

stories.Headline: Quantum, fusion and AI stand out during DOE leader’s campus visit - UW–Madison News
stories.Summary:
On Monday, October 26, 2026, Under Secretary for Science Darío Gil of the U.S. Department of Energy spent a daylong visit touring laboratories and research spaces at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. Hosted by Vice Chancellor for Research Dorota Brzezinska, the visit showcased the university's work in quantum science, fusion energy, national security, critical minerals and biotechnology. Gil also toured the Proteus autonomous laboratory at the Wisconsin Energy Institute, along with the Great Lakes Bioenergy Research Center and the Wisconsin Crop Innovation Center. Discussions centered on the growing role of artificial intelligence in research and teaching, which one campus leader said has changed everything about the classroom.

The visit also tied into the university's part in the Department of Energy's Genesis Mission, under which UW–Madison recently received five Round 1 awards. Those awards support projects in artificial intelligence, fusion energy, critical mineral recovery and advanced computing. According to the article, the university earned more Genesis awards than any public university in the nation, tying Stanford University and trailing only the Massachusetts Institute of Technology. Gil urged participants to become an integral part of the Genesis platform and to align campus strengths with national scientific priorities.

Participants also stressed the university's longstanding leadership in Department of Energy-supported bioenergy research. A session with early-career faculty, graduate students and postdoctoral researchers explored how federal investment and AI, machine learning and advanced computing are being used to tackle research challenges. Rose Cersonsky, a chemical and biological engineering professor, said AI has changed the faculty's responsibility in preparing students for the world beyond campus. A fusion energy roundtable highlighted a plan to build a fusion innovation hub based on the university's plasma physics expertise and its WHAM prototype device, which operates with Realta.

Participants called for collaboration among universities, industry, government agencies and national laboratories. Gil challenged attendees to think boldly about where their research could stand in five to 10 years. Brzezinska said the work is about more than university growth, describing it as a way to build a statewide, regional and national ecosystem for translating research, strengthening supply chains, developing workforce and expanding manufacturing. The article does not describe any next steps beyond the visit itself.

Articles.Title: Quantum, fusion and AI stand out during DOE leader’s campus visit - UW–Madison News

stories.Headline: USF combines AI-powered mapping and community outreach to fight dengue
stories.Summary:
Hillsborough County is facing its largest dengue outbreak on record, with more than 350 locally acquired cases reported this year, and University of South Florida faculty and students are helping public health officials respond. Their work combines predictive mapping, mosquito control training, neighborhood outreach and multilingual public education. Dengue is a viral infection spread by the bites of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes, and its symptoms include high fever, headache, joint pain and rash. Local officials declared a state of emergency in early October, and the county went on to account for roughly 84% of Florida's dengue cases.

The effort relies on geographic artificial intelligence, or Geo-AI, to predict where mosquito breeding habitats are likely to emerge rather than only reacting to reported cases. Benjamin Jacob, an associate professor of biostatistics and data science, leads a team that analyzes satellite imagery and environmental data, including rainfall, temperature and weather patterns, to flag areas at elevated risk. The team also trained Florida Department of Health and Hillsborough County personnel at USF Riverfront Park to use GIS, GPS and satellite imagery to locate potential breeding sites and record their coordinates for field crews. Separately, USF students and volunteers, working with the Florida Department of Health, went door to door in affected neighborhoods, leaving information on preventing mosquito breeding around homes.

Jacob said the models could help agencies focus mosquito control, public education and disease surveillance where they are needed most, and could later be adapted for West Nile virus, Zika virus and chikungunya. Caitlin Wolfe, director of the COPH Bull Professional Engagement Network, said the outreach stressed the message "spray, drain and cover," arguing that reducing standing water reduces mosquito breeding and lowers dengue risk. Claudia Parvanta, director of the USF Center for Social Marketing, led the creation of plain-language dengue materials drawn from Florida Department of Health, CDC and EPA guidance and reviewed by USF experts. Those materials were translated into Spanish, Haitian Creole, Farsi, Arabic, Portuguese and Russian, the last by a volunteer through the Largo Library ESL program, after requests from the Tampa Bay Refugee Task Force.

Articles.Title: USF combines AI-powered mapping and community outreach to fight dengue

stories.Headline: Body Sensors and AI May Lead to New Kinds of Learning
stories.Summary:
Researchers at NJIT have proposed a concept called Minds and Machines: A Neuro-Adaptive AI Learning Companion, which combines physiological sensors, AI and extended reality to help students stay on track in their studies. The idea was reported on October 28, 2026, by NJIT News, with Evan Koblentz as the writer. Under the concept, students would wear a wrist device or headset that detects bodily signs of distress, such as overloaded brain waves measured by electroencephalogram, during lectures or other lessons. The article presents this as a way to spot students who may be falling behind or who are highly engaged and ready for harder material. The project is funded by a $50,000 university grant.

When those signs appear, an AI system would choose a different way to present the topic, drawing on preprogrammed knowledge of educational best practices and student motivation. The new material could be delivered in real time or later, and it could use augmented or virtual reality to make concepts more vivid. The approach could also extend beyond classrooms into hands-on settings such as NJIT's makerspace. Jessica Simon, a neuroscientist and pedagogical and instructional innovation specialist at the Center for Educational and Innovation and Excellence, is joint principal investigator with Zhifeng Kou, associate chair of biomedical engineering. Simon said personalized teaching has been shown to raise performance by at least two standard deviations, though the article notes the field of neuroscience-informed education is still young.

Kou said his interest grew from years of using AI for biomedical imaging analysis, and that when large language models emerged, he saw a way to help students learn. The team now faces the main hurdle of making the parts work together in a live classroom rather than only in a laboratory. They must separate useful body signals from background electrical noise and handle several signals while customizing instruction in real time. The researchers must also decide whether students are comfortable sharing body data and make sure that data stays private. Once the technical problems are solved, they plan to turn the research into a product that could be shared with other universities.

Several other faculty members are co-principal investigators on the project: Nicole Bosca, Elisa Kallioniemi, Bryan Pfister, Mengjia Xu and Lin Zhao. Kou emphasized that the goal is to build something practical and impactful, not only scientific. The article does not give a timeline for when the product might reach students or describe any results from testing with students. It frames the work as an early-stage effort in a growing field that combines education and neuroscience.

Articles.Title: Body Sensors and AI May Lead to New Kinds of Learning

stories.Headline: Miami Dade College to Host XI Presidential Dialogue on Democracy, Freedom and Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Miami Dade College will host the XI Presidential Dialogue of Grupo IDEA on Tuesday, November 10, 2026, at its Wolfson Campus in downtown Miami. The event runs from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m., brings together former presidents and other leaders from the Americas and Spain, and will be conducted in Spanish with simultaneous English interpretation. It will also be streamed on MDC Live. The announcement was published by the college on October 28, 2026.

The dialogue centers on the theme of how societies can protect public well-being without giving up freedom in the age of digital technology and artificial intelligence. Two panels are planned, one on freedom and the rule of law compared with stability in the Americas, and another on freedom of expression, corporate power and digital surveillance. The program closes with a declaration from the IDEA Group and the presentation of the 2026 Sebastián Piñera Prize for Freedom to María Corina Machado, the Venezuelan opposition leader and Nobel Peace Prize laureate. Speakers listed include José María Aznar, Laura Chinchilla, Jamil Mahuad, Jeanine Áñez, Hipólito Mejía, Federico Franco, Jorge Quiroga, Miguel Ángel Rodríguez, Álvaro Uribe and Luis Almagro, along with Dominican Foreign Minister Víctor Bisono.

Miami Dade College President Madeline Pumariega said the college is proud to host the event and that its focus on artificial intelligence fits the college's role as a leader in AI education and workforce development. She said the college hopes to engage students, faculty, staff and fellows of its Institute for Freedom in the Americas in discussions about using AI responsibly while protecting individual freedoms and democratic institutions. Asdrúbal Aguiar, Secretary General of IDEA Group, argued that the democratic constitutional state and rule of law appear to be weakening, and warned that the West risks being drawn toward alternative authoritarian models. Media representatives must register in advance, and the college says further logistics will be sent to confirmed attendees.

Articles.Title: Miami Dade College to Host XI Presidential Dialogue on Democracy, Freedom and Artificial Intelligence

stories.Headline: Outskirts In: A Doctoral Student Brings UVM Together on AI - University of Vermont
stories.Summary:
A doctoral student at the University of Vermont has organized a campus forum on artificial intelligence, drawing students, faculty, and community members from across disciplines. The first Community Forum on Artificial Intelligence was held on a Friday afternoon in a packed partitioned ballroom, and the event was funded by a $10,000 grant from UVM's AI Innovation Fund. The grant was received in 2026 by Frances Starn, a second-year PhD student in the College of Education and Social Services, together with Rigo Melgar, a PhD student in the Rubenstein School of Environment and Natural Resources. Starn said she joined the university's AI Taskforce in 2025 because she saw little shared understanding of how the campus was engaging with the technology. The article was published on October 29, 2026.

The forum was built to be low tech, with laptops and phones discouraged and graduate facilitators supplying markers and sticky notes. Three speakers presented: Julia Zimmerman, a postdoctoral researcher at the Vermont Complex Systems Institute, who discussed how large language models produce useful output without the human processes that created language; Vermont State Representative Brian Cina, who described the state's AI governance work; and Melgar, who led a closing exercise on the deeper economic and ecological systems beneath AI. Participants at each table weighed the decisions people face about AI and generally agreed that the technology is being adopted faster than society can understand it. Cina said Vermont's task force, which traveled the state collecting input, informed Act 132, passed in 2022, which made Vermont among the first states to establish an AI division to oversee AI use across state government.

Starn said she was pleased with how the event drew people from different disciplines, and she hopes more undergraduates will attend the next forum. That forum is scheduled for February 2027, with the exact date and speaker lineup still being arranged, and Starn said a third event may take the form of a more focused summit. Justin Garwood, Starn's advisor on the grant, said AI raises questions that no single discipline can answer alone and that bringing students and faculty together helps the university think critically about responsible use. He also said the conversations can help the College of Education and Social Services move beyond abstract debate toward practical ideas for how UVM should respond. The article's closing remarks frame the work as a reminder that the university is still at the beginning of its engagement with AI.

Articles.Title: Outskirts In: A Doctoral Student Brings UVM Together on AI - University of Vermont

stories.Headline: Oracle launches AI consulting practice with OpenAI
stories.Summary:
Oracle has launched an AI consulting practice built on OpenAI technology, reported on October 29, 2026. The unit sits within Oracle Customer Success Services and is called the Oracle AI Services Practice. Oracle's consulting teams will lead customer engagements, while OpenAI will help train those teams on its models and tools. The move reflects large organisations moving from testing AI tools to using them in daily operations. Oracle said customers want faster deployment, tighter cost control and clearer business results.

The practice covers four areas. The first is Oracle Fusion Cloud Applications, where customers can build AI agents using OpenAI models, either built-in or their own supported large language models. The second is AI application development on Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, using OpenAI Codex and APIs with OCI Enterprise AI to run production systems. The third focuses on enterprise data, linking Oracle's data platforms and databases with foundation models, including OpenAI's, to build agents across internal and external sources. The fourth is security testing, where Oracle AI Security Mesh uses OpenAI cyber models to find vulnerabilities before attackers do, with customers setting the testing scope.

Oracle says the practice supports customers through the full adoption process, from finding high-impact uses and validating systems to setting governance controls and supporting use after launch. Oracle Customer Success Services will use its Innovation Studios to identify use cases, and its specialists will design, build, test and deploy systems. Oracle also plans, with OpenAI, to train and certify one million developers and professionals through Oracle University, covering consultants, customers and partners. The curriculum includes role-based learning, hands-on Codex training and certifications. Oracle described the goal as building practical expertise among the people who design, implement and run its systems.

Oracle's announcement is part of a wider pattern in which technology groups package consulting, governance and training with AI software sales as customers seek help moving from pilots to wider rollouts. For Oracle, the practice deepens its commercial alignment with OpenAI by linking OpenAI models and coding tools more closely to its applications, infrastructure and support services. The articles do not give financial terms of the partnership or a timeline for rollout beyond the training target. Oracle said that enterprise AI adoption depends on skilled people who understand both AI and the business processes it is meant to improve.
