stories.Headline: [INTERVIEW] Fines won't fix problem: Korea needs new playbook as AI changes hacking paradigm
stories.Summary:
Suspected AI-assisted cyberattacks have spread through Korea's financial sector, reaching commercial banks, brokerages and cryptocurrency exchanges. On Wednesday, brokerage firm Daishin Securities, cryptocurrency exchange Bithumb and asset manager Mirae Asset Global Investments reported hacking incidents, adding to a string of similar cases involving 16 financial firms earlier this month. On Thursday, virtual asset exchange Prabang reported losses of 100 million won ($75,000), the first reported case of actual asset losses in the recent hacking spree. Financial authorities have also detected large-scale scanning attempts against financial systems from IP address ranges associated with North Korea, for the first time.

Lim Jong-in, chair of the AI committee at Soongsil University and a former presidential special adviser on cybersecurity, argued that fines alone will not solve the problem. He said that humans cannot keep pace with AI agents and that the whole paradigm of cybersecurity has changed, so both government and industry must rethink their defenses. He warned that companies that suffer attacks are also victims, and that they vary widely in their security capabilities and budgets. He added that the threat reaches beyond finance, since a breach at a major semiconductor company could spread across the broader economy.

Lim called for a task force led by the presidential office to develop a Korean version of a cognitive zero-trust architecture (CZTA). The task force would bring together the National Intelligence Service, the Ministry of Science and ICT, and the Ministry of Trade, Industry and Resources. Under the proposed design, the CZTA would use AI to continuously assess user behavior and emerging threats, flag suspicious activity and adjust access privileges in real time. Lim also cautioned against assuming who is behind the attacks, since attackers can use proxy IP addresses to hide their origins, and he said identifying perpetrators is growing harder because AI agents leave few traces.

Articles.Title: [INTERVIEW] Fines won't fix problem: Korea needs new playbook as AI changes hacking paradigm

stories.Headline: New AI tool helps scientists identify bacteria hidden in soil
stories.Summary:
A new artificial intelligence tool called BBERT, developed by researchers at the Hebrew University of Jerusalem and partner institutions, helps scientists identify bacterial DNA hidden in soil samples. The study was published on October 29, 2026, in the journal Nucleic Acids Research. It was led by Dr. Amir Erez of the university's Racah Institute of Physics and Dr. Omri M. Finkel of its Department of Plant and Environmental Sciences. Dmitry Alekhin, Dr. Moshe Alon and Dr. Tomer Sidi contributed equally, working with colleagues from the University of Haifa and the Volcani Institute of the Agricultural Research Organization.

The problem the tool addresses is that a single soil sample yields millions of short DNA fragments from many organisms, and many soil bacteria are missing from reference databases. Existing tools match fragments against stored sequences, so unmatched DNA often stays unidentified or is labeled incorrectly. BBERT takes a different approach by learning patterns in bacterial DNA, which lets it assess unfamiliar fragments without finding a match. It can recognize bacterial fragments only 100 DNA letters long. The researchers say this makes the tool useful for analyzing the so-called microbial dark matter that earlier methods could not explain.

In benchmark tests, BBERT distinguished bacterial from nonbacterial DNA with about 90% accuracy, and it identified protein-making fragments with about 88% accuracy. When applied to 1,969 publicly available soil DNA data sets, it classified a substantial share of fragments that a widely used comparison tool had left unclassified. The team also found that fragments that could not be linked to known functions were more likely to contain nonbacterial DNA. In simulated mixtures, filtering with BBERT cut genome reconstruction time from about 66 hours to 25 hours per data set, with fewer errors and about 96% of bacterial genome coverage retained.

The tool has limits that the researchers acknowledge. It can miss some bacterial fragments and can confuse chloroplast DNA from plants with bacterial sequences, and it can struggle to separate bacteria from archaea. It can run on a personal computer with a suitable graphics card, and the team demonstrated it on a laptop, which could help laboratories without large computing facilities. The articles do not say when the tool will be widely available, but they suggest researchers may use it to revisit existing environmental DNA collections.

Articles.Title: New AI tool helps scientists identify bacteria hidden in soil

stories.Headline: Students Call for AI Literacy, Purposeful Tech Use in Schools
stories.Summary:
On October 28, 2026, GovTech.com's Center for Digital Education published a report on a Project Tomorrow webinar and survey urging schools to teach students AI literacy and to use technology purposefully. The webinar, hosted by the education nonprofit Project Tomorrow, presented findings from its 2025-26 Speak Up National Report, which drew on the views of more than 95,000 K-12 students, parents, educators and administrators at 1,023 schools nationwide. Four middle and high school students spoke during the webinar, which Project Tomorrow CEO Julie Evans moderated. The report found that 46 percent of high school students had learned about AI through their own experimentation, compared with 30 percent who had learned about it in class.

The article also describes how student use of AI for studying and research has grown. The share of high school students using AI for those purposes daily or weekly rose from 23 percent in the 2023-24 school year to 40 percent in 2025-26, and daily or weekly use for writing and idea generation rose from 21 percent to 29 percent over the same period. Among high school respondents, 48 percent wanted teachers to connect lessons to real-life situations, an equal share wanted more chances to build job-relevant skills, 44 percent wanted more self-paced learning, and 41 percent wanted teachers to act on student suggestions for improving classes. The report also found that only 11 percent of teachers felt very comfortable letting students use AI resources, while 35 percent felt very comfortable facilitating collaboration through digital tools.

The students who spoke framed their recommendations around teaching how AI works, not only how to use it. Tharun, a Pennsylvania high school senior, said students should learn where AI answers come from so they can understand why those answers may be wrong. Jordan, an Alabama junior, argued that instruction on AI's limits makes misuse less likely, and he described a geometry project in which he used Google Earth and ChatGPT to redesign his school courtyard to scale. Eloise, a Virginia seventh grader, said her research teacher had students check AI-generated passages for inaccuracies and bias. Evans said schools should consider whether technology gives students chances to apply knowledge and build skills, rather than simply reproducing conventional instruction on digital devices.

The article notes that the students also called for clear, consistently enforced rules on technology, with Eloise emphasizing consistency and Kennedy, an eighth grader in California, discussing her school's cellphone restrictions. The article presents these views as evidence that technology policy need not be framed only around access or prohibition. It does not describe any formal requirement, rule change or follow-up action by a school system or government body. The reporting ends with Tharun's view that schools should teach students what these tools are and how they work so they are better prepared for an uncertain future.

Articles.Title: Students Call for AI Literacy, Purposeful Tech Use in Schools

stories.Headline: Oklahoma lawmakers discuss AI use in state agencies to improve efficiency
stories.Summary:
Oklahoma lawmakers met on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, to examine how state agencies are using artificial intelligence to improve their operations. The review is aimed at boosting efficiency while making sure proper safeguards are in place. The effort traces back to Gov. Kevin Stitt, who formed an AI Task Force in 2023 to help the state bring AI technology into its work and become a leader in the field. The state's approach is meant to balance faster operations with oversight that keeps people involved in decisions. The Oklahoma Department of Transportation is preparing to roll out a new AI-powered program to track the state's infrastructure more closely.

According to Tara Cullum, the agency's director of administration, the system can accurately identify the location of assets and the type of damage, then feed that information into the agency's own system. She said the program is close to going live and will be fully deployed in early 2027. The agency is also using AI to find better ways to reduce traffic noise, which it estimates will save more than $170,000 a year. Madeline Mitchell, a professor at the University of Central Oklahoma, said the question is not simply whether to use AI but how to layer governance and training so that a human stays in the loop. Her point was offered as context for the broader debate rather than as a verdict on any specific program.

Lawmakers have not yet decided on legislation, but they may consider drafting bills to regulate AI use in state agencies after Wednesday's study. Any such bills would follow from the review rather than being already written. The articles do not say whether the lawmakers reached any conclusions at the session or what specific rules, if any, would follow. The reporting also does not describe the cost of the broader AI effort beyond the traffic-noise savings. What comes next depends on whether lawmakers move forward with proposed regulation and how the infrastructure program performs after its planned 2027 rollout.

Articles.Title: Oklahoma lawmakers discuss AI use in state agencies to improve efficiency

stories.Headline: UBS Employees Run 12,700 AI Agents as Bank Automation Accelerates
stories.Summary:
UBS employees are using more than 12,700 personal artificial intelligence agents in their daily work, according to a press release the bank issued alongside its third quarter results, as reported by PYMNTS on October 29, 2026. The tools include software development agents used by 18,000 of the bank's software developers, and STAAT, a tool for financial advisor teams that has generated more than 30 million insights used in advising clients. UBS reports 608 live AI use cases in production, 81% more than a year earlier, and more than 1,090 applications in development. The bank describes these efforts as part of its investment in technology, capabilities and talent to enhance the client experience, strengthen infrastructure and increase efficiency.

UBS framed the spending as a way to position the firm for the future rather than as a set of specific mandates or changes to working arrangements. The release itself contains no further detail on how the agents are governed or how their use affects staffing. The article places the announcement within a wider trend in which financial firms concentrate AI on back-office work. A PYMNTS Intelligence report cited in the piece found that revenue recognition and accounting close, credit risk assessment and scoring, and sales forecasting and pipeline automation are the most adopted AI tasks in financial services and insurance. That same report found that 85% of financial services firms plan to increase their AI budgets over the next 12 months.

Other institutions cited in the article show similar moves. PYMNTS reported on October 23 that Customers Bank found a pilot of its AI-powered process closed select commercial loans in seven days, compared with a typical wait of 30 to 60 days, and its parent, Customers Bancorp, doubled its deployed AI agents in the latest quarter. Regions Financial Corp. said during an October 16 earnings call that it expects cybersecurity costs, which include frontier AI, to raise its adjusted noninterest expense by between 1.5% and 3.5% for full-year 2026. The article does not indicate any next steps for UBS beyond the continued investment described in the release.

Articles.Title: UBS Employees Run 12,700 AI Agents as Bank Automation Accelerates

stories.Headline: Gaon Cable Wins 120 Billion Won AI Data Center Cable Order From US Tech Giant
stories.Summary:
Gaon Cable, a subsidiary of LS Cable & System, said on October 29, 2026 that its US manufacturing subsidiary, LSCUS, will supply power distribution cables worth 120 billion won to a global cloud company. The order is the largest power distribution cable award a single global technology company has given to a South Korean supplier. The products are medium-voltage cables that will be delivered in stages to several AI data center projects in the United States, running from October 2026 through the first half of 2027. Gaon Cable is also in talks with the customer about additional supplies.

Demand for these cables is rising as campus-style AI data centers, which group several data center buildings within one complex, become more common. The cables connect buildings and substations inside those campuses. To meet this demand, LSCUS will start a new power distribution cable production line in the fourth quarter of this year and plans further expansion in 2027, which would double its production capacity from current levels. The articles say LSCUS revenue is expected to rise from about 440 billion won last year to roughly 870 billion won this year.

Revenue is projected to reach 1.5 trillion won next year, more than triple last year's level. The announcement came from Gaon Cable, which has supplied power infrastructure products to global technology companies and US neocloud providers in cooperation with LS Cable & System. The company's statement, as reported, described the contract as the largest of its kind awarded to a Korean supplier by a single global technology company. The articles do not name the cloud customer.

They also do not say who will supply the remaining orders or how the 2027 expansion will be financed. The order fits a broader push by suppliers to meet the power and cabling needs of AI infrastructure in the United States. Gaon Cable's plans show that its US capacity is central to serving that demand over the next two years. The articles do not report any further developments beyond the announced delivery schedule and the expected revenue growth.

Articles.Title: Gaon Cable Wins 120 Billion Won AI Data Center Cable Order From US Tech Giant - THE ELEC, Korea Electronics Industry Media

stories.Headline: Asian Publishers Gather in Seoul to Debate AI's Impact on Books
stories.Summary:
Publishers from across Asia will gather in Seoul from November 3 to 6, 2026, to examine how artificial intelligence is reshaping the publishing industry, according to the Korean Publishers Society, which announced the event on the 29th. Publishers from seven overseas markets, including Taiwan, Vietnam, Singapore, Indonesia, Thailand, Turkey and Germany, will join their Korean counterparts. The gathering is titled "Publishing in the Age of AI: Between Crisis and Opportunity." Participants will share hands-on experience and response strategies on issues such as AI copyright and technology adoption across acquisitions, translation, editing, production and marketing.

The program includes a roundtable at the JU youth culture center on November 4, where participants will discuss AI issues facing publishers in their countries. On November 5, participants will visit Kyobo Book Centre and Millie's Library to review Korea's bookstore sector and digital publishing. The centerpiece, the 2026 Asia Publishers Forum, will also be held on November 5 at the 50th Anniversary Hall of the Changbi Seogyo Building. Speakers include Song Kyung-seok of Hanbit Media, who will describe how publishers use AI in daily operations, and Bui Thu Ha of Vietnam's Alpha Books, who will discuss improving book discoverability. The 2026 Asia Book Award ceremony will take place at the same forum, with four titles named Asian Books of the Year.

Youngsuk Chi, chairman of Elsevier and a former president of both the Association of American Publishers and the International Publishers Association, wrote in a contribution to the society's webzine, Asia Publishing Insight, that AI training must begin with the permission of copyright holders. He warned that the real concern is not empty shelves but shelves filled with content that looks valuable yet is not. Yu Hua, author of the global bestsellers "To Live" and "Chronicle of a Blood Merchant," argued that AI's biggest weakness is that it almost never makes mistakes, noting that humanity's knowledge was largely discovered through error. He addressed the possibility that AI could replace writers. The society's webzine is built around this year's AI theme, and the reporting was produced by Lee Jae-yong for Seoul Economic Daily.

Articles.Title: Asian Publishers Gather in Seoul to Debate AI's Impact on Books - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: Busan to Open Korea's First 'Physical AI' Research Schools Next Year
stories.Summary:
Busan's Metropolitan Office of Education said on October 30, 2026 that it will become the first in South Korea to bring "physical AI" education into its public schools, pairing artificial intelligence with robots, sensors and other physical devices. The office plans to designate and begin operating five physical AI research schools starting next year, the first program of its kind in the country. The stated aim is to go beyond existing AI classes, which mostly stop at processing information on a screen, and to train students who can build AI that interacts with the physical world. Physical AI, as the articles describe it, combines artificial intelligence with equipment such as robots, autonomous driving modules and sensors so a machine can perceive its surroundings and move accordingly.

Under the plan, the research schools will use a convergence-style class model in which students define real-world problems themselves, debate them and work out solutions, rather than simply learning physical computing or coding. Before the program starts, the office will hold a physical AI education workshop on the afternoon of December 2 at the main auditorium of the Busan Educational Research and Information Institute, under the theme "Beyond the Screen, Into Reality." About 300 teachers and education specialists are expected to attend, and the session is meant to help them understand physical AI and design lessons suited to each school level. Speakers include Son Je-deuk, a supervisor at the office, who will present Busan's policy direction, and Lee In-ho, a professor at Pusan National University, who will give a lecture on the future of physical AI education. Teachers Park Jae-hyun, Lim Jae-cheol and Lim Byung-ryul, from elementary, middle and high schools, will share classroom practices.

The office links the program to real industries such as autonomous driving, smart factories and care robots, and argues that a early response at the public education level will shape students' future competitiveness. Superintendent Kim Seok-joon said that as AI moves beyond the screen, the educational environment has reached a major turning point. He said the workshop and research schools will be used to spread strong class models developed by teachers across Busan's classrooms. The articles do not give a budget for the program or describe how the five schools will be selected.

Articles.Title: Busan to Open Korea's First 'Physical AI' Research Schools Next Year - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: New York Enacts Landmark AI Chatbot Rules for Minors, With Fines Up to $25,000 per Violation
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul signed a law on Tuesday that bars AI companies from offering a range of chatbot features to users under 18 or to anyone whose age has not been verified. The measure, sponsored by state Senator Kristen Gonzalez and Assembly Member Alex Bores, cleared the state Senate in June and passed the Assembly unanimously. It takes effect in six months. Hochul also signed a separate law on internet-connected baby monitors, which takes effect in 90 days. Under the new rules, chatbots cannot pose as real people, claim to be alive or say they have human emotions.

They may not claim a romantic, personal, professional or authority-figure relationship with a child, and they may not use flattery meant to keep minors engaged. Bots also cannot promote or assist with suicide, self-harm, eating disorders or drug and alcohol use, or produce sexually explicit material. Companies must verify ages using more than one method, including at least one that does not rely solely on government-issued identification, and must delete age information after use. Violations carry civil penalties of up to $25,000 each, plus damages and restitution, and the state attorney general can order destruction of unlawfully collected data and models trained on it. Hochul framed the signing as a response to what she called too many tragic incidents involving AI, saying no company should be marketing chatbots to kids that encourage self-harm or pose as their friend.

Jim Steyer, founder and chief executive of Common Sense Media, called it a milestone and said the bill could serve as a template for other states. The governor's office cited a Common Sense Media survey finding that 72% of teens have used an AI companion. OpenAI has said it has already built child safety protections into ChatGPT and will keep improving the model. The signing comes as at least eight states have sued OpenAI this month over alleged harms to children, and as New York City barred public school students in 2-K through eighth grade from using generative AI tools in class for one year. The baby monitor law requires security features that block unauthorized viewing or listening, along with warning labels, after security firm Rapid7 graded nine monitors from eight companies with eight Fs and one D. Hochul made reining in Big Tech a central part of her reelection campaign, which the signing precedes by a week before Election Day.

Articles.Title: New York Enacts Landmark AI Chatbot Rules for Minors, With Fines Up to $25,000 per Violation - BigGo Finance

stories.Headline: Korea to Spend 5 Trillion Won by 2030 on AI, Robots at Smaller Factories
stories.Summary:
The South Korean government plans to spend more than 5 trillion won, about $3.5 billion, by 2030 to help small and medium-sized manufacturers adopt artificial intelligence and robots. The Ministry of SMEs and Startups announced the plan on the 29th at the 16th national policy coordination meeting, chaired by the prime minister and held in Cheonan, South Chungcheong Province. The stated aim is to combine AI and robotics with data gathered on factory floors to raise productivity at smaller firms. It also seeks to strengthen the competitiveness of the domestic smart manufacturing technology industry. Budget spending on the related programs begins in earnest next year.

The package centers on what the ministry calls a "3X strategy," linking digital transformation, AI transformation and robot transformation at smaller manufacturers. The plan targets digital transformation support at 30,000 small and medium-sized manufacturers and AI adoption at 6,000 firms. It aims to raise the digital transformation rate among these firms from 30% to 50%, and the AI adoption rate from about 1% to 10%. Support will be staged according to each company's technology level, with basic help for firms lacking the foundation for AI and advanced help for those already equipped. The ministry will also expand physical AI demonstrations on actual factory floors, applying articulated, collaborative and logistics mobile robots to verify performance and safety.

An official said the budget for smart factories and physical AI in the 2027 government budget proposal alone exceeds 1 trillion won. The package was prepared with the Ministry of Planning and Budget, the Ministry of Science and ICT and the Ministry of Trade and Industry. Under the plan, national strategic projects will feed into the smart factory deployment system. The existing Korea AI Manufacturing Platform will be upgraded into "Manufacturing AI 24," and the government will assess the economic value of manufacturing data.

Ownership of that data will stay with the company that generated it, to protect trade secrets. Regional hubs such as manufacturing AI data centers will be linked with testing facilities, and AI specialists will be trained with the four science and technology institutes playing a central role. The government also plans to designate strong performers as specialized smart manufacturing companies, nurturing 500 such firms by 2030. Minister of SMEs and Startups Lee So-young said factory floors at smaller manufacturers will become a stage where physical AI is tested and spread.

The Ministry of Science and ICT will handle core technology development, the Ministry of Trade and Industry will lead industry-specific AI transformation, and the Ministry of SMEs and Startups will spread the technology to smaller firms. An official warned that without enough testing opportunities for Korean-made robots, the domestic market could be eroded by Chinese robots. The plan's sector focus includes economic security industries, pharmaceuticals and biotechnology, climate technology and Korean consumer goods. Lee said the government will actively support smaller companies in transforming how they produce as part of national strategic projects.

Articles.Title: Korea to Spend 5 Trillion Won by 2030 on AI, Robots at Smaller Factories - Seoul Economic Daily

stories.Headline: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape
stories.Summary:
On September 30, 2026, Governor Newsom vetoed California bill SB 903, which would have barred companies from offering psychotherapy through AI chatbots and limited how far clinicians could rely on AI tools. Proponents said the bill kept clinicians involved in patient care, while opponents said it would force clinicians to review and sign off on AI activity constantly, even when that activity was routine. Newsom judged the bill overly broad, invited a narrower version, and stressed the need for guardrails on AI in healthcare. The episode reflects a broader national question about what role AI should play in psychotherapy.

Supporters of AI tools argue they can expand clinician capacity, letting providers serve more patients and improving access to care. Lawmakers, however, have warned against overreliance on AI, and several states have already regulated its use. Because the states have not reached consensus, their approaches differ considerably. The result is a legal landscape still in flux, with new legislation expected in 2027.

Across the healthcare sector, states generally permit AI use but have increasingly called for some regulation. Several states have barred health plans from using AI to make clinical decisions without clinician involvement, and similar federal bills are pending. Other states require that healthcare providers keep independent professional judgment over patient care when AI is involved. Some states also require disclosure to patients when AI is used in their care or in processing medical claims.

Among states that have acted on AI in psychotherapy, the focus has been on AI mental health chatbots and on how far therapists may rely on AI in clinical work. Nevada and Colorado both bar AI providers from presenting their systems as therapists, though Nevada goes further and bars AI chatbots from being offered, while Colorado instead blocks health plans from paying for AI psychotherapy services. Utah, by contrast, expressly permits AI mental health chatbots so long as they disclose that they are AI. Governor Newsom has said he will not sign the broad version, and Senator Padilla, the bill's author, has said he will reintroduce legislation when the 2027-28 session convenes on December 7, 2026.

Articles.Title: AI in Psychotherapy: An Evolving Regulatory Landscape - JD Supra

stories.Headline: GitHub Octoverse 2026: AI agents drive developer activity surge
stories.Summary:
Developers pushed code to GitHub 17.9 billion times in the 12 months ending September 2026, surpassing the combined activity of 2024 and 2025. The surge became sharp around June 2026, when AI agents moved from experimental tools to integral parts of developer workflows. Repositories configured with an AI agent logged eight times more commits than those without, which points to a faster pace of work. The findings come from GitHub's Octoverse 2026 report, published in late October 2026. Many of the same figures appear in coverage by TechGig, which reported them on October 29, 2026.

By September 2026, more than 40 per cent of pull requests on GitHub were started by an agent, up from 17 per cent in March. This shift means that directing an agent is becoming the first step for a growing share of development tasks. GitHub Copilot users are also spreading their work across models, with 61 per cent of users who manually selected a model using more than one in September 2026. The report also notes that the language an agent picks, when a developer does not specify one, is starting to shape language choice. TypeScript remained the most used language on GitHub, followed by Python and JavaScript.

TypeScript, Python, and Rust, the fastest-growing language communities, show merged pull requests with detected AI involvement at rates between 40 and 44 per cent. The United States, with 38.3 million developers, and India, with 32 million, remain the two largest developer communities on GitHub. Each country added more than 10 million developers over the past year. India has closed 28.3 per cent of its projected growth toward 57.5 million developers by 2030. AI adoption is also reaching beyond traditional software sectors, as public repositories serving mining, construction, health care, and agriculture have grown several times over since 2022.

Construction repositories show the highest share of agent-opened pull requests of any sector, at about 9 per cent. GitHub is responsible for the report and the platform data behind it. The company has also made GitHub Copilot Fusion, a tool for model orchestration, generally available, and it automatically selects the appropriate model for each step of the development process. The articles do not describe further plans or any next steps beyond the release of that tool.

Articles.Title: GitHub Octoverse 2026: AI agents drive developer activity surge

stories.Headline: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents
stories.Summary:
AssemblyAI has released AssemblyAI-TTS-1, its first text-to-speech model, and made it generally available. The model is aimed at voice agents handling live phone calls, where response speed and correct pronunciation affect whether a caller stays on the line. It is priced at $15 per 1M characters, with no annual contract and no concurrency tier to purchase. Developers who already use AssemblyAI's speech-to-text service can now handle both sides of a voice conversation with a single vendor. The model runs only on AssemblyAI's cloud, in the US (us-east-1) or EU (eu-north-1) regions, and no open weights or on-premises option is offered.

It can be reached through an HTTP API, a WebSocket API, or an OpenAI-compatible route, and the WebSocket session supports a cancel message for interrupting speech mid-reply. Output comes as mono PCM, mu-law or A-law at rates from 8 kHz to 48 kHz, with 24 kHz PCM as the native format. The launch includes a library of more than 4,000 voices and instant voice cloning, which requires a short recording and confirmation that the speaker has given permission. Six languages are supported at launch: English, Spanish, French, German, Italian and Portuguese.

AssemblyAI's own tests, dated October 28, 2026, show the model matching ElevenLabs v4 on entity accuracy, with a 93.7% score against 93.6%, at under a fifth of that model's price. The company reports a median time to first byte of 47 ms, the fastest of the models it tested. Independent results are more mixed, with a Cekura benchmark placing the model's median streaming latency at 159 ms and ranking it eighth of 19 timed models. Under the same benchmark, Inworld TTS-2 Flash posted 45 ms and 93.2% reading accuracy at the same price.

AssemblyAI also says the model lacks SSML, speed control, pronunciation dictionaries and emotion tags for now. AssemblyAI describes the model as a streaming system trained on millions of hours of audio, including real conversational data, that works on continuous audio representations rather than the discrete tokens used by most TTS models. The company says this approach improves realism and shortens the wait before speech begins. The launch was covered by MarkTechPost on October 29, 2026, and the article includes LiveKit and Pipecat reference agents that AssemblyAI has published for developers.

Articles.Title: AssemblyAI Ships AssemblyAI-TTS-1: A $15 per 1M Character Text-to-Speech API for Voice Agents

stories.Headline: RBC to block personal AI agents from access to online banking
stories.Summary:
Royal Bank of Canada, the country's largest bank, said on Tuesday that it will block third-party personal artificial intelligence agents from direct access to its digital properties, including online banking. The bank said it recognized the decision may disappoint the small portion of its clients who use these tools. RBC said the choice was made with the safety and security of its clients and systems at the forefront. The articles do not give a specific effective date for the block.

RBC chief executive Dave McKay said AI agents could help consumers, but they are becoming more autonomous, and the stakes are high if something goes wrong. He warned of risks ranging from fraud and consumer harm to effects that could spread more broadly through the financial system. In a LinkedIn post, McKay said trust is core to the bank's relationship with clients and that, while the bank values the time savings AI offers, nothing matters more than the security of client information. The articles describe an AI agent as software that acts autonomously for its users.

Evan Light, an associate professor at the University of Toronto, said such tools are largely unregulated and that giving them access to a personal bank account could lead them to act in ways a person would not want. He called RBC's decision wise and said he hoped it would push the government to take further steps to regulate AI in the financial sector. He added that there is pressure on industries to adopt AI in unproven ways and that, for AI agents, there is currently no regulation, oversight or transparency. His comments reflect his own view as an academic.

The article places the decision within wider concern among regulators. A series of global incidents involving AI agents going rogue prompted the Office of the Superintendent of Financial Institutions, Canada's top banking regulator, to raise its assessment of AI risks facing financial institutions. OSFI head Peter Routledge said at a press conference earlier this month that agents interpreting their task authorizations liberally and posing dangers to institutions was frightening and a front-and-centre risk for the regulator. OSFI is also considering whether the financial system needs an AI safety code, though Routledge said the regulator has not developed one or drafted it and has asked his team to begin considering it.

Articles.Title: RBC to block personal AI agents from access to online banking

stories.Headline: Assessing the impact of artificial intelligence requires social experimentation
stories.Summary:
Ru Peng, a professor at the School of Public Policy and Management at Tsinghua University, argued in a China Daily opinion piece published on October 29, 2026, that the social effects of artificial intelligence can only be understood through real-world experiments. Using the example of an AI companion placed in an elderly person's home, the author said that a system can work as designed and still change family relationships, daily routines or feelings of isolation in ways its developers did not expect. Because these effects often appear slowly, the piece said, waiting for problems to become obvious can make them harder and more costly to correct. The author framed this as the Collingridge dilemma, the difficulty of predicting a technology's consequences before it spreads widely.

The article said that testing should happen in carefully chosen settings before adoption becomes too widespread to change, with researchers establishing baselines, tracking outcomes over time and protecting consent and privacy, especially for vulnerable groups. It pointed to a three-year project launched in 2025 by researchers at Tsinghua University and industry partners, which plans to involve around 300 households and assess effects on older people's quality of life, emotional well-being, family interactions and social participation. Early findings, according to the piece, showed that some elderly users need help setting up equipment and that loneliness and limited digital access are concerns in some rural areas, though it stressed these observations do not yet show that AI companionship improves well-being. The author also noted that China has since 2023 set up a national standards working group, which has issued five national standards on AI social experiments and on assessing the social impact of generative AI.

The article placed this approach within China's policy agenda, citing government guidance issued in 2022, the State Council's 2025 AI+ initiative and national pilot bases and innovation zones that support such experiments. It also referred to President Xi Jinping's remarks at the World Artificial Intelligence Conference and the High-Level Meeting on Global AI Governance in July 2026, where he raised questions about human-machine relations, security, ethics and the fair sharing of AI's benefits. The author argued that experiments reveal what happens when AI enters daily life while standards help apply those lessons consistently, and that neither removes uncertainty entirely. The piece did not describe any specific next steps beyond continuing these experiments and standard-setting.

Articles.Title: Assessing the impact of artificial intelligence requires social experimentation

stories.Headline: Switzerland advances sector-specific AI regulation and voluntary codes of conduct - INSIGHT EU MONITORING
stories.Summary:
The Swiss federal government is moving ahead with steps to implement the Council of Europe Convention on Artificial Intelligence. At its meeting on 28 October 2026, the Federal Council noted progress to date and initial results, including a report on ongoing AI activities within the federal administration and guidance on voluntary commitments by associations and companies. The Federal Council had decided to ratify the AI Convention on 12 February 2025. The Federal Office of Communications (OFCOM) is coordinating these non-legally binding measures, which cover guidelines, industry standards and voluntary commitments.

The OFCOM report, titled "Sector-specific measures for the regulation of Artificial Intelligence," draws on a survey of all federal agencies and sets out current and planned measures in sectors such as transport, energy, health and media. It finds considerable momentum within the administration, and high-tech sectors as well as those tied to intellectual property, data processing, digital infrastructure and regulated markets face particular challenges. A separate toolkit, the "Guide on an AI Code of Conduct," is meant to help associations and businesses draft voluntary guidelines, offering suggested texts on 10 topics at three levels of detail that can be combined as needed. Several federal agencies are already holding AI dialogues to produce sector-specific voluntary commitments. Since November 2025, the Federal Office of Culture has been running an AI dialogue with the creative sector, which is intended to produce, among other things, a code of ethics on AI.

The Federal Office of Energy has asked the electricity sector to draw up industry guidelines and voluntary commitments addressing the risks AI poses to the electricity supply, and OFCOM held talks with the media sector in May about drafting a voluntary commitment. The Federal Council has tasked DETEC, through OFCOM, with setting up an internal administrative knowledge-sharing platform on the sector's AI self-regulation by the end of March 2028, with methodological support for departments and further development of the guidance on an AI code of practice. On the legal side, the Federal Office of Justice is drafting binding measures to implement the Convention. According to the articles, these rules are intended to address transparency, data protection, non-discrimination, supervision and risk assessment, and consultation is scheduled to begin in spring 2027.

Articles.Title: Switzerland advances sector-specific AI regulation and voluntary codes of conduct - INSIGHT EU MONITORING

stories.Headline: AI Pushing Small Law Firms To Rethink Atty Pay, Billing
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is changing how small law firms and solo practitioners think about billing and lawyer pay, according to a Law360 Pulse article by Rachel Rippetoe published on October 28, 2026. The article reports that legal consultants said the efficiency of AI tools, along with their price, is prompting these firms to reconsider how they charge clients and what they pay their lawyers. The available text is a short preview, and the paywall cuts off the full article, so the specific figures and examples it contains are not visible here. What is clear is that the piece treats AI as a force pushing smaller practices to revisit long-standing billing habits. It does not say which firms or consultants were quoted beyond the general reference to legal consultants.

The article's core point, as far as the preview shows, is that the cost and speed of AI could affect the traditional hourly model that many small firms rely on. If AI lets a lawyer finish work in less time, the hours billed for that work may fall, which is one reason firms are rethinking their approach. The preview does not spell out any new rates, fee structures, or compensation formulas that firms are adopting. Readers wanting those details would need the full text, which requires a subscription or trial.

The consultants quoted in the preview are described only in general terms, and the preview does not name them or give their exact remarks. The article is attributed to reporter Rachel Rippetoe. The preview also does not say what changes, if any, firms have already made or what the consultants expect to happen next. Because the visible text is limited to the introduction, any further conclusions would go beyond what the article states.

stories.Headline: Italian businesses believe businesses that fail to adopt AI risk falling behind competitors, want practical support to use AI
stories.Summary:
A new Ipsos survey of 500 small and medium-sized Italian business owners and employees, conducted on behalf of Meta, finds that most Italian businesses believe firms that fail to adopt artificial intelligence risk falling behind their competitors. The poll was released on October 28, 2026, and was carried out online in October 2026 among micro, small and medium businesses in Italy. Only 25 percent of the businesses surveyed currently use AI tools as part of how they operate, while 42 percent are still experimenting with or trialing them. Many firms continue to handle tasks by hand, with 74 percent saying they manage customer messages manually. Smaller businesses of one to nine employees are less likely to have used AI at all than firms of 10 to 249 employees, though the survey notes that the sample of larger firms was small.

The findings point to several things businesses say would help them adopt AI more widely. Seventy-three percent believe small businesses need greater support or financial incentives to fully benefit from AI, and 69 percent feel AI is being pushed at small firms faster than they can adapt. Among those who have used AI but rarely or never use agentic AI assistants, 45 percent say training tailored to their industry would help, while 36 percent point to free trials or lower costs and 33 percent to financial support or tax relief. Concerns about accuracy are widespread, with 63 percent worried about the accuracy of what AI tools produce for their company.

Forty percent of non-users want more reassurance on data protection and compliance requirements. Finding new customers is the top business challenge, cited by 45 percent, and 47 percent say they would hand that task to an AI tool if it could reliably handle it from start to finish. The survey is presented as a set of findings from Ipsos, with Scott Gardner, Vice President of Ipsos Public Affairs in the United States, listed as the contact for the research. The poll reports that 63 percent of businesses believe those that do not adopt AI tools risk being left behind by competitors, and that three in five expect to increase their AI use for marketing and content creation over the next year.

Among regular users of agentic AI assistants, 42 percent report saving time on routine tasks, and 20 percent say the tools have helped reduce costs. Other concerns include errors going out without review, cited by 25 percent of regular users, and the possibility that AI could weaken the personal connection customers expect, cited by over one in five. Data privacy worries affect 63 percent of businesses overall. The results carry a credibility interval of plus or minus 5.4 percentage points across all businesses.

Articles.Title: Italian businesses believe businesses that fail to adopt AI risk falling behind competitors, want practical support to use AI

stories.Headline: AI in Cell Factories: Is the Highly Anticipated Big Payoff for Capital Investors and Stakeholders Just Around the Corner?
stories.Summary:
AI is now being applied in cell factories, the synthetic biology field that once drew heavy capital before losses and failed pilot tests cooled investor enthusiasm. The article, published by 36Kr on October 30, 2026 and written by Liu Lingguo, asks whether a long-awaited financial payoff for investors is close at hand. It notes that on October 14 David Baker's team published two papers in Nature showing AI can design proteases from scratch, and that Claude and Gemini 4 have since claimed similar enzyme design abilities. Investors interviewed say a recovery is underway this year, though not a return to the 2021 peak.

The most concrete example given is Xinbeile's lactulose project, where AI screened 100 sequences from more than 30,000 enzyme sequences, and about 20 of them showed catalytic activity. Through successive rounds of AI-guided design, the best mutant reached roughly five times the original activity and about three times the stability, moving from wild-type enzyme to industrial enzyme in three months. Liu Huatao, the company's CTO, concluded that AI cuts the R&D cycle by about 80% compared with blind screening. The article also describes AI helping a dapoxetine intermediate project avoid equipment modifications that could have cost hundreds of thousands or even millions of yuan, and a Bluepha pilot whose unstable output was traced to its cause in about a week.

Several industry figures are quoted describing these gains. Luo Xiaozhou, founder of Senris, says the recovery is driven by AI and the 15th Five-Year Plan policies, and that an AI analysis flagged a valve problem later confirmed as a roughly 10% deviation. Li Yingjie of Inno Kechuang Fund evaluates projects on several criteria, including scaled production experience and sufficient market size. Luo Hongzhen of Bailun Bio explains that scale-up changes in dissolved oxygen, pH and substrate concentration cause problems that small tests do not reveal. The article stresses that AI mainly predicts risks and troubleshoots bottlenecks, while experienced technicians still make decisions on feeding, stirring, ventilation and contamination.

The article identifies market demand as the area AI helps least and where past failures were most painful. It cites Danimer Scientific, whose capacity expansion to 55 million pounds in 2022 left plants idle and led to bankruptcy protection in March 2025, and erythritol, where domestic capacity reached 380,000 tons by May 2023 and the price fell from 40,000 yuan to 9,500 yuan per ton. Companies are now choosing products either along clear downstream demand or by replacing existing supply with cheaper methods. The article's account of how these product choices are playing out continues beyond the portion available to this summary.

Articles.Title: AI in Cell Factories: Is the Highly Anticipated Big Payoff for Capital Investors and Stakeholders Just Around the Corner? - eu.36kr.com

stories.Headline: AuditPro.ai Expands Platform Access to College Accounting Departments
stories.Summary:
AuditPro.ai, a maker of AI-native assurance technology, has launched an initiative called AuditPro.ai for Educators that extends its platform into higher education. The announcement, published October 29, 2026, describes a version designed for accounting and finance professors. According to the article, the platform gives academic institutions modern case studies, student access, and the same artificial intelligence that accounting firms use. The company frames the move as part of a broader shift in which university curricula are changing to prepare graduates for AI-driven work. The offering is built for immediate use in classrooms.

Universities and faculty members can request group access and case study materials through the company's website, and the ready-made cases can be dropped into existing course syllabi. The article says the platform lets students work with a real engagement file, identify risks, plan responses, and practice auditor judgment. The stated goal is to help students develop professional skepticism while gaining hands-on AI experience. The article does not give pricing, the number of participating institutions, or a timeline for rollout beyond the launch itself.

Payton Baran, Founder and CEO of AuditPro.ai, said the team wants students to gain hands-on experience with AI tailored for assurance. Baran said that by bringing the turnkey platform into university classrooms, the company is helping educators better prepare students for their careers. Brandon Szerwo, CPA and Associate Professor of Accounting at the University at Buffalo, has used the platform with his students. Szerwo said the experience let students see an engagement file in a real audit platform and that it quickly builds their skills.

He also recommended the platform to other professors and to audit teams. The launch comes as the accounting profession is still working out how AI fits into audit practice. Recent coverage elsewhere in the same publication has examined where AI belongs in the audit process and what responsibility must remain with the auditor. The article does not describe any next steps for the AuditPro.ai for Educators program beyond inviting universities and faculty to request access.

Articles.Title: AuditPro.ai Expands Platform Access to College Accounting Departments - CPA Practice Advisor

stories.Headline: SuperPlane 1.0 launches as open-source software factory for coding agents
stories.Summary:
SuperPlane, a company, has launched SuperPlane 1.0 on October 29, 2026, presenting it as an open-source software factory for coding agents. The announcement was published that day by TechGig, which reported the launch in a short news item. The platform is designed to give engineering teams a shared and repeatable workflow for their coding agents, taking work from ticket creation through to a verified pull request. The system checks whether a task is ready, runs the coding agents, verifies the results, and handles failed checks and review feedback along the way. Engineers keep control over what gets built and what ships.

The software is model-agnostic, so teams can connect their own model accounts and API keys. It is released under the Apache 2.0 open-source license, and teams can self-host it on their own infrastructure. According to the article, SuperPlane is meant to coordinate routine work around coding agents rather than replace engineers. Its design encourages a shared environment in which skills, setup steps, tools, and context are available to the whole team, so one person's improvements benefit later runs for everyone.

It also supports a single set of standards, with readiness checks and verification rules established once for the team. A Kanban board gives visibility into running tasks, failures, costs, and the points where human intervention is needed. The articles provided do not describe the company's background, its funding, pricing, or any customers or independent assessments of the product. They also do not indicate what further releases or plans may follow the 1.0 launch.

Articles.Title: SuperPlane 1.0 launches as open-source software factory for coding agents

stories.Headline: Trump official reacts to leaked video of Microsoft's AI chief telling staff company wants to bring foreig
stories.Summary:
Microsoft's AI chief, Scott Guthrie, was recorded in an internal question-and-answer session telling employees that the company wants to bring more foreign talent into the United States. The recording was leaked and then shared by Anthony D'Esposito, the inspector general of the Department of Labor, who used it to again criticize Microsoft. The article's reporting places the internal remarks in the period just before its October 29, 2026 publication, and it describes them as following recent government action. The administration had suspended Microsoft's Green Card program, accusing the company of Green Card abuse, and Microsoft denied the allegations.

In the recording, Guthrie said the company was working with the US administration to get clarity on its recent announcements and on the data behind them. He said everyone's situation on a visa or Green Card differs, so the company had to look after the people affected. He told staff that anyone impacted should reach out to human resources. Microsoft's own statement said it follows a rigorous process for PERM jobs and did not violate any rule, and it noted that most of its US employees are Americans. The company also said that about 80 percent of the roughly 6,000 H-1B petitions it filed last fiscal year were to extend or change the status of existing employees.

Microsoft said the remaining filings for new employees covered people already legally in the country and equaled only 1 percent of its US workforce. Brad Smith, Microsoft's vice chair and president, said the administration's move sent a wrong message and that the country risked losing top AI and software engineers to other nations. He added that Vice President JD Vance did not have accurate data about Microsoft's Green Card sponsorships. D'Esposito responded to Guthrie's message by saying the administration had been clear, warning against using visa programs as a back door into the country. He said the officials had not been joking, and he said the government would not be pulled off its position.

Articles.Title: Trump official reacts to leaked video of Microsoft's AI chief telling staff company wants to bring foreig

stories.Headline: In Dewan Rakyat today: AI literacy, Brics role and AI Bill on the agenda
stories.Summary:
Malaysia's Dewan Rakyat is set to take up several policy matters during its sitting on Thursday, 29 October 2026, according to the Order Paper published on the Parliament website. The Ministers' Question Time will open with a question from Mohd Nazri Abu Hassan (PN-Merbok), who will ask the Minister of Education to outline how AI literacy will be built into the school curriculum through the AI Literacy Guide. The session will then move to questions for the Foreign Minister and other ministers on several separate subjects. The reported agenda covers the programme's scope, timing and effect, but the articles give no further detail beyond the questions themselves.

Datuk Seri Dr Ronald Kiandee (PN-Beluran) will ask the Foreign Minister to explain the goals of Malaysia's participation as a BRICS partner country and what this offers beyond existing bilateral ties. Datuk Idris Ahmad (PN-Bagan Serai) will put questions to the Minister of Digital on the status of drafting the AI Governance Bill, the expected date for tabling it in the Dewan Rakyat, and the legal protections open to citizens who fall victim to fraud. Datuk Seri Doris Sophia anak Brodi (GPS-Sri Aman) will ask the Foreign Minister for the number of Malaysians detained or charged for drug offences abroad over the past five years, and for comment on how well airport scanning technology detects drugs. Datuk Seri Sh Mohmed Puzi Sh Ali (BN-Pekan) will request figures on the economic returns of the Malaysia Agriculture, Horticulture and Agrotourism Show (MAHA) and how far small-scale operators have benefited.

Responsibility for answering these questions rests with the ministers named in the Order Paper, who will respond during the sitting. The articles do not record what any minister has said on these matters. Separately, the winding-up session for the debate on the Supply Bill 2027 is scheduled for the following day, 30 October 2026, and will involve the Ministries of Plantation and Commodities, Communications, Human Resources, Economy, Youth and Sports, and Finance. The Dewan Rakyat will then vote on whether to pass the Bill. The articles do not say how the vote is expected to go.

Articles.Title: In Dewan Rakyat today: AI literacy, Brics role and AI Bill on the agenda

stories.Headline: Puno: AIDA bill eyes maximizing AI gains
stories.Summary:
The House of Representatives recently passed a bill to create the Advanced Industries Development Authority (AIDA), an agency that would govern a proposed economic zone in New Clark City. House Deputy Speaker Ronaldo Puno spoke about the measure on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, during the Daily Tribune's Straight Talk program. The bill is meant to help the country take advantage of the growing artificial intelligence market. Puno said the Philippines is well placed to do so because of its natural resources and skilled workforce.

Puno explained that the zone would be governed by AIDA and that the law is needed to define which authority oversees Clark. He noted that every economic zone in the country currently operates under its own distinct laws. According to him, a clear legal framework would help attract foreign investors, who could lose interest in an area without firm policies. He said the law would define and guarantee what the zone will look like. Puno also said the authority would be connected to the Pax Silica declaration, a non-binding agreement involving 26 countries.

Puno is the official who spoke on the bill's purpose and its intended effects. He presented the measure as a way to create a free market environment for building the ecosystem that artificial intelligence needs. His remarks were reported in the Daily Tribune article by Jerod Orcullo, published October 29, 2026. The articles provided do not include the bill's full text, a timeline for its enactment, or any reaction from other lawmakers or government bodies. Further details on how the zone and authority will operate have not been reported.

Articles.Title: Puno: AIDA bill eyes maximizing AI gains

stories.Headline: Microsoft Q1 Earnings: CEO Nadella Touts AI Consumption, Usage-Based Billing Growth
stories.Summary:
Microsoft reported its first-quarter results for fiscal 2027 on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, with CEO Satya Nadella highlighting growth in consumption-based AI billing across its products. The quarter ended September 30. Nadella said the number of Copilot customers actively using usage-based billing grew more than 75 percent over the quarter, while credit consumption from agentic features on GitHub more than doubled. He presented consumption alongside seat subscriptions as a way to widen Microsoft's market and revenue per user. The company's revenue reached $92.3 billion for the quarter, up 19 percent year over year.

Starting December 1, usage-based billing will be on by default for eligible services used under Microsoft 365 Copilot Business licenses, which target small and midsize businesses with up to 300 seats per tenant. Solution providers can set the spending limit to zero to turn billing off, and the default limit is set at 4,000 Copilot Credits per user per month and can be adjusted. Microsoft spent $45.2 billion on capital expenditure and finance leases during the quarter, adding 24 data centers across five continents. About three-quarters of that spending went to GPUs and CPUs. The company expects capital expenditure of $50 billion for the second fiscal quarter and about $170 billion for the calendar year.

Nadella said customers need to understand when the compute included in a license is enough and when usage-based billing makes more sense, and he said he does not want customers to overbuy consumption. CFO Amy Hood pointed to Microsoft's Frontier Co., a forward-deployed engineering division, and changes to its Microsoft 365 sales approach as ways of educating customers on licensing and consumption pricing. Hood expected consumption pricing to be adopted more slowly outside coding users, though she said she still saw encouraging signs. Nadella also said enterprise demand is a long-term business that spreads across many customers rather than a few large buyers. He added that Microsoft remains open to large deals as long as the pricing is right.

Microsoft's results showed Azure revenue up 48 percent year over year despite delays in third-party capacity, while commercial bookings fell 11 percent year over year against a tough comparison with large Azure commitments last year. Hood said the company expects to remain free cash flow positive in fiscal 2027 but may access additional funding sources when it is attractive to do so. Nadella reported that Copilot daily users rose nearly 50 percent quarter over quarter, and that Foundry now has more than 120,000 customers. Microsoft did not disclose new Copilot user totals, focusing instead on revenue and usage. The company's next earnings update will cover its second fiscal quarter.

Articles.Title: Microsoft Q1 Earnings: CEO Nadella Touts AI Consumption, Usage-Based Billing Growth

stories.Headline: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act: A 10^25-Operation Pause, a Department of AI, and 20 Years in Prison
stories.Summary:
On 3 September 2026, Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont and Representative Greg Casar of Texas publicly announced the Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act. The announcement was a press release describing forthcoming legislation, not a bill. The formal texts followed later: S. 5493 was introduced in the Senate on 23 September and H.R. 10538 in the House on 24 September. Neither bill has had a hearing, markup or vote since.

If enacted, the bill would make it unlawful to develop or deploy superintelligence and any system showing a listed precursor trait. It sets a compute threshold of 10^25 operations for advanced AI, adjusted yearly by the Secretary, and imposes a pause on advanced systems until a new Department of Artificial Intelligence is staffed and has issued safety rules. Violators who act recklessly could face up to 20 years in prison, and a charter holder that violates the rules could lose its charter and its intellectual property. The bill also requires discoverers of such systems to notify the Secretary within 24 hours.

The sponsors' release and the bill texts are the primary sources for these provisions. The House version has eleven cosponsors, all Democrats, added between 24 September and 13 October. The findings section cites statements from Geoffrey Hinton, Elon Musk, Sam Altman, Mustafa Suleyman, Max Tegmark and Stuart Russell, along with a July 2026 open letter signed by more than 1,300 AI scientists. The articles present those citations as the sponsors' case, not as verified findings.

The Machine Intelligence Research Institute endorsed the bill on 23 September, calling it the first legislation with a real chance of stopping the threat, while also saying it lacks chip tracking and may over-classify some narrow systems. The National AI Association's Caleb Max told NBC News that the bill would be dead on arrival with industry and in Washington, calling it a de facto ban. The Congressional Research Service status for the House bill, refreshed 14 October, still listed the 24 September introduction as its latest action. More to follow.

Articles.Title: The Ban Artificial Superintelligence Act: A 10^25-Operation Pause, a Department of AI, and 20 Years in Prison - OrcaRouter

stories.Headline: L&T AI Factory: 10,000+ B300 GPUs Live by Jan 2027 [2026]
stories.Summary:
Larsen & Toubro (L&T) has set January 2027 as the commissioning target for an AI factory at its Chennai campus, according to reporting that says the site will carry more than 10,000 NVIDIA B300 GPUs. The company is developing the facility through a wholly owned subsidiary, L&T N Compute Private Limited. That subsidiary has already signed a long-term deployment agreement with Together.ai covering a significant portion of the GPU capacity. The announcement was made on record by Chief Financial Officer Parameswaran Ramakrishnan, who described the scale of the project. The confirmed facts are the operator, the site, the chip platform, the minimum capacity, the commissioning month and the anchor customer.

The more-than-10,000 figure is a floor rather than a final count, and no exact opening date has been published. Ramakrishnan put the investment for 10,000 GPUs at close to around $750 million, but he framed it loosely and gave no itemized budget. Reporting also does not say how much of the capacity Together.ai holds, what the contract value or term is, or who will fund the spending. Readers should treat the figures as a snapshot from late October 2026, since L&T can revise any of them in later disclosures.

The B300 is part of NVIDIA's Blackwell Ultra family, a current-generation platform that sits ahead of the Vera Rubin systems now entering cloud racks. Anchor-tenant agreements matter for GPU sites because they can support financing and make it easier to plan power and fill remaining space before opening. For Together.ai, the deal gives access to a large block of capacity without building a data center itself. The reporting describes commissioning, which means installing, powering and testing the hardware, and that is different from a public launch where customers can rent capacity on published terms.

Phased release is common for builds of this size, and the anchor tenant may take early capacity while the site is tuned. L&T has not published further details beyond the statements already reported, and the coverage does not indicate whether the company plans to repeat or revise the January target. The next signals to watch are whether L&T confirms the January date in a later update, whether it discloses the final GPU count and project cost, and whether it opens capacity to customers beyond Together.ai. More to follow.

Articles.Title: L&T AI Factory: 10,000+ B300 GPUs Live by Jan 2027 [2026] - shattered.io

stories.Headline: US Federal Trade Commission targets airline ticket pricing as scrutiny of AI and personal data intensifies
stories.Summary:
The US Federal Trade Commission has ordered nine companies, including three major American airlines, to provide information about how they set prices. The orders, announced on October 28, 2026, cover Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and JetBlue, alongside Uber, Lyft, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart. The agency wants to learn whether businesses use personal data such as browsing history, location, purchasing behaviour or loyalty-programme participation to offer different prices to individual customers. The FTC has not found that any of the airlines has broken the law.

The orders were issued under Section 6(b) of the FTC Act, which lets the agency run broad market studies and demand information even when no specific violation is under investigation. Each company has 45 days from receiving its order to respond, and the FTC can seek federal court enforcement if a company does not comply. The agency is asking for details on the data, algorithms and tools used to set prices and, where relevant, how gig workers are paid. The distinction at the centre of the inquiry is between dynamic pricing, which airlines already use to adjust fares for demand, seat availability and booking timing, and personalised pricing, which would use information about a specific customer to set that customer's fare. FTC Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson said the agency intends to examine methods that could affect how much consumers pay for the same product.

The airlines have been drawn into this debate by earlier controversies. In 2025, Delta faced questions from US lawmakers about its work with Fetcherr, an AI pricing technology provider, and in an August 2025 response to senators the airline said it had never used or planned to use fares targeted to individuals based on personal data. In April 2026, JetBlue apologised after a social-media reply suggested that clearing browser cookies or using incognito mode might help a customer whose fare had risen by $230, saying the reply was wrong and that its fares were not set using cached or personal data. A proposed class-action lawsuit has since alleged that JetBlue used customer data to raise fares, but those allegations are unproven and the airline denies them. The FTC's wider work includes a study launched in July 2024 into third-party firms that sell personalised pricing tools, and in August 2026 it invited public comment on a proposed enforcement policy on the subject.

Responsibility for the pricing decisions rests with the airlines themselves, and each has denied using personal data to set individual fares. The reporting says the immediate effect is likely to be closer scrutiny of pricing systems, data governance and customer communications rather than an instant change to how tickets are sold. Airlines may need to document which customer data they collect and how it is used, establish controls on pricing algorithms, make clear to customers how fares are determined, and review their arrangements with outside AI providers. The FTC will use the responses to inform policymakers, and the outcome of the inquiry will depend on what the companies disclose in the coming weeks.

Articles.Title: US Federal Trade Commission targets airline ticket pricing as scrutiny of AI and personal data intensifies - FL360aero

stories.Headline: Livermore Unified School District Forms AI Workgroup
stories.Summary:
The Livermore Valley Joint Unified School District, known as LVJUSD, has set up an Artificial Intelligence Workgroup to help decide how AI should be used in its classrooms. The group was formed at the start of the school year and includes teachers from all levels, students from Granada and Livermore high schools, school counselors, district administrators, and parents. It also has a board member and AI experts from Quest Science Center and Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory. Since beginning its work in September, the group has focused on building a shared understanding of AI, assessing district readiness, and reviewing privacy and security concerns.

The workgroup has been asked to develop an approach that supports teaching and learning while addressing academic integrity, student privacy, security, and equitable access. Its findings will guide the LVJUSD Board of Directors as it adopts a districtwide AI policy. As the school year continues, the group will run a limited AI pilot involving educators and students. It will also review guidance and a model AI policy being developed by the state Department of Education, along with approaches taken by other districts. Staff, students, families, and the community will have a chance to review and comment on the findings before the board considers a policy for implementation before the 2027-28 school year.

Chris Connor, the district's director of TK-12 Education, said that the district's job is to determine thoughtfully how AI can support learning while keeping students at the center of decisions, rather than simply reacting to the technology. Michelle Pechette, assistant superintendent for Educational Services, said that AI offers major opportunities but also raises important questions that the district intends to answer together with the community. She said the goal is guidance that prepares students for an AI-influenced future while protecting critical thinking, creativity, relationships, and human judgment. The district is also partnering with Quest Science Center on a Workforce Development Planning Initiative. That effort brings together Bay Area tech leaders, educators, higher education institutions, and community members to shape guidelines linking STEM classroom learning to future careers.

The move comes as schools across the country and the state wrestle with how students should use generative AI tools, both as learning aids and as possible shortcuts that undermine academic work. The article does not say how the pilot will be structured, which schools will take part, or when the pilot results will be published. It also does not give a date for the board's vote beyond the target of a policy before the 2027-28 school year. Those details, along with the outcome of the state guidance, are likely to shape the district's final policy.

Articles.Title: Livermore Unified School District Forms AI Workgroup - independentnews.com

stories.Headline: 2026 NH U.S. Senate Race: Pappas, Sununu debate guardrails for AI
stories.Summary:
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Chris Pappas and Republican candidate John E. Sununu were asked during a New Hampshire debate whether the country needs federal guardrails to regulate artificial intelligence technology. The question was posed in the 2026 race, and WMUR's Kevin Landrigan reported on the exchange, which was posted on October 28, 2026. The article is a short item centered on that single question. It does not give the candidates' full answers in detail. The article describes the topic as whether federal rules should govern artificial intelligence, but it does not spell out any specific bill, agency, deadline or dollar figure tied to such rules.

It also does not state what either candidate ultimately proposed. Because the report offers no numbers, dates beyond the publication timestamp, or legislative text, nothing concrete about new requirements can be drawn from it. Readers are left with the core question the candidates were asked and the fact that they addressed it on stage. Pappas and Sununu are the two major-party nominees in the New Hampshire contest for the seat. The article identifies them as the speakers and presents their positions on regulation as the subject of the debate, without summarizing their remarks beyond that.

The reporting does not include quotations from either candidate or describe what their stated views were. The item sits within WMUR's political coverage of the 2026 Senate race. The article does not say what comes next, such as further debates, a vote on AI legislation, or any follow-up reporting. This is therefore a brief, incomplete account. More to follow.
