stories.Headline: How to make the most of AI tools without feeling overwhelmed
stories.Summary:
Small business owners are being pressed to keep up with a constant flood of new AI models, agents and apps, a trend that a Stacker and Wix article published by KESQ on October 29, 2026 says can become a second job in itself. Experts quoted in the piece, including Avery Chi of Made4Vital and Kristin Ginn of trnsfrmAItn, argue that owners do not need to track every development to grow their businesses. Instead, the article says, they should focus on where their operations are getting stuck and whether a tool would create more value than the cost and complexity it adds. The article draws on a study in Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence that interviewed 15 young professionals in IT, marketing, finance, and research and development about generative AI and workplace stress. Those researchers found that AI can make employees more efficient but can also add pressure, such as the need to stay informed and to adopt changing technology.

The article calls this technostress and notes that the tools meant to lighten the load can add to it. Its central advice is that the fix is not more tools but being more selective about which ones to use. Several specific practices are recommended. Behavioral psychologist Bob Hutchins, PhD, suggests an "annoyance audit," in which owners log for one work week every task that irritates them, such as copying data between systems or repeating follow-up messages, and then look for patterns to guide their choices. The article also advises checking existing subscriptions for overlap, testing one new tool at a time instead of several at once, and choosing a calm moment to evaluate options rather than deciding right after a sales pitch.

Hutchins adds that a tool that is opened repeatedly without accomplishing its purpose should be dropped, and that tools owners open on their own, without prompts, are likely the ones working well. The article also recommends letting AI handle repetitive, low-judgment work while keeping human approval for major decisions, such as sending customer communications, making purchases or changing important business information. Hutchins advises deciding which customer interactions should stay personal, such as responses to complaints or thank-you notes, and making it easy to reach a human whenever a customer asks. Customers should also be told whether they are speaking with AI or a real person, since the article warns that trapping customers in automated systems can erode trust. Overall, the piece concludes that making the most of AI means knowing where a business is stuck rather than chasing every tool that promises to save time.

stories.Headline: As AI in politics becomes more common, here's how voters can stay vigilant
stories.Summary:
Experts warn that AI-made political content is spreading faster and looking more realistic as the election season moves forward. The Associated Press reported on Wednesday that social media videos believed to be made with AI and linked to Russia are using real people's names and photographs to spread disinformation about two Democratic Senate candidates in close races, Sherrod Brown in Ohio and James Talarico in Texas. Ari Lightman, a digital media and marketing professor at Carnegie Mellon University, said foreign adversaries are using increasingly advanced tools to push polarization and favor certain political outcomes. The use is not limited to foreign actors, since political groups in the United States are also using AI in campaign ads.

The Wesleyan Media Project has tracked 220 midterm election ads generated at least in part with AI tools, a count it called almost certainly an undercount. Most of those ads came from Republican candidates and organizations, though stakeholders in both parties used them. Spending on AI-generated ads had exceeded $137 million as of earlier this month, compared with less than $50,000 in the 2024 cycle, according to the project's co-director, Erika Franklin Fowler. She said much of the AI use goes undisclosed through any kind of disclaimer. Thirty-one states have enacted laws regulating deepfakes in political messaging, though some have been challenged in court on free speech grounds, and there are still no federal disclosure requirements.

Experts say voters cannot rely on visual clues alone, such as misshapen hands, unnaturally smooth skin, or misaligned shadows, because the technology has grown too sophisticated for most people to spot these flaws. Lightman advised voters to check the credentials and context behind potential AI content and to verify information through independent sources. He also said voters should be wary of content designed to provoke an immediate emotional response and should think twice before sharing it on social media. OpenAI confirmed on Wednesday that it is launching an Election Operations Center this week to track misinformation and address potential misuse of tools like ChatGPT, running until all votes are counted, according to Politico. A new Brennan Center report found OpenAI was the only company that significantly improved protections against generating fake election content since the center tested six popular models earlier this year.

stories.Headline: China's new export curbs draw a line around its AI crown jewels
stories.Summary:
China has proposed new rules on artificial intelligence exports that would keep its most valuable AI technology at home while still letting foreign customers use its services. The draft rules were released on October 16, 2026, and China is expected to adopt them by the end of 2026, with implementation guidelines to follow later. They would add 23 AI-related technologies to the list of items banned or restricted from export, including advanced models, autonomous agents and chip-design tools. A temporary requirement to register certain transfers has already taken effect.

Under the proposals, overseas users could broadly access Chinese AI through websites and cloud platforms, but some transfers of underlying technology or overseas deployments would need government approval. The draft sets three tests for which models would be covered: training computation above 10 to the power of 26 calculations, a size of at least 2 trillion parameters, or a place among the world's top 10 in certain performance, use or efficiency assessments. The rules also cover methods for coordinating more than 10,000 AI chips and offer simplified approvals for Chinese firms running their own computing facilities abroad. The proposals are open for public comment until November 15.

The rules were drafted by Chinese authorities, and the China commerce ministry did not respond to a request for comment. Alfredo Montufar-Helu, a managing director at consultancy Ankura in Beijing, said the leadership prefers keeping research and intellectual property onshore while selling operations and access abroad. He also said security concerns, including keeping powerful cyberattack capabilities and sensitive data in China, accompany the commercial goal of protecting technological advantages. Yang Jingru, a partner at law firm Jincheng Tongda & Neal, described the approach as a counterpart to US restrictions on China's access to advanced chips and investment. Liu Jing of Beijing Dacheng Law Offices said companies want more clarity on which models would be covered.

The approach is set against intensifying rivalry with the United States, where Nvidia's most advanced processors cannot be exported to China. Some Chinese AI developers have used overseas computing facilities to reach such chips, and researchers at major labs are seeking clarity on whether they can train or run their most advanced models on foreign-owned servers. In a worst case, developers might have to maintain separate domestic and overseas versions of the same downloadable model. The rules could also reach corporate deals, with registration requirements covering transfers that put Chinese technology under foreign ownership or control, including transactions already underway. Beijing earlier this year ordered Meta to unwind its more than $2 billion acquisition of the Chinese-founded startup Manus, which shows the risks for foreign buyers.

stories.Headline: Is AI Overhyped? Apollo Economist Sees "Zero Financial Payoff" Beyond Tech Companies
stories.Summary:
Apollo Global Management's chief economist, Torsten Slok, published research on Saturday, October 25, 2026, arguing that artificial intelligence has so far produced no financial gains for companies outside the tech sector. His analysis found that the "Magnificent Seven" tech firms, including Alphabet, Microsoft, and Meta, are seeing rising revenue per worker and profit margins from AI, while the other 493 companies in the S&P 500 are not. Slok reported that revenue per employee at tech firms climbed from about $550,000 to nearly $800,000 since 2022, while the figure for the rest of the index has stayed near $550,000 for seven years. Profit margins for those other companies have stagnated at about 10%, and productivity growth across the economy has not jumped as AI optimists predicted.

The findings matter because the AI boom rests on the hope that huge investments in data centers and models will eventually raise profits across many industries by cutting costs and improving processes. Slok wrote that mainstream companies are beginning to see token spending as a cost that weighs on margins rather than a source of growth. He framed the open question as whether corporate America can turn increasingly cheap intelligence into higher revenue and margins, and he said that may be harder than it sounds. Commentary from the Motley Fool notes that if this pattern holds, today's highly valued tech stocks could be overpriced, and a sell-off could follow if companies cut AI spending.

Slok, a partner and chief economist at Apollo, presented the research as a warning about the current trajectory rather than a final verdict. The Motley Fool's Ben Gran, writing on October 28, 2026, pointed out that other forecasters are more optimistic, and Vanguard research suggests gains from AI could reach companies across many industries over the long run. Gran's advice for investors who share Apollo's concern was to consider a broadly diversified S&P 500 fund instead of a tech-heavy one. He also noted that such a fund still holds major tech names and would not be fully shielded from an AI-driven downturn.

Gran cited the Vanguard S&P 500 ETF, which has delivered annualized returns of about 13.8% over the past five years, including through the 2022 bear market when the index fell about 18.2%. Business Insider's Truman Dickerson reported the Apollo findings in a similar vein, emphasizing that the broader economy has not yet seen the widespread productivity gains that AI supporters have promised. Both outlets framed the research as a test of whether the AI boom will spread beyond a handful of large companies. The coming quarters of corporate earnings and AI spending will show whether Slok's view holds or whether broader gains emerge.

stories.Headline: What to consider if a company that made AI-related job cuts wants you back
stories.Summary:
Companies across the world are increasingly citing artificial intelligence when cutting jobs, and some firms that made such cuts are now bringing workers back. Microsoft, Barclays Bank and Kroger are among the recent employers to announce AI-related workforce reductions this year, sometimes to eliminate roles seen as redundant and sometimes to free money for AI investment. Some of those companies found that AI models, applications and agents did not perform as well as expected and rehired laid-off staff, a pattern now called the "AI boomerang." It is unclear how common these reversals are, though they are happening often enough to attract attention.

Hiring managers in finance, marketing, law and health told the staffing firm Robert Half earlier this year that their companies had cut roles because of AI or automation and then hired again for the same or similar work. The main reasons given for restoring jobs were that the technology needed more human oversight than anticipated and could not replicate institutional knowledge. Klarna, the Swedish buy now, pay later provider, began recruiting human customer service representatives again last year after its CEO acknowledged that relying on an AI chatbot to cut costs had gone too far. In June, Ford said it had hired or promoted 350 veteran engineers after AI tools it used for quality control did not perform at the expected level.

Experts quoted in the article say companies often miss the invisible work employees do beyond their formal job descriptions. Betsy Summers, a principal analyst at Forrester, said that work includes sensing moods, holding impromptu meetings and building trust within teams, none of which is usually counted when tasks are handed to AI. Brooks Holtom, a management professor at Georgetown University, said many organizations do not document their processes well enough to know where people add value. He also said AI chatbots often need to pass complex or emotional problems to human workers who can respond creatively within policy limits. Beaumont of SHL added that companies may not publicize such reversals, since they may prefer not to admit they were not ready for the change.

For workers considering an offer to return, the experts suggested several steps. Holtom advised them to explain how they would add value in a new role that uses the technology along with their own expertise, and to seek a one-year renewable contract with a buyout clause if the job ends early. Beaumont said returning workers often ask for more pay, more training and clear information about how AI may affect future staffing, though she noted that trust in the employer is hard to rebuild. Summers urged workers to stress human qualities such as motivation, curiosity and empathy, which the technology has not fully mastered. More to follow.

stories.Headline: Cash is king as investors draw new battle lines in AI spending boom
stories.Summary:
Investors on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, sharply separated companies they see as profiting from artificial intelligence from those struggling to control its costs. Microsoft and Oracle were rewarded for showing they could fund their large AI plans without repeatedly turning to investors for money. Alphabet, Google's parent, was punished for burning through cash, and slower growth in Google Search raised worries that rivals were hurting the business that pays for its AI push. By Thursday's premarket trading, Microsoft shares had risen more than 2 per cent while Alphabet had fallen nearly 11 per cent.

The split reflects a shift in what investors want to see after years of rewarding firms for spending heavily on computing capacity, often with borrowed money. Now they are asking for proof that the growth from those investments can pay for the next round of spending. Meta gave an early signal the week before, when better-than-expected revenue and an upbeat outlook were overshadowed by its cash burn. Oracle, by contrast, closed nearly 11 per cent higher on Wednesday after saying it would cap external financing and expected its cash flow to turn positive in the second half of fiscal 2028.

Melissa Otto, head of research at S&P Global Visible Alpha, said the two companies looked like night and day, describing Microsoft's growth as disciplined while Google was burning cash and its core business fell short of expectations. She suggested investors might now ask whether AI was taking some share from Google Search. The figures behind the concern are stark: Alphabet put 121.4 per cent of its operating cash flow into capital spending in the September quarter, against 68 per cent at Microsoft, excluding finance leases. Google Search revenue grew 12 per cent in that quarter, below the 14.7 per cent analysts had expected, even though CEO Sundar Pichai said queries were growing at their fastest pace in five years. Alphabet's capital spending could reach as much as $205 billion this year and rise significantly in 2027, according to CFO Anat Ashkenazi.

Alphabet's cloud business offered a counterpoint, as Google Cloud revenue more than doubled to $30.71 billion, though spending overwhelmed that gain and cash burn reached $9.07 billion. Jeremy Saltzberg of Check Capital, which owns Alphabet shares, defended the spending as necessary to compete with OpenAI and Anthropic. Microsoft generated $18.6 billion in free cash flow in its fiscal first quarter, nearly $10 billion above Wall Street's expectations, while investing $45.2 billion in computing infrastructure. Its Azure revenue rose 48 per cent, and CEO Satya Nadella said businesses were moving past experiments toward long-term AI contracts.

stories.Headline: What Argentina Needs to Fulfill its AI Ambitions
stories.Summary:
Argentina's President Javier Milei proposed at the UN General Assembly last month that the world develop artificial intelligence in Argentina, offering tax breaks, limited liability for companies operating AI agents, and a pledge not to regulate the technology preemptively. The author, Soledad Guilera, writes that the appeal is understandable because good ideas in Argentina often stall in paperwork. She notes that the European Union has had to delay parts of its own AI law because the technical standards needed to comply were not ready. Milei's ambition is admirable, she says, and the country has real strengths, including engineers who have founded global companies and a knowledge services industry that earned a record $9.6 billion in exports last year.

Guilera argues that Argentina's AI sector hinges less on deregulation than on steps that build certainty for everyone involved. She points out that Chile, Brazil and Uruguay lead the 2026 Latin American AI Index, while Argentina ranks sixth out of 20, even though all of them score the same on the index's regulation indicator. The country holds just 2.3% of the region's GPUs and 1.1% of its processing power, and it has seven certified data centers compared with Chile's 37. Federal science spending is on track to fall to about 0.16% of GDP this year, from 0.30% in 2023, and staff at the main federal science agencies fell 13% between December 2023 and August 2026.

Argentina's data protection law dates from 2000 and caps fines at 100,000 pesos, about $65. The author also describes an announced data center in Patagonia, worth up to $25 billion and based on a letter of intent between OpenAI and a local energy company, which does not appear among the projects approved under the incentive regime a year later. A new incentive law for AI and data centers passed the lower house in June and still awaits a Senate vote, and a bill allowing companies to operate through AI agents has sat in a Senate committee since June without a formal report. Guilera says consumers, from doctors to loan officers to retirees, need answers about responsibility, data use and human review before they trust these systems.

She proposes four steps: funded transmission lines and computing power tied to every incentive, joint programs to train AI talent and protect core research teams, a modernized data protection law such as the one the national authority drafted in 2023, and public-sector transparency about the algorithms the state uses. Guilera concludes that these measures would not follow the European rulebook but would give both capital and people the certainty they need to commit to Argentina. She argues that the president's idea of companies run by AI agents would be far easier to accept if everyone knows who answers for them. In her view, investors will not come on a promise alone, and Argentines will not trust a technology that no one answers for.

stories.Headline: Trump says US will beat China in AI as technology emerges
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence has become the main point of disagreement between the United States and China, and President Donald Trump says the United States will win the AI competition. Speaking on September 13 in Ireland, Trump said the United States was leading China in AI and called it the most sophisticated country in the world. He said he wanted to keep that lead because whoever wins AI wins. The remarks came as the two countries, the world's two largest economies, have been caught in a trade war during both of Trump's terms.

The reporting shows that Trump has treated the relationship with Chinese President Xi Jinping as a warm one. During a state visit to Beijing in May, Trump praised Xi and said the two had gotten along and worked out past difficulties. In September, Xi visited the White House for a state visit, and Trump described the strides the two had made on national security, trade and technology. At that summit, the countries agreed to extend a trade truce until January. However, no agreement was reached on putting safeguards for AI into practice.

Trump is the central figure in these comments, and he is the one who has called AI "super intelligence" and insisted on American victory. Trump said during his presidential campaign that tariffs would form the core of the bilateral relationship. The articles frame these statements as his own positions rather than as a joint policy. They report that he and Xi are set to meet again in China next month.

The articles place the dispute in the context of an ongoing trade conflict, which has shaped the relationship through both of Trump's terms in office. They do not describe any new rules or changes arising from the AI discussions, beyond the unresolved question of safeguards. The next step named in the reporting is the planned meeting in China in November. Beyond that meeting, the articles do not say what will follow.

stories.Headline: Alfieholdingslimited Launches AI-Powered Market Intelligence and Financial Analytics Platform
stories.Summary:
Alfieholdingslimited, a company based in Brussels, announced on October 28, 2026 the commercial launch of an AI-powered financial analytics and market intelligence platform aimed at European enterprises and analysts. The cloud-based system pairs structured economic indicators with machine-learning models to turn complex market data into non-transactional research reports. The company says the platform is built for information analysis rather than trade execution or investment management. It is positioned as an alternative to trading platforms and investment services, focusing on information rather than financial transactions. The company describes several functions for the platform, including analysing market data and economic indicators, identifying patterns across financial information, and supporting research through AI-assisted workflows.

It states that the platform is not a brokerage, does not accept investment deposits or process withdrawals, and does not guarantee financial returns. Security is presented as central to the design, with encryption, access controls, audit logging, verified data providers and AI model validation named as the main measures. The company also acknowledges that no digital system can eliminate every security risk. Alfieholdingslimited says it is responsible for the platform and emphasises transparency about what the tools do and their limits. In its own words, AI can help spot patterns and organise large datasets, but its outputs do not guarantee future market performance.

The company also distinguishes itself from several organisations with similar names, including ALFIE FX LTD, Alfie Group and Alfie Group Ltd, stating that it has no affiliation with them and that no claims are made about their activities. Readers are directed to the company's support address, support@alfieholdingslimited.com, for further questions. The announcement is framed within a broader European interest in data-driven financial research, with the company citing relevance to markets in Malta, Belgium, the Netherlands and Romania. The articles present the launch as part of a wider sector trend in which artificial intelligence plays a growing role in financial analytics. The release does not describe any regulatory review, customer numbers or pricing, and it notes that the press release was paid content distributed by its issuer.

stories.Headline: Echo launches Frontier to patch AI-found zero-days
stories.Summary:
Echo, a security company, has launched a product called Echo Frontier that turns zero-day vulnerabilities found by advanced AI models into private software patches before they are publicly disclosed. The launch was announced on October 28, 2026, and the service is now generally available. The announcement came as security researchers reported that newer open-weight AI models are getting better at finding and exploiting software flaws. Anthropic research cited by Echo found that Zhipu AI's GLM-5.3 produced working end-to-end exploits in 50 of 410 attempts on the ExploitBench benchmark, compared with 56 for Claude Mythos Preview. Because GLM-5.3 is openly available, flaws could be discovered and exploited before a CVE is assigned, before detection signatures exist, or before a maintainer releases an upstream fix.

Frontier works by checking each vulnerability against a working exploit, then building and testing a fix across the full application before delivering it. Patches reach customers through their existing JFrog or Nexus repositories, and customers move to the official upstream fix once one is available. The service covers reproducing a flaw with a proof of concept, identifying affected versions, notifying maintainers, developing and backporting fixes, and distributing the patched software privately. Echo also provides documentation of the detection and remediation process for compliance purposes. The company pointed to 1Password's Off-by-1 Labs research, which found that 54% of 6,080 AI-generated patches failed to fix the vulnerability, introduced a new one, or did both, as evidence that fixing flaws safely is hard.

Echo's chief executive, Eilon Elhadad, said AI is changing the vulnerability lifecycle, so the traditional sequence of a flaw becoming public, receiving a CVE and then getting a fix no longer holds. Eylam Milner, the company's chief technology officer, said that finding zero-days without the means to fix them creates new liabilities, and that the product is meant to make discovered flaws safe to run in an enterprise quickly. Echo acts as an authorised CVE Numbering Authority and coordinates disclosure. It cited a recent case involving OpenEXR, the open-source image file format library, in which it found a high-severity denial-of-service vulnerability, validated it and protected customers in about two days, roughly two months before an upstream fix became available.

The launch reflects a broader concern that organisations may need an intermediate layer of remediation when AI-driven discovery outpaces standard vulnerability management. Echo builds on its existing work vetting, patching, rebuilding and delivering open-source software used in containers, libraries, operating system packages and virtual machines. For software suppliers, the articles suggest the challenge is not only finding unknown flaws but proving that a patch can be applied safely and quickly across the versions and environments customers already use. The articles do not describe any further developments beyond the launch itself.

stories.Headline: FORVIA and Raiqon enter strategic AI partnership
stories.Summary:
FORVIA, a global automotive supplier, and Raiqon GmbH, a specialist in scalable AI solutions for regulated engineering environments, have entered a strategic partnership to apply artificial intelligence in automotive engineering. The announcement was issued as a press release from Nanterre, France, on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The two companies say the work centers on Requirements Engineering, a stage of product development in which technical requirements are defined, analyzed and managed. Depending on product complexity, a single development project can involve as many as 15,000 individual requirements.

The jointly developed solution automates the analysis, assessment and processing of those requirements, which the companies say will raise productivity and speed up development. It runs on Raiqon's multi-agent AI platform inside FORVIA's secure IT environment and plugs into FORVIA's existing IBM DOORS setup without disrupting established workflows. The platform pulls data from several engineering applications and is being adapted to the needs of FORVIA HELLA and Faurecia Clarion Electronics. Its tasks include analyzing requirements, spotting similarities, reusing earlier assessments, detecting inconsistencies and creating missing links automatically. By cutting manual effort, the companies say engineers can devote more time to new requirements.

FORVIA's CEO, Martin Fischer, said AI is becoming a key enabler of innovation and competitiveness in the automotive industry and linked the collaboration to the company's IGNITE transformation program. Joerg Weisgerber, Managing Director Electronics at FORVIA HELLA, said the AI-based automation is meant to make the company faster and more efficient and to let teams handle a much larger volume of requirements. Raiqon's CEO, Szabi Koppany, said the automotive industry faces growing international pressure to shorten development cycles, improve economic efficiency and manage rising complexity. He described the shared goal as improving the efficiency and quality of engineering processes and strengthening FORVIA's leadership position.

FORVIA describes itself as a global automotive technology supplier formed from the Faurecia and HELLA businesses, with more than 137,500 employees, over 12,000 R&D engineers across more than 40 countries and a patent portfolio of over 12,400. The company reported consolidated revenue of 26.2 billion euros in 2025 before IFRS 5 adjustments. The articles do not say when the platform will be fully deployed or what financial terms the partnership carries. More to follow.

stories.Headline: AI reshaping product research, but trust remains key
stories.Summary:
A new survey from Lyssna, a research platform company, finds that AI is now a routine part of product research, though many professionals remain wary of trusting it. The findings are based on responses from 428 attendees surveyed at Future Product Days in Copenhagen. Of those surveyed, 94% said they use AI somewhere in their research workflow, with 55% using it throughout the research-to-decision process. Designers made up 46% of respondents and product managers 28%, while only 4% identified as researchers.

The survey suggests AI is changing how research gets done inside product teams rather than replacing the work. Nearly half of respondents, 47%, said AI has led them to do more research, while 20% now rely on AI more than on doing the research themselves. Some 49% said they had connected an AI assistant directly to their research or product tools, with engineers most likely to do so at 72%, compared with 55% of product managers and 39% of designers. Respondents also pointed to the work that comes after a study as the biggest slowdown, with manual synthesis or write-up named by 32%. Checking AI-generated output for errors and bias has emerged as a new burden, and 81% said they would value an AI-generated, decision-ready report based on their research data.

Trust is the central obstacle the survey identifies. Asked about barriers to using AI directly with research data, 27% cited data privacy and 25% pointed to trust in accuracy. The concern was sharpest among people who had connected an AI assistant to their tools but rarely used it, with 40% in that group naming accuracy as the main barrier. Some respondents said company policy prevented them from linking AI tools to internal systems. In an open question that drew 258 responses, people said they wanted AI to spot patterns they might miss and to act as a critical partner, with one respondent asking the tool to "challenge me instead of agreeing with everything."

Tristan Gamilis, Chief Product Officer and Co-Founder at Lyssna, said AI has not replaced research but has changed who is doing it, and that designers and product managers are running more studies than ever. He said the main challenge now is trust, and that teams need assurance that what their AI tells them comes from real people. Mateja Milosavljevic, Chief Executive Officer and Co-Founder at Lyssna, said the teams that benefit most will keep AI grounded in what real people said and did, which she argued lets them move quickly while still making decisions they can defend. Lyssna also cautioned that its audience was self-selected and unscreened, and that the 18 researchers in the sample mean findings about that group should be treated as directional rather than conclusive.

stories.Headline: Envision Energy Unveils AI-powered New Energy System for Mining and Smelting Industry at All Energy Australia
stories.Summary:
Envision Energy, a green technology company, unveiled an AI-powered new energy system for the mining and smelting industry at All Energy Australia in Melbourne, Australia, with the announcement dated October 28, 2026. The system combines wind, solar, battery storage, and gas turbines that run on green hydrogen or green ammonia, all coordinated by an integrated dispatch and control system. The company says the aim is to lower energy costs, keep power supply reliable, and speed up decarbonisation. It is designed for remote mining sites with weak or no grid connection, where delivering affordable and reliable green power has been a central problem.

Envision's approach links renewable generation, battery storage, and backup power into one integrated energy system. Its weather and energy AI foundation models, together with the EnOS AI platform, handle renewable generation forecasting, load forecasting, system planning, and real-time dispatch. These tools adjust the coordination of generation, storage, and industrial loads as weather and operating conditions change. The system is also built for safety and reliability across grid-connected, weak-grid, and off-grid sites. Wind-storage integrated turbines smooth wind output, grid-forming battery storage supports stability, and a seven-layer protection and control framework manages sudden load changes and restores supply after an outage.

Envision also says it is exploring green hydrogen or green ammonia gas turbines as alternatives to diesel generators for backup power, which would further cut emissions. Its energy and carbon management capabilities support product carbon-footprint accounting and supply data for green certification, which the company says can help producers meet customer demand for lower-carbon minerals and metals. The offering covers planning, engineering, delivery, ongoing operations, and financing options. Depending on local resources, configuration, and production needs, the company targets around 20% lower overall energy costs, a renewable electricity share above 80%, and power supply reliability above 99.95%.

Envision is already applying these solutions in the sector. In Western Australia's Pilbara region, it is supplying wind turbines for Fortescue's Nullagine Wind Project, which supports the miner's Real Zero strategy. In Baotou, China, it integrated wind power, battery storage, and loads into a system for green alloy production that meets more than 70% of electricity needs with renewables and cuts annual carbon dioxide emissions by over 200,000 tonnes. At All Energy Australia, the company is talking with mining and smelting producers and project partners about developing systems tailored to local resources and decarbonisation goals.

stories.Headline: Bessent Plays Down Concerns Over AI Financing, Fed Rate Policy
stories.Summary:
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said on Wednesday that he and his team are monitoring financing for the artificial intelligence build-out, and he downplayed recent signs of concern. In a CNBC interview, he responded to questions about yields on some AI-related debt climbing into double digits. He said the neoclouds, which rent out AI infrastructure, make up only a small part of the wider ecosystem, so he did not see the situation as a problem. CoreWeave Inc., a major AI computing provider, has become the focus of growing worry about how durable the boom is and the hundreds of billions of dollars borrowed to fund it.

Bessent said financing deals are still getting done, and he pointed to companies such as Meta choosing to raise money through equity. He spoke shortly after the Federal Reserve's latest rate decision, where the central bank held rates steady after raising its key rate in September. He also restated his confidence, and that of President Donald Trump, in Fed Chairman Kevin Warsh. Asked whether a future rate increase would be a policy mistake, Bessent said that was not necessarily the case, citing strong economic growth.

He again urged policymakers to keep an open mind about whether the energy shock to inflation would prove temporary. Yields on US debt have pulled back from their highest levels in more than two decades in recent weeks, though 10-year rates remain above 5 percent. Bessent linked those yield levels to the Fed's decision before the 2024 presidential election to cut rates, starting with a 50 basis point move. He said the 10-year yield had never turned back and that the bond market had done much of the tightening for the Fed.

Many market participants, however, say the AI financing boom has added to strain on Treasuries, as AI companies have flooded corporate debt markets with a combined trillions of dollars in new issuance. Bessent also said he and Trump expect the oil market to be well supplied once the US gets past the Iran conflict. He argued that this would help ease inflation and bring down borrowing costs. The articles do not say what specific steps, if any, the Treasury will take in response to the AI financing concerns, and they do not describe any further Fed decisions beyond the hold announced this week.

stories.Headline: Sources: AI coding startup Cognition weighs a new funding round before year's end after receiving offers valuing it at $70B-$80B, up from $48B in September (Katie Roof/Business Insider)
stories.Summary:
Cognition, an AI coding startup, is weighing a new funding round before the end of 2026 after receiving investor offers that value it at between $70 billion and $80 billion. That is a steep rise from the $48 billion valuation it secured in September, only weeks earlier. According to sources familiar with the matter, the company is seriously considering the round, though talks are still early and the valuation targets could change. Business Insider first reported the story on October 28, 2026. The company's founders are Scott Wu, Steven Hao, and Walden Yan, who started it in 2023.

Cognition is best known for Devin, an AI coding agent built to automate software engineering work. The San Francisco-based company counts a16z, Accel, Founders Fund, Khosla Ventures, Elad Gil, and Pear VC among its existing investors. The reported valuation range reflects how intensely investors are competing for stakes in AI coding, one of the most crowded and expensive areas of the AI market. Companies are racing to sell agents that can take over more of what engineers do, and investors are paying premium prices for the few startups they believe could lead. The article notes that a $75 billion figure would not be out of line, since SpaceX recently bought the rival AI coding company Cursor for $60 billion.

The article also describes a public dispute from last month between Cognition and Factory AI. Factory accused Cognition employees of posing as job applicants to obtain product information, and it criticized a former Factory adviser for meeting with Cognition executives. Cognition and the former adviser both denied that any confidential information was sought or shared. Business Insider's reporter, Katie Roof, invited tips by email and through the Signal messaging app. The article does not say when the new round would close or how much money it would raise.

stories.Headline: Early Anthropic member recalls burnout and big ambitions in the AI lab's early days
stories.Summary:
Ivan Vendrov, a former member of Anthropic's technical staff, has published a Substack post describing his time at the AI lab from late 2022 to mid-2023. In the post, he recalls an intense, safety-focused workplace where fears of AI catastrophe competed with the push to build safe AGI for commercial use. He wrote that he later felt burned out and disillusioned. The account arrives days after Anthropic filed to go public, and Anthropic declined to comment on the story.

Vendrov said he was weighing offers from OpenAI and Anthropic in 2022 when a cofounder told him over lunch that the company was already talking with regulators in Washington. A recruiter then asked whether he would pledge two-thirds of his equity to charity, and said all the cofounders had made that pledge. Vendrov said he was unsure if the offer depended on his agreement, so he said yes. Anthropic's S-1 filing describes a donation-matching program in which workers can pledge a "meaningful portion" of their equity awards, and reports that 50% of employees are included.

Vendrov described a cramped, unattractive office stocked with fresh croissants, and said a popular masseuse visited twice a week but was always fully booked when he tried to schedule. He also recalled one visit from an FBI agent, who warned that Anthropic was probably already a target of several foreign intelligence agencies. When the company hosted a sushi chef, he said a cofounder complained in Slack the next day that the event set the wrong tone. The cofounder reportedly said the company was not there to get rich and eat caviar, and suggested future dinners of rice and beans instead.

Vendrov's post describes sleepless nights, walks with other stressed colleagues, and a sense that he could not be fully honest about his feelings at work. Eight months after signing, he wrote a resignation letter, and he said he considered voicing his doubts but worried about unsettling colleagues he regarded as more capable and better intentioned than himself. Instead, he praised Anthropic as an unbelievably good organization. Vendrov has not responded to requests for comment, and he cautioned that his account is his memory of events, reconstructed from one junior employee's experience during a short period.

stories.Headline: Circana Puts AI to Work: Engages Ode with Anthropic to Build a Faster, Smarter Market Intelligence Engine
stories.Summary:
On October 29, 2026, Circana, a Chicago-based company that turns consumer data into growth insights, announced it had engaged Ode with Anthropic, an enterprise AI transformation company, to modernize how it produces and delivers market intelligence. The stated aim is to give Circana's clients faster, more flexible and more actionable insights. The two companies are building a governed agent platform where teams can build, test and deploy agents in one place. Each agent is measured against expert-verified cases, and work the system finds uncertain is sent to Circana specialists.

The collaboration also involves end-to-end workflows guided by experts, with data processing, trend forecasting and product classification as the first three focus areas. Ode is training Circana engineers to build and deploy agents of their own, and operators will own the goals and quality of the agents in their areas. Circana describes these as production-ready capabilities on a reusable foundation rather than standalone productivity tools. The company says this should speed up its ability to develop and deliver new solutions to clients. Circana also says it will share results and case studies as the work scales.

Stuart Aitken, Circana's president and CEO, said AI matters only if it improves clients' decisions and speed, and that the firm is turning complex manual processes into scalable workflows centered on its data and industry expertise. Michael Rosenthal, president of Operations at Circana, said removing manual steps and routing exceptions to experts allows faster, more consistent work without sacrificing the oversight clients expect. Chris Taylor, CEO of Ode, said AI works best when it gives experts more room to apply judgment and that he is pleased to work alongside Circana's analysts. The announcement notes that Circana grew from IRI and The NPD Group and has spent decades using technology and data science to help clients understand consumers.

Circana describes itself as a provider of technology, AI and data to fast-moving consumer packaged goods companies, durables manufacturers and retailers. Its platform, Liquid Data, relies on a large data set and algorithms trained on six decades of domain expertise. Ode was formally launched in 2026 through a partnership between Anthropic, Blackstone, Hellman & Friedman and a group of global investors, and it helps organizations move AI from experimentation to full deployment. It pairs Anthropic's frontier models with experienced AI engineers to find high-impact uses and build the systems that deliver them. The articles do not give financial terms of the engagement or a timeline for completion.

stories.Headline: Meta launches two new AI apps, including one aimed at kids
stories.Summary:
Meta launched two new AI-powered apps in the week covered by this report, as the company uses its own AI models to generate app code faster. One of them, Waddle World, is aimed at kids and gives users a virtual pet that can remember things they say and create content based on their interests. The other, Style Sketch, uses AI to suggest outfit combinations from clothes users already own. Meta describes Waddle World as a cozy, 16-bit pet care game with no streaks or scores to chase. The article notes that Waddle World is currently only available to users in the Philippines.

Style Sketch builds a virtual wardrobe by integrating with Instagram and pulling clothing items from images users have shared there. Users can also add items by hand, and the app then builds looks from those pieces. According to analyst Matt Navarra, Style Sketch is only available in Indonesia, Singapore and Thailand. The article says Waddle World collects personal data including location, contact information and user ID, according to the app's iOS page. Both launches come amid ongoing concerns about AI tools making potentially dangerous recommendations to users.

The article describes Meta as experimenting in this way because AI tools make it much easier to build and release new apps and see which ones gain traction. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said on the company's July earnings call that AI is speeding up product development, pointing to recent launches including Instagram Instants, Forum and Seller. The article lists other test apps Meta has released or is working on, including Pocket, Vibes, StoryKit and a prediction markets app called Arena. It says whether Arena reaches a full launch remains to be seen.

The writer argues that most of these experimental apps are unlikely to last long, though a few may help Meta keep people engaged on its platforms. The article also points to Meta adding parental oversight to its Meta AI app as related coverage. Against that backdrop, the writer calls Waddle World's cute design somewhat disingenuous given how the company uses such tools to gather data. The article does not describe any formal regulatory response or announced changes to either app's data practices.

stories.Headline: Qualys launches TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 with AI remediation
stories.Summary:
Qualys has launched TruRisk Eliminate 2.0 with TruConfidence, now generally available as an upgrade for existing customers of TruRisk Eliminate. The release adds a remediation intelligence and orchestration engine to the company's security platform, supporting what it calls Autonomous RemOps, a model meant to automate how organisations fix cyber exposures. The update lets security and IT teams choose among patching, applying a compensating control, uninstalling software, isolating affected assets or using a custom fix. It reaches beyond managed endpoints to perimeter devices, cloud environments and applications, including assets that cannot run an agent, which can be handled through scanners and existing integrations.

The launch comes as security teams face pressure to close vulnerabilities faster, since AI tools are speeding up both discovery and exploitation. At the centre of the system is Agent Sara, an AI component that builds wave-based deployment plans by analysing asset criticality, operational dependencies and traffic patterns. Updates roll out in stages so problems can surface in smaller groups before wider deployment. Qualys said the system draws on data from half a billion patch deployments, with less than 0.1% rollback, and that 40% of those deployments were carried out autonomously. The product also includes a Patch Reliability Score, which estimates the likely success of a patch before it is deployed, along with patch failure analysis that can explain failed attempts and suggest steps such as a localised rollback.

Where patching is not immediately practical, the system first checks which risks existing security controls already cover, then identifies remaining gaps. It then looks for third-party mitigations that can be applied through tools already in use on endpoints and perimeter systems. This reflects a wider move in vulnerability management toward alternatives to immediate patching for sensitive or hard-to-offline systems. Qualys also said the system monitors system health after remediation through integrations with observability providers including Dynatrace, Datadog and New Relic, looking for anomalies such as CPU spikes, memory leaks and service-impacting conditions.

Jon Nelson, Principal Advisory Director in the Security & Privacy Practise at Info-Tech Research Group, said the handoff between security teams that find vulnerabilities and IT teams that patch them has become harder to manage as AI shortens exploitation timelines to hours. He argued that neither team can close that gap alone and said the product offers a path to remediation at machine speed. Sumedh Thakar, President and Chief Executive Officer of Qualys, said customer hesitation about automation is mainly about the risk of outages rather than automation itself. He said the company wants to give organisations confidence to reduce cyber risk quickly through the Risk Operations Centre framework, which unifies telemetry, asset visibility and validation. The release sits within Qualys' wider push into a market where vendors are being pressed to show they can act on findings with less human coordination and lower disruption risk.

stories.Headline: Nvidia's web of AI bets: smart strategy or bubble risk?
stories.Summary:
Nvidia announced on Tuesday, October 27, 2026, a $3 billion investment in Meta's share sale, the latest addition to a growing portfolio of stakes, loans and guarantees tied to the artificial intelligence boom. The chip giant has taken positions in OpenAI, Anthropic and Elon Musk's xAI, now part of SpaceX, along with neocloud firms such as CoreWeave and Nebius that rent out computing power built on its chips. Its reach also extends to Europe, where it has backed Mistral and Wayve, and to Asia, where it has teamed up with South Korea's SK Group on data centers. Beyond equity, Nvidia acts as a customer of last resort, having committed to buy up to $6.3 billion of unused CoreWeave capacity, and it reportedly holds about $36 billion in cloud backstops plus a guarantee of up to $105 billion tied to an OpenAI data center. Some analysts now call the company the central bank of the AI boom.

Experts see these deals as a rational use of Nvidia's large profits. Michael Cusumano of the MIT Sloan School of Management said the company is in effect becoming a bank and that steering money into infrastructure that buys its own equipment is a smart move. He added that running its own data centers would bring it into conflict with its biggest customers and could invite antitrust complaints. Gil Luria of D.A. Davidson said Nvidia is filling gaps where other parts of the AI ecosystem are underinvesting, calling the approach unprecedented but workable. Chief executive Jensen Huang has defended the strategy by arguing that leading AI labs need tens of billions of dollars to get started, and Nvidia's money gives them time to succeed.

Critics, however, compare the arrangements to the dot-com era, when firms inflated growth by funding startups that then bought their products. Paulo Carvão of the Harvard Kennedy School said there is nothing inherently wrong with Nvidia helping clients, but the closer the ties, the harder it becomes to judge how much demand is genuine and sustainable. Luria argued that demand is not equal in quality, since Nvidia money cycling back through a neocloud is weaker than a major cloud provider buying chips for paying enterprise customers. The sharper risk is concentration: two direct customers made up 22 percent and 14 percent of Nvidia's revenue in fiscal 2026, according to its annual report. Carvão warned that a weaker partner such as CoreWeave running into trouble could spread losses across chipmakers, data-center builders and their financiers at once.

Those worries surfaced in October, when shares of several Nvidia-linked neocloud companies, including CoreWeave, Nebius and IREN, fell at least 30 percent amid concern about tighter credit for AI projects. Carvão estimated that demand for AI chips, still constrained by supply, would keep rising for another 12 to 18 months before leveling off. Cusumano expected strong demand for Nvidia chips to last three to five years. Whether the web of deals proves a sound strategy or a bubble will therefore depend largely on how long AI spending holds up.

stories.Headline: How AI drones are influencing the course of the Ukraine war
stories.Summary:
Yaroslav Azhnyuk, a Ukrainian tech entrepreneur, turned to drone warfare after Russia launched its full-scale invasion in 2022. His companies, The Fourth Law and Odd Systems, are among the leading producers of AI-powered drones in Ukraine, and dozens of Ukrainian military units already use their autonomous drone, the Lupynis-10-TFL-1. The reporting describes a broader shift in which artificial intelligence is making drones faster and more capable. Russia is also deploying AI-enabled drones against Ukraine.

The Lupynis-10-TFL-1 is a small, affordable first-person-view drone paired with an autonomous terminal guidance unit. For the last 500 meters, or 0.3 miles, of a flight, an onboard computer and AI technology take control from the human operator. The system relies on relatively simple image recognition tools rather than the large AI systems used in data centers or self-driving cars. Azhnyuk says this lets a drone navigate without a person, select a target, or fly toward one on its own. The company's testers say the drone's microcomputer runs a deep-learning network trained on hours of combat footage to recognize vehicles, armored vehicles, tanks and flying objects.

Azhnyuk argues that AI gives a smaller military an asymmetric advantage, claiming it can make a drone "10,000 times more effective." He acknowledges concern about destructive weapons but says the worry is not specific to AI, comparing it to earlier tools like fire or steel that can be used for good or bad. The company's test and integration lead, who uses the call sign Stab, says safeguards are in place so the drones will not go rogue and that humans select the targets. Azhnyuk rejects comparisons to killer robots, calling the systems "just sort of calculators," though he concedes that future drones might one day make their own targeting decisions. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that AI could lead decisions on the battlefield as soon as next year.

Azhnyuk's main argument is that Ukraine cannot afford to refuse AI in defense when adversaries are already using it for offensive decisions. He says Russian systems can decide in microseconds while human control takes minutes, hours or sometimes days, and he warns that if Ukraine loses, there would be no room to debate the ethics of AI. The company names its weapons after Ukrainian intellectuals and artists killed or persecuted by Russians, with the Lupynis drone honoring a poet who endured Soviet imprisonment. The articles do not describe any specific outcome beyond these claims or set out formal rules governing the use of such drones.

stories.Headline: SAP swaps costly AI models for cheaper alternatives, targets over €2 bln in gains - ET CIO
stories.Summary:
SAP, the German software maker whose products are used by many of the world's largest companies, is replacing some of the expensive artificial-intelligence models that power its products with cheaper alternatives. The company expects the switch to generate more than €2 billion in efficiency gains over the next two years. The shift was described in an interview with Reuters published on October 29, 2026. The reporting covers the change without detailing a single starting date for the swap.

CFO Dominik Asam told Reuters that the company had removed some of the most expensive AI models from products including its internal consulting assistant. He said the replacements were lower-cost models used where performance stayed strong. SAP uses more than 70 AI models from providers including OpenAI, Anthropic and Google. Asam said the company increasingly picks the cheapest model able to perform a task to the required standard. He also said overall spending on AI is still expected to rise as adoption grows.

SAP said in written answers to Reuters that its goal is healthy margins as it scales, not an absolute cut in AI spending. The company said it charges customers for completed tasks rather than for the computing resources used to generate responses. Under that model, lower operating costs can help improve profitability, according to the reporting. Asam is the executive quoted on the cost figures and the model changes.

The reporting also notes that customers are paying closer attention to where AI models come from. Asam said government agencies and companies in regulated industries increasingly set specific requirements and exclude models based on origin. He said European customers are increasingly demanding local solutions. The articles do not say how much of SAP's AI work will move to these alternatives or whether any further changes are planned beyond the two-year window.

stories.Headline: AI giants’ funding ambitions test Wall Street’s appetite for risk
stories.Summary:
Anthropic filed paperwork for its initial public offering on Monday, Oct 26, 2026, paving the way for a share sale reportedly worth US$100 billion as early as November. The same day, Meta unveiled a plan that could bring it as much as US$97.5 billion through equity offerings over the coming months. Both moves come as the largest AI companies press ahead with enormous funding needs, a bet that investors' fear of missing out on future returns will outweigh their fear of overpaying. Markets were also expecting signs of fundraising plans when Microsoft and Alphabet reported earnings later that Wednesday.

Meta's plan involves creating a new class of stock to fund share sales, and its shares have fallen more than 11 per cent since it was announced on Oct 21. The company also reported its first quarterly cash burn in more than a decade. Anthropic's revenue has grown sharply, which eased some concerns about AI growth, but its net loss widened to US$80.7 billion in the first half of 2026 from US$13 billion a year earlier. Smaller firms face sharper pressure: CoreWeave has seen its bond yields soar, and its shares hit their lowest level since May 2025 last week before rebounding about 10 per cent this week.

Analysts quoted in the article voiced the concern that investors are no longer willing to fund ambition alone. Matt Kennedy of Renaissance Capital said not even Anthropic would get a blank check, while Matthew Tuttle of Tuttle Capital Management warned that CoreWeave's next loan, and how soon it is needed, matters as much as its price. SpaceX chief executive Elon Musk said neocloud companies could face significant consolidation and failures, and he ruled out any SpaceX acquisition of a neocloud company, calling such a deal pointless. Ehren Stanhope of Franklin Templeton's Canvas said the growth of the AI ecosystem was astounding but that such firms compounding earnings at triple digits for years seemed to defy economic logic.

The context is a market heavily dependent on AI, with AI stocks accounting for nearly 75 per cent of the S&P 500 index's return in the first half of 2026, according to Carson Group. Data from JP Morgan showed that this year's AI capital spending by Amazon, Alphabet, Meta, Oracle and Microsoft would likely equal their cumulative spending since ChatGPT launched in November 2022. Dubravko Lakos-Bujas of JP Morgan wrote that the Street appeared to be underwriting the AI data centre monetisation case. The article also notes growing circular financing, in which money invested in AI companies can flow back to investors through spending on computing infrastructure and services. The article does not say what the outcome of the earnings reports or the planned share sales will be.

stories.Headline: 2 Millionaire-Maker Custom Silicon Stocks Powering the AI Infrastructure Supercycle
stories.Summary:
Broadcom and Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing, known as TSMC, were highlighted in a Motley Fool piece published on October 28, 2026, as two leading companies in the custom silicon market for artificial intelligence. The article explains that graphics processing units are the main hardware for training AI models, while application specific integrated circuits, or ASICs, are chips built for narrower tasks that can be more powerful and efficient at those tasks. Broadcom designs custom ASICs and has partnered with Alphabet on its Tensor Processing Units, with Meta Platforms, OpenAI and Anthropic also named as customers. The author, Keith Noonan, presents the two companies as having delivered large gains for investors.

The article reports that Broadcom's artificial intelligence semiconductor revenue rose 221 percent year over year to $16.7 billion in the third quarter, while net income rose roughly 216 percent to about $13.1 billion. For the fourth quarter, the company expected AI revenue to reach $21.7 billion, an increase of 236 percent from a year earlier. Over 15 years, Broadcom's dividend-adjusted total return is put at roughly 13,470 percent, and the stock trades at about 28 times expected earnings and 15 times expected sales. TSMC does not design chips but manufactures them for customers such as Broadcom and Marvell Technology, and the article estimates it controls over 90 percent of the market for high-end AI and high-performance computing chips. TSMC's stock is described as returning roughly 4,720 percent over 15 years.

The article attributes its views to Keith Noonan, who has no position in the stocks discussed, and notes that The Motley Fool holds positions in and recommends Alphabet, Broadcom, Marvell Technology, Meta Platforms and TSMC. It says both companies have seen valuation pullbacks amid broader concerns about an AI valuation bubble. The author argues that Broadcom's strong net income margins and revenue growth could support further valuation gains, and that TSMC's dominant manufacturing position and strong demand could help its stock reach new highs. The piece is promotional in tone, pitching the Motley Fool's Stock Advisor service, and the article does not say what will happen next.

stories.Headline: Delta Air Lines among companies FTC investigating for potential price-setting using AI - WSB-TV
stories.Summary:
The Federal Trade Commission has opened an inquiry into nine companies, including Atlanta-based Delta Air Lines, over how they set prices for customers. The agency announced the probe on Wednesday, October 29, 2026, and it targets Delta, United Airlines, JetBlue, Lyft, Uber, DoorDash, Instacart, Target and Walmart. The announcement noted that DoorDash and Instacart had recently announced a $17 billion merger. The inquiry is aimed at learning whether these firms use personal data to set individual prices.

The FTC ordered the companies to provide detailed information about their use of personal data in setting prices and compensation. Each company has 45 days from receiving the order to respond, which means they must either provide the data or contest it in court by December 12. The agency is trying to determine whether airfares, ride share fees, food delivery costs or other services vary depending on loyalty program participation or other personal data. The FTC described these methods as "superintelligence algorithms," the federal term now used in place of the more common phrase artificial intelligence, a shift that President Donald Trump introduced at the United Nations in September. If a company refuses to comply, the commission said it would seek to compel compliance in federal court.

FTC Chairman Andrew N. Ferguson said the agency intends to examine the opaque methods some companies may use to decide what consumers pay or what gig workers earn for the same work. He said consumers should know whether their web browsing or other personal data is used to estimate the highest price they can be charged, and that workers should know whether their pay is affected in the same way. The FTC noted that a 2024 study on personalized pricing examined only middlemen consultancies, not companies like those named in this inquiry that set prices directly. Delta responded to a request for comment by pointing to an earlier statement, saying it has never used, tested or planned to use fares that target customers with individualized offers based on personal data. A Delta spokesperson said the airline has zero tolerance for discriminatory or predatory pricing and complies with applicable privacy, pricing and advertising laws.

stories.Headline: Opinion: AI, Musk, Trump and our freedom in these uncertain times
stories.Summary:
The article is a first-person opinion piece by Narain Batra, a Upper Valley resident and author, published by the Concord Monitor on October 28, 2026. It recounts a four-session seminar on freedom he taught at the Osher Institute at Dartmouth College, where participants were asked whether AI, Elon Musk or Donald Trump posed the greatest threat to American democracy. The group's consensus was that all three were, in different ways, a serious menace. Batra frames this as a moment when many Americans are being asked to hold two ideas at once: that democracy is fragile, yet strong enough to withstand powerful pressures. The piece appeared days before the 2026 midterm elections.

The author lays out the case for concern about executive power and private wealth. He notes that critics such as Liz Cheney and Robert Kagan have warned of a slide toward dictatorship under Trump, while Peter Berkowitz has argued that institutions constrain such moves and that history offers little evidence of democracies collapsing without broad cooperation from the military, bureaucracy, business, media and universities. Batra then points to spending figures reported by Reuters: Musk has spent roughly $366 million on this election cycle, $276 million of it since July, which would make him the largest single donor of the 2026 races. He also raises concern about Musk's social media platform X, which he describes as operating without the legal constraints and gatekeepers of traditional media. The article connects these points to the wider debate over the spread of influence through money and platforms.

Batra writes that AI-generated speech has already affected New Hampshire, recalling robocalls in January 2024 that imitated President Biden's voice and urged voters to skip the primary. He says the calls were later traced to a political consultant, Steve Kramer, who claimed he meant to expose the dangers of AI deepfakes and cast his act as civil disobedience. A court ruled that Kramer's AI robocall was protected under the First Amendment, a result the author presents as part of the slow and messy working of American democracy. He also describes Trump's December 11 executive order blocking states from regulating the AI industry, quoting MIT Technology Review's account that the move was a qualified victory for tech companies who argued that a patchwork of state laws would stifle innovation. Batra argues that the rules being written in state capitals and action by Congress may shape how the technology develops, though he says such hopes should not be naive.

Batra concludes that American democracy faces a stress test from three converging forces: an executive branch increasingly willing to bypass constitutional norms, wealthy individuals who wield foreign-policy-like influence, as Ian Bremmer and Mustafa Suleyman argued in Foreign Affairs, and AI companies pressing for little regulatory oversight. He frames the central question as how much of democratic institutions can survive these pressures rather than how the republic will govern them. He closes by suggesting the midterm results may indicate which way the wind is blowing. Batra is the author of "The First Freedoms and America's Culture of Innovation."

stories.Headline: Steve Eisman gets more conservative with portfolio as AI trade nears 'tipping point'
stories.Summary:
Steve Eisman, the investor known for The Big Short, said on CNBC's Squawk Box on Thursday that the artificial intelligence trade is nearing a "tipping point," though he has not yet bet against it outright. He told the network that he has grown more conservative in his own portfolio and has shorted against the box across many positions, so his risk is much lower. He stopped short of calling himself net short, however. The comments came a day after Alphabet's stock fell following its earnings report, which showed a large pullback in its core advertising business.

Eisman's main worry concerns the frontier AI model makers, which he believes are using fear about their technology to build a competitive regulatory moat against cheaper rivals and to hide weakening fundamentals. He pointed to Anthropic's recently filed S-1, where the company left its latest revenue figures blank in its initial IPO filing. Eisman expects those numbers to show a significant slowdown from the prior quarter. He also cited an analysis showing the ratio of revenue to equipment expense fell from 2.08 in the second quarter to 1.7 in the third, which he described as a significant change in trajectory.

Eisman said he was reluctant to make a definitive bet against the AI trade because the sector is so intertwined with the broader market, calling it impossible to isolate technology from the rest of equities and the economy. He argued that much of the market remains on the other side and is still reading tea leaves, adding that Alphabet's numbers had frightened people. Google executives said Wednesday that AI mode queries were growing strongly but monetizing at lower rates, and that the company was running ad experiments that had shown promising results. Eisman described parts of Anthropic's filing as extremely negative because it lacked many metrics for the coming quarter.

stories.Headline: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported third-quarter earnings that fell short of Wall Street expectations, and its stock dropped about 10% in extended trading. The clearest weakness was in search and other revenue, which grew 12% from a year earlier to roughly $63 billion but came in below estimates for the second straight quarter. The results were released on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, and the report also showed negative free cash flow of $9 billion, three times the estimated deficit. Alphabet executives blamed foreign exchange as the biggest factor behind the slowdown in search revenue. Even so, the company said search query growth was the strongest it has been in five years.

The gap between heavy search usage and slowing revenue is raising concern that AI tools are pulling people away from traditional search. Analysts have long predicted that AI would eclipse traditional search, and Google has been warned it must find new ways to make money. Search revenue growth slid from 19% in the first quarter to 17% in the second, then to 12% in the third. Analysts at UBS wrote that the results will bring fears of search cannibalization back to the forefront. Mizuho analyst Jordan Klein said the numbers raise worries about search and YouTube as AI and agentic tools take share.

Google's leaders, including Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler, pointed to AI as a driver of growth in its advertising business. Schindler said the company made its biggest update to product listing ads in a decade during the quarter and that Gemini models helped advertisers generate more than 1.5 billion campaign assets, up more than sevenfold from a year earlier. Deepwater Asset Management's Gene Munster said the new AI-powered services will be a significant force and could become the starting point for commerce for many people. Alphabet also said its cloud business more than doubled in the quarter to nearly $31 billion, with a backlog of roughly $560 billion.

The company kept its full-year 2026 capital expenditure forecast at $195 billion to $205 billion and said spending will rise significantly in 2027. Chief Financial Officer Anat Ashkenazi explained that cash goes out while Alphabet builds inventory for its tensor processing units, which it began selling to outside customers in the second quarter, and cash comes in once those systems are delivered and billed. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said investors will now worry that AI has finally reached Google's core business. He wrote that one quarter should not be the basis for firm conclusions, but the company will need to reassess what agentic commerce means for it. More details on the company's next steps are expected as the story develops.

Articles.Title: Alphabet earnings miss reflects first real sign that AI is taking a bite out of search

stories.Headline: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round
stories.Summary:
Wabi, a startup that describes its product as a "personal agent," said on Thursday that it has raised $55 million at a $1.25 billion valuation. The company was founded by Eugenia Kuyda, who previously founded the AI companion startup Replika. Wabi first focused on letting anyone build apps from prompts, but last month it announced a shift toward becoming an AI messenger. The article does not say whether the round has closed or who else is leading it beyond what is listed below.

The new version, called Wabi 2.0, is meant to build the interfaces a user needs to get things done as part of its role as a personal AI agent. The company suggests it could create mini apps for meal planning, tracking local restaurants, planning date nights, building fitness plans, and designing specialized trivia games. The funding suggests investors see potential in this agentic direction. The article notes that the market for AI agents is hot right now, citing the viral agent Instinct, which raised another billion at a $10 billion valuation in September. It also mentions Tolan, an AI companion that just raised $30 million.

Alex Lim, a general partner at IVP, which led the round, praised Kuyda's sense for where AI is headed and her track record in building it. Lim said she has a clear vision for how people will interact with AI, one that goes beyond the text box or command line. Lim described Wabi as the expression of that vision and said IVP was thrilled to support her. Other participants included Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), Forerunner, the Amazon Alexa Fund, and angel investors such as Shopify CEO Tobi Lütke, Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff, former Yahoo head Marissa Mayer, former Twitter CEO Dick Costolo, and Alex Pall of The Chainsmokers.

Articles.Title: Wabi, the AI agent that builds mini apps, now valued at $1.25B after latest round

stories.Headline: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
stories.Summary:
Proton, the Swiss company behind Proton Mail and a suite of privacy and security products, is pushing its staff hard toward AI, according to a 404 Media investigation published on October 29, 2026. The reporting draws on interviews with eight current employees and one former employee, along with Slack chats, meeting recordings, and an AI manifesto written by the company's chief technology officer, Bart Butler. The article says that in late August, CEO Andy Yen told an engineer who wanted a few days of security testing before code went live that such caution was "loser thinking," and urged the team to "stop lovingly handcrafting all our code and use AI more." Other steps reported include an address where staff can flag anything slowing AI adoption, software that tracks how much AI-generated code is produced, and Yen's statement that this will be the last year Proton hires engineers.

The article says that Proton has moved from banning AI internally to approving it for many uses, including processing financial data, drafting customer replies on Reddit and LinkedIn, and writing code, with exceptions for source code that could give a competitor an immediate advantage or that relates to research and development. Butler reportedly said in a meeting in October that 90 percent of Proton's code that month was written by AI, and multiple employees said much of it is produced with Anthropic's Claude. Butler's manifesto, posted to Slack one Friday afternoon last month, told engineers that their old job was gone, that the company must get to the point where most code is reviewed by AI rather than humans, and that failing to change posed an existential threat to its mission. The article also reports that Proton has said it will re-interview staff about their AI use, with the implication that willingness to embrace AI could affect whether someone keeps their job.

Several employees described a climate of fear in which concerns about security or about building security products with AI are rarely voiced, because Yen might berate them in front of colleagues or threaten their jobs. One source said the CEO was in "full AI psychosis." An internal document cited in the article says Proton is not on track to meet its annual recurring revenue target because of "insufficient velocity," and calls the company underperforming by the metrics that matter. A Proton spokesperson did not dispute the reporting and said some people are unhappy with the direction or misunderstand it, that the company had sometimes been too blunt or too slow in explaining itself, and that it would work on that because staff questions are the ones it most needs to answer. The article places this in the wider context of companies across the security field grappling with AI, some carefully and others chasing profit quickly, and notes that Proton has launched its own privacy-focused chatbot, Lumo.

Articles.Title: Manifestos, Fear, and ‘Loser Thinking’: Inside Proton’s AI Reckoning
