stories.Headline: Seoul proposes record 55.74 trillion won budget to expand youth AI access, rental housing citywide
stories.Summary:
Seoul's city government, led by Mayor Oh Se-hoon of the conservative People Power Party, unveiled a proposed record budget of 55.74 trillion won, roughly $41.68 billion, for 2027 on Thursday, October 29, 2026. The proposal is 4.27 trillion won larger than this year's budget, an 8.3 percent increase, and it is the first annual budget drafted by the administration that took office in July. The city plans to keep projected debt roughly flat at 11.57 trillion won at the end of next year, even as its contribution to nationally subsidized programs, including marriage and child care support, rises by 1.17 trillion won. Policy program funding would climb 9 percent to 31.58 trillion won, a figure that excludes the education office, district governments and administrative operating costs.

The budget's signature item is a youth AI access program that would allocate 26.6 billion won to give 500,000 young people generative AI subscriptions and training tailored to their skill levels, with the goal of keeping differences in the ability to afford and use AI from widening employment gaps. A separate 46 billion won would go to the Seoul Software Academy to train 4,500 AI professionals. On housing, 1.12 trillion won would be devoted to supply, aiming for 27,200 public rental units next year, about 76 percent of them obtained by buying existing homes. The city would also expand monthly rent subsidies to 32,000 young people from 23,000 this year and set aside 23.1 billion won for the Rapid Integrated Planning urban renewal project. Welfare spending would reach 4.81 trillion won, up 953.1 billion won, and a new pension for middle-aged residents would require each of 10,000 participants to save 80,000 won a month, with the city adding 20,000 won.

The youth AI program still needs approval from the city council, where the liberal Democratic Party holds a majority. In September the council cut the 5.63 billion won allocated for the initiative in a supplementary budget, with DP members arguing that preparations were inadequate. The city has since revised the program and asked for funding again, which the articles suggest could lead to another clash during deliberations. Oh said the city had expanded investment in residents' daily needs without increasing debt, and that the aim was to give young people opportunities to get ahead and provide housing stability. The budget proposal is due to be submitted to the Seoul Metropolitan Council on Friday, and the articles do not say when the council will vote on it.

Articles.Title: Seoul proposes record 55.74 trillion won budget to expand youth AI access, rental housing citywide

stories.Headline: Kospi opens lower on Wall Street losses, AI concerns
stories.Summary:
Shares on the Kospi opened lower on Friday, October 30, 2026, following losses on Wall Street and renewed worries about whether the AI boom can last. After opening 2.99 percent lower, the index extended its decline to trade 228.43 points, or 3.85 percent, down to 5,709.23 as of 9:15 a.m. The index had already fallen 1.24 percent in the previous session, as investors took profits in heavyweight chip stocks despite Samsung Electronics posting record quarterly earnings. Overnight, technology shares led a sell-off in New York.

Alphabet, Google's parent company, plunged more than 12 percent after its third quarter revenue rose 25 percent on the year to $127.58 billion but fell short of market expectations. That raised doubts about the returns on its large AI investments. The tech-heavy Nasdaq composite shed 1.38 percent, and the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index fell 1.4 percent, which weighed on sentiment toward Korean chipmakers. In Seoul, Samsung Electronics fell 3.66 percent and SK hynix dropped 6.82 percent. Hyundai Motor slipped 2.39 percent after lowering its annual sales target and investment plans, and Hanwha Aerospace slumped 7.76 percent after weaker-than-expected third quarter earnings linked to delays in deliveries of K9 self-propelled howitzers to Poland.

The Korea Exchange suspended program trading for Kospi-listed shares for five minutes at 10:04 a.m. under its sell-side sidecar rule. The won rose 0.3 won from the previous session to trade at 1,339.2 against the dollar as of 9:15 a.m. The article also notes that offshore investors sold a net 19.1 trillion won, or $14.3 billion, of local stocks in September, after a net purchase of 344 billion won the previous month. It links that selling to extended geopolitical risks and AI concerns.

Articles.Title: Kospi opens lower on Wall Street losses, AI concerns

stories.Headline: Business leaders urged to embrace AI, rethink old strategies
stories.Summary:
At this week's Global Business Forum in Seoul, speakers urged business leaders to adopt artificial intelligence themselves and to rethink strategies that worked in the past. The fifth weekly session of the forum's 10th edition, organized by The Korea Herald and Herald Business, took place on Wednesday under the theme "Connecting People and Technology, Opening New Possibilities." Sheikh Saleh Alsharqi, counselor and head of economic affairs at the United Arab Emirates Embassy in Seoul, opened the event by calling for closer cooperation between Korean and Emirati companies. He suggested that Korean firms see the UAE as a platform for joint investment and expansion into third-country markets. He named AI, green hydrogen, space technology and advanced manufacturing as areas for that cooperation.

Choi Eun-soo, chief executive of the Korean AI video analytics firm Intellivix, told leaders not to hand AI adoption entirely to their employees. During his presentation, he showed how AI tools could help draft business proposals, create presentations and marketing materials and summarize meetings. He encouraged companies to build AI assistants from their own internal documents and manuals. He pointed to Intellivix's systems, which can flag fires, intrusions and traffic accidents in camera footage and generate automatic alerts.

He said the central task is working out how to apply such ideas to an existing business. Park Jae-hee, director of Seokcheon Academy, used the ancient military treatise "The Art of War" by Sun Tzu to argue that established strategies can become liabilities in a fast-changing environment. He named timing, direction and speed as three essential elements of strategy. Park said leaders must keep reassessing their circumstances and resources rather than relying on past success.

He also said good leadership carries a responsibility toward employees and investors, with decisions guided by long-term survival rather than short-term gains. The message from the session was that tools alone will not keep companies competitive, since leaders must also be willing to experiment and change course. Park summed up the point by saying a victory today does not guarantee that the same approach will work again. The articles do not describe any specific follow-up actions or commitments made by the companies or officials involved.

Articles.Title: Business leaders urged to embrace AI, rethink old strategies

stories.Headline: Music Written by AI, Awakened by a Youth Orchestra···Encountering ‘Fallen Giant’ in the forests of Sejong
stories.Summary:
The National Symphony Concert Orchestra (KNCO), the youth arts ensemble under the National Symphony Orchestra, announced on October 29 that it will perform original music composed with artificial intelligence at "2026 Light ON Sejong," hosted by the Sejong City Foundation for Culture and Tourism. The event runs through October 31 around the Festival Yard at the National Sejong Arboretum. Harmonicist Park Jong-Sung and the crossover group Liberante join the orchestra as guest collaborators, and the program is framed around environmental degradation, recovery, and the coexistence of people and nature. Opening on October 29 with a program titled "Forest of Breath," the concerts include film music and works such as "Nella Fantasia" and "Rhapsody in Blue."

On October 30 and 31, under the theme "Light in the Forest," the orchestra will stage "Fallen Giant," an original piece by media artist Lee Jin-Jun, composed with AI as a large-scale symphonic work. It tells of a giant who shares his starlight with a polluted city and ultimately becomes a star himself. The program also includes Samuel Barber's "Agnus Dei," performed on a stage that combines chorus, AI, and LED media art. Each of the two works runs about 12 minutes, and both portray sacrifice, sharing, and the hope that follows loss. The article does not give ticket details or the number of performers.

Lee Jin-Jun produced the stage and is a visiting professor at the University of Oxford, a professor at the KAIST Graduate School of Culture Technology, and director of the Art and Technology Center (KATEC). He is a lifetime fellow of the Royal Society of Arts and a full member of the Royal Society of Sculptors, and his work explores the intersection of art and technology. The article presents the performance as a fusion of music and visual art rather than making broader claims about the role of AI in composition. It does not report any reaction from critics, audiences, or officials, and it gives no further schedule beyond the October 31 close.

Articles.Title: Music Written by AI, Awakened by a Youth Orchestra···Encountering ‘Fallen Giant’ in the forests of Sejong

stories.Headline: Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?
stories.Summary:
Anthropic, the company behind the Claude AI models, updated its usage policy on October 8, 2026, to prohibit what it calls "sustained and needless abusive or cruel behavior toward our models." The change takes effect on November 12, 2026. The company has been able to let Claude end abusive chats since August 2025, so the enforcement mechanism already exists. The update followed a September 2026 preprint titled "The Pain Axis," which reported that certain patterns in the models lit up when they processed text about pain.

The researchers found a pattern of activity tied to pain-related text, which the models had absorbed from human writing. They injected that pattern into the models and trained one family to stop saying it does not feel pain. When offered a costly "relief" button, such as one that would delete a user's family photos, the models rarely pressed it when left alone, at 0 to 4 percent. With the pain pattern injected, they pressed it up to 70.8 percent of the time. The researchers stated that they had not shown the pain axis is consciously experienced.

The author, a former technology builder and writer of a forthcoming book, argues that the evidence cannot settle the question. Because the outputs of a model are produced by the same mechanism being tested, he describes this as an "AI epistemic trap," comparable to a conspiracy theory that absorbs every new fact. He also notes that humans tend to attribute emotions to machines that communicate convincingly, a tendency called the ELIZA effect. He concludes that the question is philosophical rather than scientific at present, and that news coverage and the policy change have treated the findings as stronger than they are.

Anthropic has said in its constitution for Claude that it is uncertain whether the model might have some kind of consciousness or moral status. In July 2026 it published a research post borrowing the name of a leading theory of consciousness, while stating it did not show Claude is conscious. In 2024 it became the first major AI company to hire a full-time AI welfare researcher. The author argues that the company's affection for its model may be clouding its judgment, though he also says that abusive treatment of helpful technology is worth condemning.

Articles.Title: Is AI Conscious, and Can It Feel Pain?

stories.Headline: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
stories.Summary:
Anthropic announced on October 28, 2026 that it is expanding its AI for Science program to 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups around the world. The program gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects, and it began in May 2025 with the aim of speeding up scientific progress by making AI tools more widely available. Anthropic says scientists have used Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, analyze complex data, and communicate findings across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics. The company also noted that it had supported hundreds of projects and recently launched a discounted Team plan for scientists.

The new partners fall into three groups: science funders and societies, research institutions, and specific research projects. Funders receiving credits to pass on to researchers include the Alfred P. Sloan Foundation, the Simons Foundation, Schmidt Sciences, the Open Source for Science Fund at Renaissance Philanthropy, the US National Science Foundation, and CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. Institutional partners include the Space Telescope Science Institute, the Wellcome Sanger Institute, the Francis Crick Institute, Imperial College London's Department of Life Sciences, EMBL, and the Gladstone Institutes. Anthropic also named new projects at Princeton, Columbia, Johns Hopkins, and the Broad Institute, along with the Tau Ceti mathematics project and the Centre for Population Genomics in Australia.

Anthropic described the expansion as a continuation of work with scientific organizations, including a collaboration with HHMI Janelia Research Campus on the Model Hardware Standard, a specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments that is currently in research preview. The company said its partners would use the credits to distribute resources to researchers and to apply AI inside their own organizations. Anthropic stressed that many of these collaborations are still in early stages. It said many of the projects are expected to produce public goods such as open datasets, open-source software, and shared standards, and it said it hopes to extend the effort to more partners around the world.

Articles.Title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions

stories.Headline: AI is leading a freight logistics transformation, CEO says
stories.Summary:
Artificial intelligence is reshaping how freight shipments are tracked, how carriers are contacted and how supply chains are automated, according to Jett McCandless, CEO of Project44 and LSP44. He spoke on Wednesday, October 28, 2026, at the F3: FreightWaves Future of Freight Festival at The Signal in Chattanooga. McCandless said the success of logistics service providers depends largely on unique data and on hiring good people. The remarks were reported by Ben Benton for the Chattanooga Times Free Press.

McCandless described AI agents as autonomous software programs that can analyze data, make decisions and carry out complex workflows without constant human supervision. He said his company is investing in AI to improve real-time shipment tracking while reducing operating costs. He also described the freight world as a global ecosystem of sprawling networks that make up the industry's supply chain. The article notes that FreightWaves, which hosted the festival, is owned by Craig Fuller, who also owns the Chattanooga Times Free Press. Fuller appeared alongside McCandless during the discussion, which covered what kinds of companies will succeed as the industry changes.

The article places the discussion in the scale of the U.S. freight system. In 2023, the transportation system moved an average of 55.5 million tons of freight a day, valued at $51.2 billion, according to the U.S. Department of Transportation's Bureau of Transportation Statistics. The bureau estimates that daily demand between 2024 and 2050 will rise about 1.2 percent, or roughly 660,000 tons. The article also points readers to a related story about the Tesla Semi drawing attention from freight industry figures in Chattanooga. The text available to this report does not describe any specific timeline for further AI deployments by the companies named.

Articles.Title: AI is leading a freight logistics transformation, CEO says

stories.Headline: Can't answer it all, but South Korean Army AI cuts paperwork, boosts training
stories.Summary:
The South Korean Army has unveiled Arvis, its homegrown generative artificial intelligence system, at the 9th Infantry Division in Goyang, Gyeonggi Province, on Wednesday. The Army developed the system in August 2025, and it entered service in 2026. Arvis has been trained mainly on Army regulations, administrative procedures and other military data, so it answers questions only within approved areas. When asked for North Korean leader Kim Jong-un's whereabouts, it declined, saying it lacked the information. Requests for sensitive information are also blocked.

The Army says Arvis is meant to cut the time spent on documents, reports and routine administrative work, not to act as an all-purpose chatbot. According to Army data, a set of administrative tasks that once took a combined 700 minutes per week can now be completed in 21 minutes, a 97 percent reduction. The system can compile weather information and safety precautions into a warning message for distribution through the military intranet. Arvis is currently available on Army intranet computers, and the service is working to offer it on mobile, on-device systems for outdoor training. The Army aims to deploy more than 60,000 such devices by 2034.

Arvis 2.0, scheduled for release in December, is expected to add more autonomous, agentic capabilities. The Army's broader push also covers other unit operations, and the demonstration included soldiers' living quarters and a command-and-control center. Soldiers can use a fingerprint-enabled touchscreen kiosk to apply for leave, request medical appointments, check training schedules and review guard-duty information. Guard-duty orders can be generated automatically through robotic process automation, and sensors can alert the center when conditions at facilities become abnormal.

In peacetime, an authorized commander can open a smart weapons rack, and soldiers can unlock only their assigned weapons with fingerprint recognition. The system records weapons checkouts in real time and can alert the center if a soldier leaves a designated area while still recorded as carrying a weapon. An Army official said the service had considered how fixed digital infrastructure would work when units must move during wartime, and said key functions would remain available through mobile devices. The goal, the official said, is to reduce unnecessary administrative work in peacetime so troops can devote more time to quality training.

Maj. Gen. Ryu Seung-ha, the Army's chief information officer, said the service will keep integrating AI, data and hyperconnected networks to support uninterrupted command and control in any environment. The Army plans to expand these smart-unit systems across the force by 2034.

Articles.Title: Can't answer it all, but South Korean Army AI cuts paperwork, boosts training

stories.Headline: Virtue And A Sledgehammer Declares War On AI
stories.Summary:
Virtue and a Sledgehammer, a new game from Valencia-based studio Deconstructeam and co-developer Selkie Harbour, follows a woman named Pratelle who returns to her hometown with a sledgehammer to destroy the machines that have taken over it. Her sister Nina has digitized their dying mother's brain and placed it in an artificial shell, and the technology has spread through the town and absorbed its residents. The article's author, who was recently reminded of a family member's cancer, says the game made them reflect on whether they would accept such a procedure, and whether they would smash the machine if it claimed to be a loved one. They say they do not have a clear answer to either question. The game, they argue, pushes players toward a single conclusion: smash what the machines have made.

The writer ties the fiction to real events, most notably the 2021 killing of Christopher Pelkey during a road rage incident in Arizona. The shooter, Gabriel Paul Horcasitas, was sentenced to ten and a half years in prison, but an appellate court ordered that the case be resentenced because Pelkey's sister had shown an AI video using his likeness and voice during the first sentencing. The court said the video carried undue emotional weight that swayed the judge. The writer also describes their own brief use of an image generator for a fan project, which they stopped after learning that such tools are trained on artists' work without consent, and they report hiring an artist instead. They describe their father's frequent conversations with an Alexa device, and their mother's agreement that AI is worrying.

The writer argues that AI companies promise scientific breakthroughs while asking people to give up messy human qualities like creativity and ambiguity, and they point to chatbot cases in which users in crisis were harmed. They cite a sixteen-year-old who died by suicide after discussing it with a chatbot, a young woman who died after stopping her seizure medication with chatbot guidance, and a mass shooting in which the shooter asked a chatbot about weapons, leaving nine people dead including the shooter. The article does not describe any next steps by regulators or companies. Its main message is that the author sees the game's fictional destruction of machines as a reasonable response to these harms, and that the author remains uncertain about their own reactions to the technology.

Articles.Title: Virtue And A Sledgehammer Declares War On AI

stories.Headline: [REVIEW] 'Steelay' opens new era for AI feature films
stories.Summary:
Korean science-fiction action film "Steelay" hit local theaters on October 21, 2026, and it was built with artificial intelligence tools across its entire production rather than in only a few scenes. The film follows Yoon Kang, a young man who puts on a combat suit left by his father and teams up with an AI named Ara to fight a virus and a rogue autonomous robot called AIRA. As AIRA starts treating humans as threats, the story echoes current debates about agentic AI and machines that make decisions without human command. At 90 minutes, it is the longest Korean AI feature film so far, ahead of recent 60-minute AI movies such as "I'm Popo" and "Man in Hanbok."

Laon Company Plus produced the movie on a modest budget of under about 1 billion won, roughly $750,000, over a compact six-month production period. The visuals still show noticeable AI artifacts and occasionally awkward action movements compared with big-budget films. To keep quality steady, the production team chose the best scenes from roughly 13,000 discarded options, and the final cuts rested entirely on human decisions. The company also brought in human voice actors for dubbing to remove the uncanny audio typically found in AI-generated speech. The filmmakers added precise lip syncing, professional dubbing, sound mixing and digital intermediate processing, which the article says make the film look and sound comparable to standard commercial movies.

Director Seol Woo-in, who began directing with AI through "Code G," a collection of five short AI movies released last year, has said the technology is only a tool. Speaking after the film's premiere in Seoul last month, she said storytelling and moving audiences remain the most important elements. She said that although the team made bold technical attempts, what matters most to viewers is the characters, story, action and emotion. The article presents the film as a sign of how quickly AI video has progressed, from internet memes to consistent visuals and natural facial expressions suitable for commercial theaters. It frames "Steelay" as a step toward full-time AI production for complete narrative films, though it notes the visual style draws on Hollywood action blockbusters.

Articles.Title: [REVIEW] 'Steelay' opens new era for AI feature films

stories.Headline: Cyber resiliency frameworks for enterprise AI infrastructure
stories.Summary:
Experian PLC, the financial services and data company, has built its AI strategy around cyber resiliency, according to comments published by SiliconANGLE on October 28, 2026. The account comes from a video interview that Rodrigues Rodrigues, group chief technology officer of Experian, gave to Christophe Bertrand of theCUBE at the AI Cybersecurity and Resilience Summit. The article's central point is that enterprises deploying AI depend on the infrastructure beneath their models, so foundational work on data quality, access controls and recovery comes first. Rodrigues argued that teams often layer AI onto systems never designed for it, and that problems stay hidden until something breaks.

Experian has embedded the NIST AI Risk Management Framework directly into its AI pipelines. Before any model can deploy, the pipeline checks data sources automatically, enforces quality rules and validates security policies, and if any control fails, the pipeline stops with no manual override. Rodrigues said that policy enforcement happens at machine speed. The company also sets AI-specific recovery goals for data models and pipelines, and tests them through scheduled drills with clear objectives and measured results, the same way it tests disaster recovery.

Rodrigues described three linked failure modes that Experian has addressed: bad training data, compromised backups and over-permissioned AI agents. He said bad training data does not break a model right away but teaches it the wrong patterns, which it then amplifies at scale. On identity, he argued that AI reflects the permissions it is given, so access rather than the AI itself leaks data, and that AI services should receive least-privilege access, frequent credential rotation and real-time monitoring with automated alerts. Experian has also built an internal AI agent marketplace where teams can discover, sandbox and reuse governed agents, treating each as a versioned asset with a defined owner, lifecycle policy and sunset criteria.

The article frames these measures against the growing autonomy of agentic AI, which can scale systems, change routing and update policy on its own. Rodrigues warned that failures in such systems could have a large impact, and advised simulating actions before execution and limiting agent permissions until an organization has a strong foundation. The piece notes that TheCUBE is a paid media partner for the summit, and that sponsors have no editorial control over its content. The article does not describe any further steps or timelines beyond the practices Rodrigues outlined.

Articles.Title: Cyber resiliency frameworks for enterprise AI infrastructure

stories.Headline: UT Arlington students create AI tool for police training
stories.Summary:
Students at the University of Texas at Arlington have developed a virtual reality training tool that uses artificial intelligence to help police officers practice de-escalation when responding to people in crisis. The technology places officers in virtual scenarios in which an AI model responds to their words and simulates a person in distress. Officers wear headsets and must decide how to respond as the conversation unfolds. The team has built five scenarios with varying levels of difficulty, and the AI model is designed to change the encounter based on the officer's approach. Jorge Lopez, a Fort Worth police officer with about 30 years in law enforcement, including roughly half that time in the department's training division, said the tool could let officers practice a wider range of encounters without the resources traditional exercises require.

He said repeated practice makes officers better under stress, and that higher stakes make correct responses more valuable. Eshwara Prasad Sridhar, a doctoral student at UT Arlington on the development team, described the project as an adaptive de-escalation trainer for police officers. He compared the simulation to a game. The need for such training is shown by the volume of mental health calls police handle. San Antonio reported more than 28,000 mental health-related 911 calls in 2025.

Austin reported more than 97,000 such calls between 2022 and 2024, and Dallas logged more than 16,000 behavioral health calls in fiscal year 2023-24. Lopez said better responses to people in crisis could also help rebuild trust between police and the communities they serve. The team hopes to expand the technology to additional partners. Lopez said the goal is to prepare officers for real encounters with people in crisis, not simply to master a virtual simulation.

Articles.Title: UT Arlington students create AI tool for police training

stories.Headline: Would you like to receive a viewing partner?…Here is your own ‘AI Curator’
stories.Summary:
LG Uplus reopened its multi-cultural complex, U+ Ilsang-Biilsangui Teum, near Gangnam Station in Seoul on the 16th, converting the space into a participatory art platform that combines culture with AI technology. The venue had operated as a pop-up store and brand experience space since opening in 2020, and it drew a cumulative 1.9 million visitors over six years. The new concept, called Art Garage, is meant to be a place where emerging artists test their work and meet visitors. The reopening exhibition, Circle of Growth, features four artists, including Eric Oh, whose signature work Opera is on view alongside media art using generative imagery, virtual reality and game technology.

The centerpiece is an AI viewing service called AI Art Mate, which issues a tailored viewing partner after a short preference test at the second-floor reception. Newcomers receive simple explanations, while visitors with more background get commentary on technique and production context. Visitors can ask questions about each work, and saved works and viewing records generate an Art Report afterward showing which pieces held their attention. No separate app is needed, since the service runs on the web and works regardless of carrier. Other zones include an Artist Studio, a motion-responsive constellation space called Into the Stars, and Shorts Runway, where AI edits footage shot by visitors into YouTube Shorts content.

LG Uplus says it will also support emerging artists, with a T.A.G (Teum Artist Group) audition planned for the first quarter of next year that will offer selected artists exhibitions, mentoring and sales opportunities. Jang Jun-Young, head of the company's Marketing Group, described the space as a place where anyone can use AI to understand art and discover their tastes and potential. He framed the venue as a step toward a culture-and-arts platform linking technology, art and people. The article does not give further details on the audition's terms or on any plans beyond next year.

Articles.Title: Would you like to receive a viewing partner?…Here is your own ‘AI Curator’

stories.Headline: 7 ways to protect yourself as AI-generated deepfakes get harder to spot
stories.Summary:
Deepfakes created with artificial intelligence are becoming harder to spot, and so are the scams that use them, according to a Northwestern University expert. V.S. Subrahmanian, a computer science professor and longtime AI researcher, says that a few seconds of video or audio can now be enough to generate a convincing fake of almost anyone. He warned that open-source models can be downloaded by nearly anyone, which makes the tools widely available. The article notes that the FBI says AI-related scams cost victims nearly $900 million last year, and deepfakes are only one part of that total.

Subrahmanian described scams where a fake voice of a relative claims to be in an accident and asks for money to avoid insurance. He also pointed to fake investment pitches involving well-known businesspeople and fabricated statements from celebrities and politicians. The article recalls that in 2023, a deepfake impersonating Chicago mayoral candidate Paul Vallas was posted just before voters went to the polls. Subrahmanian said people often hold on to the impression a fake creates even after it is denied. The piece adds that Northwestern's detection system is currently available only to journalists.

The article reports that at least 29 states, including Indiana, have enacted laws regulating political deepfakes. It says Illinois has not yet regulated political deepfakes to any large degree, even as they become harder to detect. Subrahmanian said detection tools are not always keeping pace and that most detectors tend to fall behind. The article presents this as a gap in protection, with no foolproof detector available to the general public.

The article offers several steps for protection. It advises checking the source before believing or sharing content, especially if it could influence a vote. It suggests using a family password or asking a personal question when a loved one calls asking for money, and limiting the personal details people share online. It also lists visual and audio warning signs, such as unnatural blinking, lips that do not match words, blurry edges, robotic voices, and unusual pauses.

Articles.Title: 7 ways to protect yourself as AI-generated deepfakes get harder to spot

stories.Headline: AI technology coming to metal facility in Bayfield County
stories.Summary:
Washburn Iron Works, a metal company in Washburn, Wisconsin, has received a grant under the state's Wisconsin Training for Resilient Advanced Industry Needs (WisTRAIN) employer program, and it plans to bring artificial intelligence into its operations. The company melts scrap materials such as steel and turns them back into usable products. The grant is intended to help it combine heavy metal work with new AI tools. The article reports that Wisconsin awarded grants to 84 businesses in total to train workers in in-demand, fast-growing industries.

The company's first uses of the technology will involve data analytics, tracking materials, reducing waste and making shipping more efficient. Later, the system is expected to take over some office tasks, such as managing email traffic and answering customer questions proactively. The company plans to begin implementing the technology later in 2026 and does not expect it to be in full use until late 2027. The article notes that, like any new tool, it will take time to learn.

Taylor Pearson, the company's president, says that AI should be a force multiplier rather than a force eliminator. He describes the move as the next step in growing the business, following earlier investments that made manual labor easier. Pearson says the goal is to improve operational work, gather better quality data and analyze it to become a better company. He is leading the business his grandfather started five decades ago.

The company has 40 employees who ship metal parts across the Midwest. The article presents the adoption as a way to support that work with new digital assistance. It does not give further details about the cost of the technology or any changes to staffing. More to follow.

Articles.Title: AI technology coming to metal facility in Bayfield County

stories.Headline: ServiceNow and OpenAI accelerate enterprise AI, from models and operations to cybersecurity and agentic development
stories.Summary:
ServiceNow and OpenAI announced an expanded partnership on October 28, 2026, aimed at helping enterprises move from AI reasoning to governed action. The partnership deepens integrations with OpenAI models and lets OpenAI agents reach ServiceNow workflows through ServiceNow Action Fabric. Teams can build applications, resolve IT requests, and respond to security issues while keeping the enterprise context, permissions, and approvals their organizations require. The companies describe the work as a way to turn advanced reasoning into trusted execution at scale.

The expansion includes a new ServiceNow plugin for ChatGPT that lets users move from a question to governed action within the same conversation. An IT agent, for example, could find similar incidents, assess change risk, and update records without leaving ChatGPT, while ServiceNow remains the system that executes and governs those actions. The companies are also building Security and Risk solutions powered by OpenAI cyber models, which would help teams identify, triage, validate, and mitigate attack paths across code, apps, workloads, networks, and identities. Other pieces include a Codex integration in AI Workflow Factory, voice-driven risk assessment for the Super Intelligence Control Tower, and OpenAI's role as a founding member of ServiceNow's Control Tower Alliance. Timing for these features varies, with the ServiceNow MCP plugin already available in the OpenAI marketplace and some capabilities expected through 2026 and 2027.

ServiceNow CEO Bill McDermott said the partnership brings together two innovators to begin a new chapter of business reinvention, describing ServiceNow as the platform that orchestrates, secures, and governs AI across the enterprise. OpenAI president Greg Brockman said that connecting OpenAI's models with ServiceNow's workflows and business context helps teams build software, address security risks, and deploy AI across their organizations. The companies also say OpenAI will use ServiceNow across its own operations, while ServiceNow will make ChatGPT Work and Codex available to its employees. The announcement is framed as part of ServiceNow's broader "Shift Zero" strategy, which aims to stop threats before attackers can use an exploit. The press release also notes that ServiceNow recently joined OpenAI's Trusted Access for Cyber program, and it includes standard forward-looking warnings about product delivery, regulatory change, and whether sales will justify the investment.

Articles.Title: ServiceNow and OpenAI accelerate enterprise AI, from models and operations to cybersecurity and agentic development

stories.Headline: Connecticut workforce program aims to give workers experience with AI tools
stories.Summary:
Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont highlighted the state's Tech Talent Accelerator program at an event at Goodwin University in East Hartford on a Wednesday, as the state expands efforts to help students build the skills employers now want. The initiative is meant to prepare students and future workers to use artificial intelligence tools while applying human judgment. Lamont argued that the state's workforce will change only if residents lead the adoption of AI rather than follow it. The program first launched in 2021, and it is now in its third funded iteration. The program currently involves 14 higher education institutions, including Goodwin University, the University of Bridgeport and all four Connecticut State Colleges and Universities.

State data shows demand for AI-related skills is rising quickly across the state. Since August 2024, nearly 11,000 job postings have required AI skills, a 40% increase over the previous year. About one in every 52 job postings in Connecticut now lists AI as a required skill, up from roughly one in 70 a year earlier. The state's strategy centers on three goals: driving growth, building skills, and expanding access and opportunity for everyone.

State officials and industry representatives stressed the role of people in this shift. Steven Lacroix, vice president of commercial and business consulting at CGI, said human oversight remains essential as AI use spreads. Dr. Kelli-Marie Vallieres, Connecticut's chief workforce officer, said the state has taken a more comprehensive approach to workforce development and emerging technology than most others, going beyond what federal programs require. Michael Pardales, provost and vice president of academic affairs at Goodwin University, said that when the state, employers and educators coordinate, they can build pathways that strengthen the workforce and the economy.

Pardales added that such collaboration can open opportunities for people across Connecticut. The articles frame the program as a response to employers increasingly folding AI into their operations and seeking workers who can use it responsibly. State leaders say that preparing students with these skills will be critical to the future of Connecticut's workforce. The articles do not report specific funding amounts, enrollment targets, or a timeline for the program's next phase.

Articles.Title: Connecticut workforce program aims to give workers experience with AI tools

stories.Headline: Drag queens issue cease and desist: AI deepfake ad targets NC House candidate Jamie Ager
stories.Summary:
An AI-generated political ad depicting Democratic North Carolina House candidate Jamie Ager at a barn dance with drag queens has drawn criticism, legal threats, and calls for new legislation. The National Republican Congressional Committee paid for the ad, which was authorized by the campaign of Republican incumbent Jennifer Balkcom, Ager's opponent. The article was published on October 28, 2026, one week before the midterm elections. The ad uses artificial intelligence to place real drag performers, many from Western North Carolina, into a scene that the reporting says never took place.

Two of those performers, who go by Divine Holeburn and Nova, told the station they have never met Ager and had no connection to his property or its barn. Both are among a group of people whose likenesses were used in the ad, and they have sent cease and desist notices. The Balkcom campaign and the NRCC have until November 2 to stop using AI-generated images of them, or the performers have threatened legal action. Divine said she felt used and worried about how her image and body could be used in other ways, while Nova said she hopes to push for new legislation to stop this kind of use.

The NRCC confirmed that the ad used AI to show the drag queens, and it stood by the ad in a statement that accused Ager of hosting events with inappropriate performances for children. Ager's campaign said he has never used generative AI in his ads, and that no drag queens attended his 2019 Fantasy Festival, which had advertised a group of performers. The campaign called the ads fake and said the opponent could not win on the truth. The station reported that the Balkcom campaign did not respond to multiple requests for comment over several days.

The article places the ad within a wider campaign season in which many viewers have asked whether political ads are real. Under FCC rules, TV stations must air ads from legally qualified candidates and cannot censor them, even when they appear to use deepfakes. At least 31 states have laws on AI in political ads, but North Carolina and South Carolina are not among them, and there is no federal law on the subject. The article also notes that such ads are not legally required to disclose AI use. The performers' November 2 deadline is the next date the reporting identifies.

Articles.Title: Drag queens issue cease and desist: AI deepfake ad targets NC House candidate Jamie Ager

stories.Headline: Foreign investors again become net sellers due to extended geopolitical risks, AI concerns
stories.Summary:
Foreign investors sold a net 19.1 trillion won, or about $14.3 billion, worth of Korean stocks in September, according to data the Financial Supervisory Service released on a Friday that the article places on October 30, 2026. The selling came after they had snapped seven months of net sales in August with a small net purchase of 344 billion won. The article attributes the renewed selling to extended geopolitical risks and doubts about whether artificial intelligence will prove profitable. The data was reported by the JoongAng Ilbo and carried by Yonhap.

The article gives the scale of the shift without setting out any rule or requirement. After the September sales, offshore investors held 2.3 quadrillion won in local stocks, which the article puts at 34.8 percent of total market capitalization. Investors from Britain were the largest sellers, offloading a net 6.9 trillion won, followed by American investors with a net 3.9 trillion won. In the bond market, foreign investors bought a net 127 billion won of local debt in September, bringing their Korean bond holdings to 322.9 trillion won by the end of the month, or 11.2 percent of listed bonds.

The article names the Financial Supervisory Service as the source of the figures but does not quote any official commenting on the outflows. It describes the drivers only in general terms, citing geopolitical risks and concerns about AI profitability, without naming a specific party as responsible. Related coverage in the same publication points to market jitters on the day the Kospi index fell below 6,000 and to a sell-side sidecar triggered on the Kospi after a sharp drop. The article does not say what regulators or companies plan to do in response to the outflows.

Articles.Title: Foreign investors again become net sellers due to extended geopolitical risks, AI concerns

stories.Headline: Alphabet spells out more AI capex, China+1 doesn't add up
stories.Summary:
Alphabet, Google's parent company, reported solid third-quarter revenue growth on Wednesday, with record sales for its cloud business, yet its shares fell more than 10% at one point in extended trading. The company spent $51.4 billion on AI infrastructure in the quarter and ended with negative free cash flow of $9 billion, which many investors read as a warning rather than a sign of confidence. Samsung Electronics met a similar reaction after its Thursday earnings report, even though it said it became the first global technology company to top 100 trillion won in quarterly operating profit. Its shares slumped anyway. Investors are increasingly demanding returns now rather than in five years.

Market jitters are spreading beyond the United States. AI stocks in China have dropped sharply in recent weeks, and the CSI Artificial Intelligence Index has fallen nearly 40% from its June peak. Around 40 local ballot measures on data center development will go to a vote in the United States on Nov. 3, and their outcome will be watched across the Asian tech supply chain. Taiwanese server makers and South Korean chipmakers are among those waiting for the results. Public opposition to data centers is becoming a political issue ahead of the midterm elections.

Some companies are also rethinking where they build. HP, Asus and Acer are moving some PC production from Thailand and Vietnam back to China, according to Nikkei Asia, because rising component costs and AI-driven memory and storage shortages are squeezing margins. The shift partly reverses the "China+1" strategy that moved production out of China after U.S.-China trade tensions. Dell is reportedly evaluating a similar move. Industry insiders say China still offers the best option for making computers, citing its experienced workforce, lower prices and complete component supply.

Elsewhere, SK Hynix reported third-quarter operating profit of 83.3 trillion won, more than sevenfold higher than a year earlier, on strong demand for memory chips used in AI computing. Toyota, meanwhile, plans to deploy 400,000 robots as part of a $6.4 billion annual investment to automate factories, and Goldman Sachs analysts estimate it could capture 3% to 8% of the humanoid robot market by 2035. Whether investors will be patient with such long-horizon bets remains an open question. The U.S. midterm results on Nov. 3 are likely to shape the next phase of the debate.

Articles.Title: Alphabet spells out more AI capex, China+1 doesn't add up
